four years before the deadline for the millennium development goals, the number of tb cases at the dawn of the new century continues to be alarming. tuberculosis is a curable disease. unfortunately, in developing countries, especially in asia and sub-saharan africa, it is a very serious problem. according to recent estimates, nearly two billion people are infected with tb, or one third of the world's population. statistically, one in ten of these people will develop tb. poor regions of the world are particularly vulnerable to the increase in tb because of poor nutrition and housing conditions, as well as stress. in many countries, access to effective treatment for the disease is limited, and there is a lack of coordination between the treatment of aids and tb. this is because governments in developing countries do not spend enough on health. in addition, rural health systems suffer from a lack of staff and resources to treat these diseases. so in countries with limited financial resources, the worst impacts are in rural areas. developed countries spend about 5 percent of their gdp on public health care, and developing countries spend about half that. that is why we cannot increase health expenditure in poor countries without outside help, as mr goerens has said. and tb is not just a medical problem, it's a socioeconomic problem, because it affects productivity and it has economic consequences. all of these things make it clear that we need to be very decisive, and we really need to do everything we can to make the vaccine more accessible.

in writing. as a member of the delegation to the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly, i support the sharing of eu research results in the field of tb vaccination development with developing countries and support for developing countries in financing treatment of tb patients. tb is one of the most common infectious diseases, along with hiv and malaria. one third of the world's population is infected with tb strains, there are 8 million new cases every year, and 2.6 to 2.9 million people die from tb. more than 95 percent of the cases are in developing countries. every second, a person dies from the tb bacteria. the disease develops in about 10% of those infected. if left untreated, it can be fatal. the highest incidence rates are in india, china, indonesia, south africa, nigeria, bangladesh, and ethiopia. in asia and africa, the incidence rates are between 100 and 120 per 100 000 population. in many countries, access to effective treatment is limited. tuberculosis is a serious economic problem. the global loss of productivity in the workforce as a result of this disease is 13 billion dollars a year. the eradication of tuberculosis is one of the millennium development goals that the union aims to achieve by 2015. we only have four years left. tuberculosis is now a fully curable disease. we need comprehensive programs to both prevent and treat tb. it is essential to launch rapidly an information campaign on tb, its prevention and treatment, and to launch a vaccination programme.

madam president! waste electrical and electronic equipment is the fastest growing waste stream in the european union. this is a multifaceted problem, because on the one hand it is about protecting the environment and human health, and on the other hand it is about managing resources and raw materials efficiently. the revision of the waste electrical and electronic equipment directive should take into account not only ambitious targets but also more realistic ones from the point of view of the new member states. in the new member states, electronic equipment such as computers, televisions and refrigerators are replaced much less frequently and these devices are used for much longer than in other member states. the amendments proposed by the rapporteur members aim to address the problem of disproportionate methodology and the disadvantageous treatment of new members of the european union. such a system takes much more account of market disparities and differences in mentality between member states. however, i believe that new regulations in this area should place greater emphasis on effective control of harvests and enforcement. in many countries, there are numerous irregularities, such as the creation of fictitious waste collection records, or so-called invoice trading. it is common to create false documents to certify that equipment has been assembled and processed, to overweight the processed equipment, or to issue a certificate that different equipment has been assembled than actually assembled. in addition, inadequate supervision and controls have resulted in a grey area in many countries where collected equipment is dismantled outside the processing plants, and such situations and practices must be strongly prevented.

in writing. − electrical and electronic waste is disposed of in a completely different way: electrical waste is dismantled and then recycled, while electronic waste is usually chemically treated after initial dismantling. the two groups differ considerably in weight, which means that electrical waste raises the so-called 'collection rate', while electronic waste, rich in gold, silver and rare earth metals, often ends up in landfills. the advancement of electrical and electronic equipment is the increase in its life span, the reduction of unit weight through miniaturization, the reduction of energy consumption. this should be part of the innovation activities, including design that facilitates recovery. unfortunately, the provisions of this directive do not stimulate innovation and waste streams are increasing at an alarming rate. to do so, the manufacturer or importer should be charged the appropriate duty when placing the product on the market. the funds thus raised can be used by innovative smes, which are market-oriented in the recovery of secondary raw materials from waste. this directive places on the member states the administrative burden of organising the collection and further processing of highly varied and difficult to dispose of complex technical structures. these products enter the markets of these countries and there they must be subject to the laws of the market. unfortunately, the lack of proper use of market mechanisms for the disposal of waste products means that this project needs to be refined, which is why i abstained.
in writing. - fellow workers! i think we should demand stricter standards for the disposal of electronic and electrical equipment. the problem of waste management is not only a european union problem but a global one. the collection and transport of waste equipment should be selective in order to ensure optimal reuse, recycling and the reduction of hazardous substances, which is of the utmost importance from the point of view of citizens. it's good that we're dealing with this issue because it's been raised many times in our regions, in local governments. we need to talk about monitoring the problem, which is why i voted in favour of the report by karl-heinz florenz.
in writing. − currently, waste electrical and electronic equipment is the fastest growing waste stream in the european union. this fact raises several issues that require a prompt solution. first, we should consider the health and environmental consequences of improper disposal of such equipment. another challenge is to reduce the level of waste of raw materials (through recycling, the industry recovers valuable secondary raw materials) and the need to intensify the collection and proper treatment of waste. according to data collected by the european commission, 85% of e-waste is now collected. although as much as 65% of the equipment sold is subsequently collected, little more than 30% of waste electrical and electronic equipment is recovered in accordance with the requirements of the directive. therefore, it is clear that the rapporteur agrees that it is the responsibility of the member states to implement the directive correctly and to establish effective procedures for the control of the storage and treatment of waste equipment. member states, manufacturers of new equipment and consumers are undoubtedly jointly responsible for pursuing a high collection rate by any means possible. i voted in favour of the report, which aims to achieve a higher selective collection rate, to reduce the loss of used equipment and to prevent illegal movements, as well as proper high-level processing.

on behalf of the s&d group. nuclear energy, as well as the whole field of technology for the production of isotopes in experimental reactors for medical and other purposes, such as the production of measuring sensors and sterilisation, requires the development of appropriate safety standards. these include the use of safe food products, animal feed, and medicines after exposure to radiation. in today's world, the risk of a radiation event is small, but it should always be minimized. the reactor failures, including the chernobyl accident, greatly increased the criteria for protection against the effects of ionizing radiation, and as it was later found, these effects were much smaller than expected. there was also minimal contamination of the soil by radioactive fallout, which contributed to some increase in the radioactivity of forestry and agricultural food products harvested in the areas at risk. but what we have here is an overreaction, and an over-expansion of the evacuation zone. now abandoned villages in the contaminated zone in belarus are populated again. it even has what some experts call the beneficial effect of hormesis, that is, the healing effects of high-energy radiation below a certain dose threshold. however, it is the linear rather than the threshold approach to radiation exposure that has led to these quasi-administrative rather than scientific approaches to these issues. the logical consequence of this is to limit radiation exposure to even lower doses than the natural ones, that is, the ones we are always exposed to. this is economic nonsense. because on average, we're already taking in about 2.4 millisieverts a year, which adds up to about 200 millisieverts after we're about 70 years old. a medical examination is therefore required to assess the simultaneous effect of the dose of contamination resulting from the radiation event and the often much higher dose resulting from natural radiation, including that of volcanic origin. the former is mainly food and affects the thyroid gland (iodine), the bones (strontium), and the muscles (cephalothorax); the latter is skin and lungs (radon).

in writing. − radiological accidents can occur wherever radioactive materials are used, stored or transported, not only in nuclear power plants but also in hospitals, universities, research laboratories, industrial plants, roads, railways, ports and shipyards. the rapporteur rightly points out that the effects of radioactive substances can be spread over many years and that the primary objective should always be to protect human life and health. today, more and more food is being irradiated to prolong its shelf life. it is worth noting that irradiation destroys up to 90% of vitamin a in chickens, 86% of vitamin b in oats and 70% of vitamin c in fruit juices. the extension of the shelf life of foodstuffs is therefore at the expense of their nutritional value. studies show that irradiation kills bacteria, but it does not kill viruses, remove dirt, or remove toxins that may have entered the meat in unsanitary and unsterile slaughterhouses and meat processing plants. irradiation also contributes to the massive, costly, and wasteful transportation of food, especially by large corporations. food produced and consumed locally does not require irradiation. i am convinced that member states should maintain and continuously improve and verify food and feed control systems against maximum permitted levels of radioactive contamination as indicated by the rapporteur.

madam president! demographic change, longer life spans and declining birth rates, the different benefits of pension systems and the economic crisis have put member states' public finances under enormous pressure. we are increasingly asking ourselves how stable and secure our current pension systems are and how they provide a decent retirement income. we conclude that reforms of pension systems within the competence of individual member states are necessary in europe. these are very time-consuming and expensive processes. in order for governments to take such steps, it is necessary for the council and the european commission to ensure that the costs of these reforms are taken into account on a permanent basis when implementing the excessive deficit procedure. any other solution could lead to a situation where countries, fearing the financial burden, abandon reforms. i would like to refer to two key aspects of the necessary reforms. first, to ensure the security of pension systems, we need to diversify revenue streams and create systems based on, among other things, public funding from capital markets and employee pension schemes. secondly, to ensure the stability of the systems, a high level of labour market activity should be ensured. member states should aim to align the effective retirement age with the statutory age and, where necessary, consider increasing the statutory retirement age, as a natural consequence of europeans living longer. however, prolonging work should be linked to appropriate labour market reforms, including provision of adequate training and healthcare for workers. i congratulate and thank the rapporteur for her help and excellent cooperation in the preparation of this report.
madam president! the debate on pension systems in some european union countries and the social emotions that accompany it show how important and difficult this is. it is not possible to adopt a single pension model that would apply in all countries of the european union. however, in times of economic crisis and demographic change, reforms of national pension systems are becoming inevitable. many countries are already struggling with rising pension costs, and this may undermine the principle of solidarity between generations. but we must remember that pensions must be secure, secure and pay our wages. and in this context, i would like us to pay more attention to the gender pay gap, because lower wages for women result in lower pension benefits.
in writing. we all know that there is no perfect model of a pension system. each country has developed its own solutions and plans for future reforms. despite the significant differences between the different systems, i believe that the european union should set a common direction for change for all member states. as has been repeatedly emphasised in committees, the financial and economic crisis of recent years has highlighted the urgency of reforming pension systems. the principles of solidarity and subsidiarity oblige us to strengthen cooperation between member states in this field. sharing experiences will help us avoid wasting time duplicating solutions that have already failed in another country, and sharing best practice will allow us to develop best strategies in an efficient way. remember that reforms cannot be limited to raising contributions or extending the period of contributions. budgetary stability, cross-border coordination of pensions, the development of minimum guarantees and gender equality are just some of the issues that should be considered in each member state. a balanced system based on interdependent and complementary pillars, covering public, labour and private, as well as capital and non-capital, should be developed across europe. i believe that this will ensure stable and equitable pension systems, while maintaining flexibility to adapt to progressive social and economic changes.
in writing. i welcome the inclusion on today's agenda of the report on the commission's green paper on adequate, stable and secure pension systems in europe. the issue of future pensions, their security and amount, is one of the most important social problems today. although the member states are responsible for shaping pension systems and the european union is not in principle empowered to act in this area, there is a need to develop some legal solutions related to pension systems at the european level. it is very important for the economic security of pensioners that the commission should draw up guidelines for the governments of the member states to set minimum levels of pensions or criteria for calculating pension benefits which would eliminate the disparity between pension benefits for women and men. women are, by their own admission, condemned to lower pensions than men because of the difference in pay for the same work or the need to take time off work to care for children and the consequent lower contributions paid for the whole period of work. therefore, in the face of threats to the stability of pension systems, the commission should not forget to seek to introduce legal arrangements that ensure equal treatment between men and women in the amount of future pensions throughout the union.
madam president! according to the world health organization, about 10 percent of the global pharmaceutical market is made up of counterfeit medicines. however, it is difficult to estimate the scale of the phenomenon in individual eu countries, for example in poland in 2009 alone, customs officers seized more than 100 thousand counterfeit products. the problems patients face are along with fake medicines lack of reliable information on the contents of the packaging, and the issue of repackaging, during which the contents may change. it is also very important for the patient to be able to obtain reliable information on the internet. unfortunately, along with much of the truth, there is also a lot of false information. in this context, it is important to establish a system of monitoring and control of medicinal products that provides reliable information to the patient. however, we are aware that even the best regulation will not have the desired effect if it does not provide for appropriate penalties for those who introduce counterfeit medicines. that's why it's so important to have this debate today and to have legislation that not only blocks the distribution of counterfeit medicines, that has a system of controls, but that, above all, imposes criminal sanctions on the manufacturers of counterfeit medicines. only such action will reduce the number of falsified medicinal products and increase their safety. finally, i would like to congratulate rapporteur matias on her excellent report. i realize it won't solve all of our problems, but it's a big step forward in improving patient safety.
in writing. - mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. counterfeit medicinal products and illicit trafficking in medicinal products are global problems in both developed and developing countries, and the scale of the phenomenon is increasing, posing a threat to the safety and life of patients. this is due, inter alia, to the fact that falsified medicinal products and medicinal products sold in unauthorised places do not meet the quality requirements laid down for medicinal products, containing unauthorised substances with unknown consequences for use. i agree that this problem requires effective and enhanced international coordination and cooperation to ensure an effective strategy against falsified medicines. i fully support the adoption of measures to minimise the marketing of falsified medicinal products, as well as the marketing of medicinal products sold in unauthorised places and other falsified products meeting the criteria for a medicinal product. attention should be paid to the need to regulate the shipping and online distribution of medicinal products. according to the world health organization, counterfeit medicines are available online and account for about 50% of the products on offer. i consider it important to plan and implement actions to share information on falsified medicines, medicines from illegal sources and to carry out public education campaigns on the risks of purchasing medicines from unauthorised places. i also believe that it is appropriate to establish safeguards to enable the identification, authenticity and traceability of medicinal products.
in writing. the counterfeiting of medicinal products is a global problem and should be addressed in this context. the causes of this are related to high drug prices, low patient awareness, but to a large extent also have a legal nature. criminal groups around the world are taking advantage of this situation. i therefore welcome the joint efforts of both the eu institutions and the almost unified position of all political groups on this issue to work out a compromise legislative act in this area. i would like to quote the words of the former secretary general of interpol, ronald noble, who put together the figures for terrorism and counterfeit medicines: in 45 years, terrorists have killed 65,000 people, counterfeit medicines have killed 200,000 people in china alone. i think that the emphasis on monitoring, control activities, tightening up standards, establishing a system of mutual recognition are good starting points. as vice-president of the envi committee, i also want to emphasise the role of patient information activities and the obligation to pharmaceutical companies to do so. patients should have access to high quality, objective information on how medicines are prescribed and their properties.

parliament today. this meeting provides a timely opportunity to review progress on croatia’s accession process and present the hungarian presidency’s plans for this first semester of the year. first and foremost, i would like to welcome parliament’s active engagement with the enlargement process, and its constructive contribution to the general debate on enlargement and on croatia’s accession process in particular. as we have underlined several times, enlargement reinforces peace, democracy and stability in europe, serves the european union’s strategic interests and helps the eu to better achieve its policy objectives in important areas which are key to economic recovery and sustainable growth. enlargement is a key driver for political and economic reform. it moves forward at a pace which is largely determined by the candidate country’s respect of the copenhagen criteria and its capacity to take on the obligations of membership. enlargement is one of the main priorities of our presidency, and our work during this semester will be to advance the policy in line with the renewed consensus on enlargement adopted by the european council in december 2006, as well as with the council conclusions of 14 december 2010, which have been endorsed by the european council. with regard to croatia, conclusion of the accession negotiations, as stated in the conclusions of the european council, is within reach, and our goal is to conclude the negotiations by the end of the hungarian presidency – provided of course that croatia completes the remaining benchmarks for closing the negotiating chapters. we would also like to finalise the accession treaty as far as possible, thereby paving the way to croatia’s accession to the eu which we look forward to. therefore, as highlighted in your resolution, this semester will be crucial for croatia’s negotiating process. let me now speak very briefly about the outstanding issues. so far, since the start of negotiations, 34 of the 35 chapters have been opened for negotiation, of which 28 have been provisionally closed. we are therefore very close to the conclusion of the negotiations. however, we still have to close a couple of difficult chapters such as competition, agriculture and rural development, fisheries, regional policy and coordination of structural instruments, the judiciary and fundamental rights, and financial and budgetary provisions, some of them of course with budgetary implications. in the council conclusions on croatia adopted last december, we highlighted key issues that require further work in these areas. you have been informed of them. we would also like to underline some points which are duly reflected in your resolution. the council has noted that encouraging progress has been made by croatia in many areas, including the rule of law and the fight against high-level corruption. at the same time, it is clear that further efforts are required. these concern judicial independence and efficiency and the fight against corruption at all levels. the council also encouraged croatia to step up its efforts to fulfil the remaining benchmarks, including the building of convincing track records, in particular as regards competition policy, as well as the judiciary and fundamental rights. in this regard, let me underline the importance we attach to the monitoring process in the alignment with – and implementation of – the acquis, with a view to ensuring administrative capacity and to building a convincing track record. in particular, the commission’s assessment of progress in the field of the judiciary and fundamental rights in march will be very important as regards the possible closing of chapter 23 later in the semester. moreover, on the international criminal tribunal for former yugoslavia (icty), the council noted croatia’s generally good cooperation with icty, while reiterating that full cooperation remains essential, in line with the negotiating framework. now that the interagency task force has started to explore important new avenues, the council has called on croatia to continue the administrative investigation in order to account for the missing military documents. in addition, the council welcomed croatia’s active role in regional cooperation as well as the improvement in its relations with neighbouring countries and its efforts aimed at reconciliation in the region. the entry into force of the arbitration agreement on the border issue with slovenia at the end of november was a very welcome development in this regard. bearing in mind the importance of good neighbourly relations, the council has encouraged croatia to build on this progress in its efforts towards resolving all outstanding bilateral and regional issues in cooperation with the countries concerned. in conclusion, let me reiterate that there is still a lot to be done during our presidency. croatia should spare no effort to fulfil the remaining benchmarks, to maintain and improve what has already been achieved and, in line with the negotiating framework, to conclusively address all other obligations still outstanding. for our part, it goes without saying that we count upon the support and cooperation of all member states, of the european commission and, of course, first and foremost, of the european parliament, in this endeavour. it is essential to keep up this momentum in order to conclude the negotiations successfully, as underlined among the priorities of the hungarian presidency until the end of june, i.e. until the end of our presidency.

president-in-office of the council. − madam president, i very much welcome this opportunity to appear before you to talk about a subject which is of particular importance for the hungarian presidency: the europe 2020 strategy. indeed, it is of particular importance for all of us. it is clear that europe has to overcome a number of serious challenges if it wishes to remain competitive with the rest of the world. some of these challenges have been generated by the financial and economic crisis, but some of them are inherent in our limited capacities and determination to fulfil the objectives and targets of the 2010 lisbon strategy. as is often said, crisis can be an opportunity – both in the ancient greek and in the chinese interpretation. it can be an opportunity for a breakthrough, for a solution and to make progress. that is why we believe that the crisis is currently a key factor in motivating member states to adopt quickly a new european strategy for jobs and smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. this is the europe 2020 strategy. i am convinced that this strategy will play an important role in helping europe recover from the crisis and emerge stronger, both internally and at international level, by boosting productivity, growth potential, social cohesion and economic governance. this is essential if we are going to be able to remain competitive globally, not least in the face of rapidly growing markets in asia. it is also essential if we are to maintain the social model, our way of life, which is a key characteristic of europe, dear to us all, and which we must preserve. the 2020 strategy confirmed five eu headline targets which constitute shared objectives guiding the action of member states and the union as regards promoting employment, improving the conditions for innovation, research and development, meeting our climate change and energy objectives, improving education levels and promoting social inclusion, in particular through the reduction of poverty. as part of meeting these targets, the commission developed and presented seven flagship initiatives containing the actions it proposes to take to strengthen the single market and to boost growth and jobs: the digital agenda for europe, innovation union, youth on the move, resource efficient europe, an industrial policy for the globalisation era, an agenda for new skills and jobs and the european platform against poverty. for each initiative, both the eu and national authorities have to coordinate their efforts so that action at national and european level is mutually reinforcing. in december 2010, the first implementation report prepared by the presidency, in close cooperation with the commission and the incoming hungarian presidency, provided an overview of work undertaken since the launch of the strategy in june. the report highlights the most important work done in the council, in all its forms, regarding the seven flagship initiatives. furthermore, the report stresses the technologies progress achieved in the various policy areas which play a major role in the new strategy: the single market, cohesion policy and agricultural policy. it also lists the activities and initiatives that have been conducted at eu level in the last six months as regards the five eu headline targets. let me emphasise some important elements concerning economic governance. the implementation of economic governance reform is a fundamental condition for fighting the crisis and boosting the european economy. this is why the 2020 strategy is closely linked with what is known as the ‘european semester’: a new key instrument of macroeconomic surveillance, to be applied for the first time under this presidency. this new process started in january 2011 with the presentation of the commission’s annual growth survey. the hungarian presidency is paying particular attention to ensuring that the european semester runs smoothly and successfully. to that end, we will organise a series of debates in all relevant council meetings in the run-up to the march european council. the general affairs council has, in particular, been tasked with preparing a synthesis report for its meeting of 21 march, which will set out the main messages on the work being undertaken in the various sectoral councils. this report will be presented to the european council in march and will form the basis for the discussions, with the aim of agreeing on a set of priorities for structural reforms and fiscal consolidation. following on from the march european council, member states will finalise the drafting of the national reform programmes and stability or convergence reports, which will be submitted to the commission in april. after that, work should be taken forward with a view to elaborating country-specific recommendations which the member states will take into account when finalising their budgets for 2012 and implementing their growth strategies. i recognise that this calendar is very tight, but we hope to complete it by june or july. the 2020 strategy is key in ensuring the future economic success of the european union. it is closely linked to economic governance reform, which will also play a key role. unless we remain competitive and can secure strong growth in the future, we will find it increasingly difficult both to maintain a sufficiently high level of social protection internally and to bring europe’s voice to bear on events externally. this is the major challenge for europe in the years to come. i am absolutely sure that we can count on the support of the european parliament to help us deliver.

in writing. the quality of human capital is crucial to the success of the eu 2020 strategy. gender mainstreaming is a key principle in the vocational education and training system. this is a prerequisite for the long-term, labour market-friendly professional development of women, the better exploitation of their potential, and the increase in the employment of women, including in particular in non-traditional occupational, low-carbon sectors of the economy and in high decision-making positions. i call for vocational education and training to be tailored to women's needs and for women to be more involved in it. at present, vocational training and education do not take into account the different needs of women, their socioeconomic conditions. this makes it much more difficult for women to return to or enter the labour market than men. in order to be effective, the vocational education and training system for women must be comprehensive, i.e. it must cover women's experiences, living situations and multidimensional training needs, including the specific needs of, for example, women with disabilities, the elderly, the poor, and immigrants. the priority is to provide flexible, affordable access to high-quality training. the incentives for employers to facilitate training for women working in small businesses and at home are also important. in line with the eu 2020 strategy, it is also necessary to better link vocational training to labour market needs in order to create new opportunities for women in science, mathematics, engineering and training.
in writing. a year has passed since the adoption of the new europe 2020 strategy and it is time to draw the first conclusions. it was greeted with a certain scepticism, which was justified by the total failure of the lisbon strategy. many commentators predicted that it too would remain a blank document, filled with ambitious but unrealistic goals. who does not remember the fundamental assumption of the lisbon strategy that the union will be the most competitive economy in the world by 2010? and where are we now? the great recession and the budgetary crises in the euro area have left the union fighting for survival, not for global economic leadership. will the europe 2020 strategy also fail? there are reasons for that! instead of thinking about how to create a knowledge-based and innovative economy, or how to reduce social exclusion, we are discussing how much funding will be reduced in the community budget. it is increasingly clear that there is a lack of political will to actually address the strategy proposed by the commission. it seems that once again the problem of the union's long-term development vision has been overshadowed by the current problems. in order to maintain its place in the world economy, to be able to compete not only with the usa and china but also with brazil and india, the community must set long-term objectives and pursue them consistently. we have a plan, now we just have to follow it.
in writing. – the euro 2020 strategy is about economic growth and employment. we must remember that a smart energy system is the future both in terms of the environment and these jobs. such a system would allow us to decouple economic growth from energy consumption. if this will be the case, we will be able to produce more for the same or less energy consumption and create thousands of jobs which can not be outsourced. we have to make sure that smart energy does not remain a dream. we are building today a whole new energy infrastructure in europe. we have to ensure this lessens the divide between western and central europe in terms of sustainable jobs. a two-speed europe on energy will not solve energy poverty or inefficiency. we should give a helping hand to those regions which are behind, even if it is not easy in today’s economic realities. we need a smart energy system for all european citizens at the same time. we must prevent a piecemeal system where some citizens only see the future 50 years after the others. simply put, we need smart energy jobs for all europeans, not just for those who would have received them even without europe.

in writing. − croatia has recently made significant progress towards membership of the european union and is likely to become an eu member state soon. in 2010, eu and croatian negotiators closed 11 chapters, bringing the total to 28 (out of the required 35). last year's achievement clearly demonstrates croatia's determination to continue reforms and will soon allow its citizens to reap the benefits of eu membership. at the last eu-croatia ministerial meeting in brussels on 22 december 2010, negotiators closed three important chapters, entitled 'justice, freedom and security'; 'foreign and defence policy'; and 'environment'. closing these chapters means strengthening the croatian legal system and making progress in several areas at once, such as greater cooperation between croatia and the international community on military and civilian missions (foreign and defence policy) or guaranteeing better air and water quality for croatian citizens (environment). negotiations on croatia's accession to the european union started in october 2005. despite some logistical problems, croatia's accession is strongly supported by eu member states, and many of them expect the remaining seven chapters to be closed quickly - by the end of 2011.

in writing. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. equality is one of the fundamental european values. this is a positive value. the only problem is that equality is interpreted in very different ways. some of these are extreme interpretations, ones that ignore the real differences that exist between people. the interpretative possibilities make it possible for ideologies directly related to this concept to emerge around equality. in the past, crimes and even genocide have been committed in the name of a specifically and doctrinally conceived equality. in the case of gender equality, the risk of dogmatism is lower, but there are some exaggerated attitudes. equality between women and men cannot be limited to political declarations and legal provisions. it is very important to implement equivalent standards. to do this, a change in mindset is necessary. we must encourage and support education, information and promotion of good practice. we need to make sure that equality is a universal thing, not an exception. true equality must be in man, in his attitude, in his daily, reflex behaviour. equality is not an isolated value either. we should not accept a formula for affirming equality that excludes other essential values like freedom, dignity or justice.

in writing. − product safety is a major concern for consumers, who want to be sure that the goods they buy do not pose a health risk. of course, the safety of products depends mainly on the manufacturers and importers who place the products on the market. market surveillance also plays a huge role in ensuring that only products that meet the necessary requirements are placed on the market. the report adopted today is a strong voice of the european parliament calling for the product safety directive to be consistent with other legislation, which guarantees a better functioning market surveillance system, clear and understandable rules for traders and gives consumers the assurance that the product they are holding in their hands is in compliance with legal requirements. however, the number of notifications in rapex is worrying, with the vast majority of notifications concerning products originating in china. in my opinion to this report in the committee on international trade, i called, inter alia, for enhanced cooperation on product safety with major trading partners and for further work on the better functioning of the rapex-china system. i hope that the strengthening of cooperation with china will translate into the quality of the products imported into the eu market from china.
in writing. − a safe internal market is a priority for our citizens and this report highlights inadequacies in the legislation on product safety and market surveillance and in the way these are implemented at both eu and national levels. the current lack of legal certainty, whereby various legal instruments apply to different categories of products, while loopholes exist in other areas, is an obstacle to market safety and to the proper functioning of the single market. the general product safety directive and rules governing market surveillance should be replaced by a single regulation, as the legal instrument guaranteeing the greatest level of clarity and uniformity. for this reason, i have identified this as one of the key priorities for inclusion in the correia de campos report on the single market act for europeans, for which i am shadow rapporteur. furthermore, in light of the fact that more and more people shop online, legislation on product safety and market surveillance must now be brought up-to-date to include measures covering online selling so as to strengthen consumer confidence in this area.

in writing. −adequate tax systems are the foundation of sustainable economic growth and monetary stability. in developing countries, where such systems are inadequate or non-existent, serious economic and political problems arise. international legal standards supporting the proper functioning of tax systems should have a positive impact on the economic situation in such countries. but remember that in no case should you impose your tax policy on others, since each country must decide its own tax systems in the light of its current social, political and economic circumstances. so let's support good tax policy, but let's not impose it.
in writing. good governance in the field of taxation is a prerequisite for the efficient functioning of the state. to function in a global economy, developing countries must integrate and reform their tax systems. in democratic countries, taxes play a distinct economic, political and social role. they are not only the main source of state revenue but also serve overriding social objectives. they finance basic services like health care, education, social security and pensions. tax revenues in developing countries can sustainably finance their development and improve the quality of life of their citizens. however, it is often insufficient to cover the costs of basic public services and to fight poverty. in the era of globalisation, taxable capital is more mobile, trade barriers are disappearing, which reduces tax revenues and poses challenges not only for poorer countries. progressive trade liberalisation, despite its obvious benefits, reduces tariff revenues. it is very important to replace foreign taxes with domestically-earned taxes. while income tax is one of the main forms of taxation in rich countries, its contribution to developing countries is minimal. most people are employed in agriculture and informally, they have irregular income, so it's difficult to effectively enforce income tax.
in writing. − today, at its plenary session in strasbourg, the european parliament adopted a resolution on eu agriculture and international trade. in recent years, a number of events have taken place which may indicate a deterioration in the situation of eu agriculture. among other things, there has been a significant decrease in the union's share of world exports of agricultural products. the agricultural trade deficit is also widening, and many of the concessions made by the eu remain unreciprocated. it is therefore essential that the eu's agricultural policy and the common commercial policy follow common and agreed lines in the fields of agriculture, trade and development. the adopted document is an important voice in defence of the eu food sector. it condemns the european commission's overly conciliatory approach and stresses that decisions to open up new markets must not have a negative impact on eu farmers.
in writing. the current state of protein crop policy in europe is disadvantageous both for farmers and producers who are forced to pay for them in the face of turbulence on the world market and for consumers who buy meat and milk from animals fed with these feeds. the geographical and climatic conditions allow the production of high protein crops in the union to change its structure and even make it advisable for biodiversity and climate change mitigation. feed imported from third countries is not subject to the same strict controls as european feed, so we cannot be 100% sure of its quality, we do not know the origin of the raw materials that make up it. therefore, urgent action is needed to change this situation, as our assurances of safe and healthy european food of the highest quality will be empty. another solution to the eu's protein shortage is to relax the rules against feeding meat and bone meal to animals. in the case of poultry and pigmeat, no risk of spreading any disease was found, and the mad cow disease ban was initially introduced against this. the possibility of using flour in livestock farming will reduce production costs, which is extremely important in view of the decline in the profitability of meat production. this would also reduce imports of high-protein feedingstuffs from the usa.

in writing. - i supported the report on women's poverty in the european union. in the last ten years, the number of women living in poverty has increased disproportionately compared to men. in the union, more than 84 million citizens live in poverty. women make up more than half of this number. this is a consequence of the economic crisis, as well as the existing gender pay gap, the difficulty of reconciling family and professional life, the longer life expectancy of women and various forms of gender discrimination, of which women are the main victims. i call for decisive action at both european and national level to combat wage discrimination and access to attractive job opportunities. i stress the need to strengthen the legal instruments to close the gender pay gap. the persistently high disparities in this area (on average 20-25% to the detriment of women) lead to high levels of poverty among single women, pensioners and widows. the europe 2020 strategy requires the adoption of union programmes for lifelong learning and vocational training for women in order to increase the participation of women in the labour market. these programmes should focus heavily on the professions of the future, eliminate stereotypes about female/male-dominated fields of education and traditional patterns in curricula.
in writing. - the issue of the feminization of poverty is a phenomenon that is increasingly observed and encountered both in europe and beyond. this is due to factors such as age, family responsibilities, ethnic origin and violence against women. the high proportion of women in low-paid or part-time jobs means that women are more likely than men to live on the edge of poverty. research on this phenomenon should be intensified at european level, as it will allow the development of precise and effective methods to combat poverty and social exclusion of women. the main method of helping women to escape poverty should be to give the appropriate direction to employment policies (e.g. flexible employment methods, vocational counselling, provision of training to improve skills, activities targeting women in rural areas). education also plays a vital role in countering this phenomenon. the eu's financial potential should be used to this end, and in particular emphasis should be placed on gender mainstreaming in the plans for overcoming the economic crisis and effectively implementing the europe 2020 strategy. eu action in this field should be an expression of social solidarity.

and i think i made it clear both in my speech and in the text on industrial policy which i presented to the commission - that enterprise and industry are only economic capital, because they are also human capital, they are the territory, the local reality in which they operate. as i said at the hearing before parliament before i was appointed as commissioner for industry, this is my vision, a broader vision that is the result of a concept that is part of the lisbon treaty, which is that of a social market economy. all our actions, in economic policy and also in the real economy, have as their ultimate aim social policy. our aim is not to enrich the entrepreneur, not to enrich the investor, but to enrich the investor as a means of giving answers to the citizens of the european union. it is now a matter of implementing and defending the choices we have made and are making which are contained in the europe 2020 document with strong action to implement the policy choices we have made. i do not hide from you, and i do not hide from you, the dangers that still exist. the speculative party is still alive and well and i do not exclude that there may still be attempts at a coup by speculators. it must be very clear that we are on the side of the real economy and that speculation which enriches only those who make a transaction is very different from the action of a company, an industry which creates wealth for many citizens. but we must remain vigilant, working and implementing our industrial policy: the european commission's industrial policy document therefore contains a series of competitiveness tests to check whether a serious industrial policy is being implemented, one which will enable our business system to meet the challenge of the global era. i shall also not shy away from the question put by mr van nistelrooij: i believe that the game should always be played on equal terms, with the same rules. president. - in writing. globalization includes the internalisation of industry and transnational corporations. when it comes to eu industrial policy, we must ask ourselves: what kind of industry does europe need - corporate industry with its subsidiaries, characterised by large-scale mass production, or small-scale industry with a regional character? what about national industry? because large multinational corporations, sometimes richer than many countries, accumulate huge profits in one place, usually at the place of origin, as well as taxes, including vat. and for those countries where production takes place, apart from employment, there are only costs. for example, fiat a multinational corporation generates a statistical revenue of 4% of poland's gdp, but its profits and the bulk of its tax revenues feed into another budget. moreover, for political and national reasons, not economic ones, the company has recently moved the production of the panda car to italy. there's a conflict of interest. the social situation in poland is deteriorating, and it is improving in italy. multinational corporations have already wreaked havoc on polish soil, buying up post-war industry for 10% of its value. the mistakes of liberal doctrinaires, including balcerowicz, resulted in the opening of poland's borders to global competition by financially resourceful corporations. and it led, at a rapid pace, to the destruction of our industry, to the elimination of competing industries, to the elimination of our scientific base, to massive unemployment. this is now a belated effect on the old eu countries. we need a sensible industrial policy, but not economic nationalism.

vice-president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as you know, at the beginning of february the commission approved the update of the european union's strategy on raw materials, and this strategy is based on three pillars. the first concerns the supply of raw materials outside the european union through agreements with the african union. we have included the raw materials issue in the agenda for meetings with the russian federation and, as i said in the previous debate, i will be in brazil, argentina and chile in june to initiate diplomatic action also with regard to these latin american countries. then i'll talk about the relationship with china. the second pillar concerns the strengthening of sustainable supply within our union. that is why we have updated the natura 2000 implementing rules, in agreement with commissioner potočnik, so that the interpretation is not detrimental to extractive activity, but at the same time continues to respect the environment. the third pillar concerns recycling and the efficient use of resources. i repeat what i said in the previous debate, that in the context of innovation policy we are planning a series of innovation partnerships in various sectors, one of which is the raw materials sector. one of the innovation partnerships focuses in particular on what we can do in the field of recycling and substitution of raw materials. the new communication focuses in particular on the supply situation of rare earths and other key raw materials. the commission therefore concluded that the chinese exporting producers were not in a position to provide sufficient evidence to justify the imposition of measures. we are assessing the situation with a view to identifying the most appropriate instruments at multilateral level, including the world trade organisation and our bilateral relations with china. we have initiated a wto dispute settlement procedure against china regarding access to nine key raw materials in 2009. the case is at an advanced stage and the conclusions will obviously be very relevant to our thinking on the launch of a wto procedure on rare earths. at bilateral level, the commission has repeatedly raised the issue with the chinese government, both politically and technically. since the end of 2010, a working group between the european union and china has been established to facilitate dialogue on rare earths and other commodities issues. the union will pursue active raw materials diplomacy, both in the framework of strategic partnerships and in the context of policy dialogues, to ensure access to raw materials, especially essential raw materials. as i said, one example is the launch of a bilateral dialogue in the context of the joint africa-european union strategy 2011-2013, which includes a section devoted to raw materials. i have already told you about our relations with russia and latin america. within the union, the commission supports the search for key raw material deposits and this objective is particularly promoted by the promine project 2009-2013 under the seventh framework programme. as regards recycling, it presents immense technological challenges, especially since the amount of raw materials contained in many products is infinitesimal. our strategy is to promote recycling through actions to improve the implementation and enforcement of eu waste legislation. in addition, we will continue to support research and innovation in the field of recycling and substitution, as has already been done under the seventh framework programme for the financing of projects concerning the substitution of rare earths. in this context, the commission is exploring the possibility of launching an innovation partnership in the field of raw materials and hopes to present a concrete proposal in the coming months. we have also started cooperation with the united states on innovation and are looking at cooperation with japan as well. we will of course continue to monitor the question of essential raw materials closely in order to define the priority actions and we believe that the security of supply of raw materials is essentially a matter for the companies. however, we are ready to discuss, in close cooperation with the member states, the costs, potential benefits and added value of a raw material storage programme. that is what we are doing, and i am of course always ready to listen to suggestions from parliament to continue to have active action by the commission on an issue which is crucial to the competitiveness of our european business system.
on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. rare earth materials are critical to hundreds of technological solutions. they are thus an essential element for further technological progress and for the european union's increased innovation. their widespread use is increasing demand without increasing production. the world now mines 124,000 tons of these metals annually, and demand is expected to increase by as much as 50 percent by 2012. the commission also found that the chinese exporting producers were not able to provide the necessary information to the commission. in august, they announced a reduction in exports of over 50% and the creation of strategic reserves. moreover, many of the companies that mine rare earths in other parts of the world are chinese. recently, australia blocked a chinese mining company from taking over a rare earth mine. this is a very serious problem with the monopoly of mining these resources. we must do everything we can to prevent the risks posed by this very important economic sector, which is the guarantee of europe's development and future.
market players are attracted to quick-return investments for competitive reasons. these are investments in plants that supply the products directly to the consumer. investments in the extraction of raw materials, especially fossil fuels, are long, costly and have a long payback period. so they can be bought by big investors, usually monopolists, who, as with rare earth metals, dictate their terms. and what do we find? europe cannot develop because of the lack of lanthanides, and especially of the samarium and neodymium needed to produce high-energy permanent magnets, which are used in wind power and electric car drives. it is time to take care of the security of raw materials in the european union, just as we do with energy security. this is not only the case for rare earth metals, but also for other rare raw materials and materials used as catalysts, such as renin and other platinum compounds, tungsten, molybdenum, lithium, selenium, etc. thank you, sir.
in writing. ladies and gentlemen, we have recently become increasingly aware of the fact that rare earth metals are crucial for technological applications and essential for the development of green technologies (such as wind turbines, hybrid vehicles, etc.). it should be noted that their operation is extremely complex. the eu industry is totally dependent on imports of rare earth metals from china, which has a virtual monopoly in this field, controlling 97% of world production. china holds 36% of the world's confirmed reserves of rare earth metals (and 59% of the estimated total reserves), while pursuing bilateral agreements to secure the world's proven reserves. the eu industry lacks both access to rare earths raw materials and scientific and industrial expertise in their processing. moreover, as global demand for rare earth metals continues to grow, china has announced drastic export restrictions which was exactly what the japanese expert group visited the european parliament in february 2011 to present in a very interesting way. in view of the indisputable need for the use of rare earths by industry in the eu countries and the need for research into them, i call for a dialogue with the people's republic of china on increasing the level of exports of these raw materials and pooling our efforts to find alternative sources of extraction.

the community. tight gas and shale gas from the us are booming. ten years ago, no one would have believed how quickly and how much the in-house production of gas from rock formations, extracted by without any definition. the theme of 'avoiding increasing dependency' is in favour, and the open market and world trade are in favour. the interests of some member states are also in favour of this. there are legislation on 'hydrocarbon resources' with the aim of non-discriminatory access and environmental protection. and there is health and safety for our eu citizens. all this needs to be taken into account. we are currently seeing potential for research and, if necessary, for funding, first in poland and then in the united kingdom and germany. but keyword germany it's also about acceptance. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the gas produced in the community is not used in the production of other fuels. the commission is monitoring the process and is follow this development without prejudice. but with all due respect, even if the resources are used, they will always play a complementary role. this means that the import of conventional gas from third countries such as norway, russia, algeria or by sea from qatar and other countries will certainly continue to be the main source of supply for the european gas market in the coming decades. therefore, infrastructure such as secure new pipelines and additional lng terminals will also remain important. i see a chance for our own gas production to supplement our gas imports, but it will certainly not be able to replace our imports.

madam president! the alternative gas deposits, especially shale gas, have allowed the united states to achieve full gas independence over the past 10 years. they've transformed the united states from a gas-importing country to a gas-exporting country. they have also brought tangible environmental benefits, for example by reducing coal mining and the resulting coal damage. scientists predict that a similar scenario could be true for the european union. the exploitation of unconventional gas in europe is the best alternative in the face of parliament's high expectations to reduce co2 emissions and thus to reduce coal extraction. moreover, we have recently seen a marked increase in the price of gas from conventional sources. the situation in the middle east is also having an effect. so, if the oil is exploited, it will actually lower the cost of energy production, as an alternative to increasingly expensive and expensive imports. extraction of unconventional gas also reduces unemployment. let's look at the united states. they have shown by experience that it pays off. in one us state alone, pennsylvania, the extraction and processing of unconventional gas has created some 200,000 jobs and generated more than $8 billion in taxes, mining contracts and concessions for the local economy each year. so let us not be left behind and take concrete action to seize this enormous opportunity and potential.

in writing. - mr president! - what are you doing? the global market is responding to the need to meet the demands of the established consumption patterns of both developed and developing societies. however, there is a 'competitiveness at any cost', i.e. a competitiveness that is not only shaped by industrial innovation and changes in consumption patterns. these adverse effects of competitiveness include: the energy- and raw-material-consumption model imposed by industry; competition based not on the superiority of solutions but on the financial advantage of rich monopoly corporations; cutting-edge competitiveness that concerns only the final processing phase and not gross competitiveness; i.e. taking into account the preparation of raw materials for production; the takeover of raw-material and energy markets by transnational, often non-european, corporations; the increase in energy (and raw-material) prices through regulation of the eu member states' emissions trading systems; non-competitive competition imposed mainly by multinational, transnational, including financial corporations. i voted in favour of this report as a good start to a very important discussion on the future of a competitive european industry, and therefore of europe.

all the objectives set by the eurogroup, which are sometimes quite reasonable, can be successfully achieved with the help of the economic, social and fiscal policies of the member states. the question therefore arises why we are expressly amending the treaty today to transfer these competences - at least in part - to the eu level. i think there are two answers: as usual, we want to share responsibility with the european union for unpopular decisions, or by the way, perhaps under the guise of reform, we simply want to shift more power to brussels. i doubt that this would have the expected effect, given that eurogroup member states tend to have more public debt and tend to have less competitive tax systems than other countries. the two-speed europe is, of course, looming over this debate. i'd like to warn those who want to speed up. in addition to speed, you need the right direction. the only thing that's going to happen is that the speed of the misdirection will only increase the scale of the disaster. at least that's my observation from the european roads.
mr president, i want to consider two issues. first, to welcome the birth of the euro plus pact, which is a welcome event. a new architecture is being born, almost a kind of economic schengen. what is important is that it should be inclusive and open for those who are able and willing to participate and that it should not create a two-speed europe. unfortunately the pact will be half open because the amendment to article 136, as debated and voted in our committee on constitutional affairs has fallen. it reads: ‘calls for the stability mechanism to be open from the outset to member states whose currency is not the euro, but who wish to participate’. it will be half open because it will be open to take obligations upon its shoulders. it will not be open for those outside the euro who want to participate in the rights. what unites us is the single market, much more so than the euro. it is not a euro crisis; it is a crisis in some euro member states. any non-euro member state could have the same public finance problem. so there is a lack of logic and a lack of consistency. a few words on libya and the southern mediterranean. firstly, i want to congratulate us – in fact not the union but some member states who are at the forefront of the defence of human rights and democracy in libya. we should be grateful to france and its leader, nicolas sarkozy, in leading the way. i think it is the beginning of moving in our foreign policy from interest-based foreign policy to value-based foreign policy. we need to follow two steps. we need to redesign the neighbourhood policy and direct it towards our societies and governments and achieve something which we call in central and eastern europe transition or transformation. it is also an alarm call to redesign and reform and strengthen the common security and defence policy so as to equip the union with common command capacities and military capacities.
mr. chairman, please! it's good that the leaders of the european union have spent so much time in recent weeks and days on what's going on in libya and other countries in north africa. i believe that these actions will lead to the fact that we will prevent the slaughter of civilians, and i believe that it will happen that the libyans themselves will overthrow the tyrant. but it is no secret that we also need to talk about internal challenges, challenges to the functioning of the european union and its institutions, to the internal functioning, to the common foreign, security and defence policy. this difference of opinion between some of the member states of the european union shows how far we are from the goal of a truly community policy in the spirit of the treaty of lisbon. it is also a challenge for the entire international community. it is good that we are working with the united states and other nato countries, it is good that we are in dialogue with the arab league, with the african union, it is good that we are in dialogue with israel. i think it is very important that what the chairman, hans-gert pöttering, has emphasized is that what is happening today in north africa, what is happening in libya, in egypt, can have very serious consequences, also for the future of the peace process. we should remember that and watch it. we should also think about the future of these countries, about the promotion of democracy and human rights, and we should not just act like firefighters putting out fires, we should also think about other countries around europe where these processes - bad processes - can happen.
in writing. we have just endorsed the treaty amendments that will allow the introduction of a permanent stabilisation mechanism for the euro area. our great success is that we have been able to express clearly our support for the community method as the main form of cooperation within the mechanism. the central role of the european commission in the process of assessing the financial situation of the member states bodes well for the future of cooperation, as it protects it from the instability that would threaten it if the intergovernmental formula were chosen. it is hoped that, once the treaty amendment has been adopted by the european council, it will be successfully ratified by the member states and that the permanent mechanism can be established as planned. the strengthening of the stabilisation mechanism in the treaty is just one of the measures taken to improve the competitiveness of the euro area in recent times. the council is also expected to accept the so-called euro pact, adopted at the euro summit on 17 march, at its meeting tomorrow. i am confident that the heads of state or government will be able to reach an agreement and that this initiative will be put into effect, allowing for closer economic cooperation in areas such as employment and public finance. it is fortunate that, despite the initial concerns of non-euro area countries, the pact has been given an open form. this has at least to some extent ensured that a two-speed europe will not emerge.
madam president! as a member of the european parliament's delegation for relations with japan, i would first of all like to express our sympathy and solidarity with the japanese people in the face of this immense disaster, which has claimed almost 10 000 lives and left more than 16 000 people missing, with the figures constantly changing. the earthquake and tsunami caused unimaginable destruction. the damage is estimated at $300 billion. although japan has not asked the european union for any help, we cannot remain passive in the face of this tragedy. the biggest concern is the damage to the fukushima nuclear power plant. the situation is, according to some experts, dangerous and a repeat of chernobyl is possible. the declaration by the hungarian presidency and mrs ashton on humanitarian and expert assistance should be completed as soon as possible in close cooperation with the japanese government.
