in writing. - madam president! - i have to go. i would like to raise the issue of the situation in japan. humanitarian aid to japan is the obvious and necessary response of the european union to the tragic disaster that has struck that country. i am in favour of giving japan and the affected regions all the necessary assistance (technical, administrative and organizational) and financial support. apart from emergency aid, it is necessary to consider the development of a systematic cooperation model with all countries at risk of disasters of various kinds, including those outside the european union. i am asking the responsible commission and council services to review the regulations in this area and to make proposals to strengthen the exchange of good practice in crisis management. more and more countries, including the european union, are suffering from natural disasters. this requires sustained, highly developed international cooperation. it is also important to review the existing legal and regulatory framework for the safety and security of nuclear installations. i would like to draw particular attention to two things: the supervision of the full implementation of the directive on the safety of nuclear installations and the adoption of the directive on radioactive waste.
in writing. the devastating earthquake and tsunami that struck japan and the pacific region on 11 march 2011 and claimed thousands of innocent lives is a tragedy that touches us all. our duty is not only to convey our deepest sympathy and condolences to the people and government of japan, but also to provide humanitarian, technical and financial assistance. i am pleased that the european union has provided this vital support almost immediately, using its best rescue teams and disaster management expertise. this assistance must be continued uninterruptedly until the situation in japan is stabilised. in view of the worrying fact that this disaster has led to a very serious nuclear accident at the fukushima nuclear power plant, which is another threat to life and health, we should review and examine the safety of nuclear power plants in the eu. although the fukushima accident is a warning to us, i don't think it should cause panic and prejudice against nuclear power. japan has repeatedly helped european nations to cope with the effects of disasters, drawing on its rich and valuable experience. it is time we took on this vital role - i am convinced that such cooperation will not only benefit the immediate relief efforts for the victims but also strengthen our relations with such an important friend as japan.
in writing. the devastating earthquake that struck japan is a clear indication that no country, even a highly developed one, can cope with the magnitude of the disaster on its own. it is our duty, along with the sympathy we extend to all japanese people today, to help the victims. an unforeseeable event like this earthquake, which, in addition to the tragedy of thousands of victims, has also created the immense threat of nuclear disaster, even though its effects do not directly affect us, requires us to learn from it. we must honestly ask ourselves how prepared european nuclear power stations are for such an eventuality. in order to avoid even unlikely but possible future risks, it is therefore necessary to review the safeguards applied to nuclear power plants in the member states of the union in order to ensure the safety of europeans.
on behalf of the ecr group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i would like to begin by thanking mr andreas schwab, rapporteur for this report, for his commitment to the draft directive. two and a half years of intensive work on this document have led to a compromise which, in its final form, will - i hope - provide greater legal certainty for consumers in the 27 member states when selling at a distance and, in particular, when making online transactions. i also hope that this directive will give consumers more confidence in cross-border trade and online shopping by enhancing and harmonising some of the new rights and making existing ones more clear. moreover, by standardising, for example, information requirements for distance and off-premises contracts, the directive also aims to encourage more businesses to enter new markets within the european union and thus improve the functioning of the internal market. i hope that it will be a positive impulse, in particular for the spread of online sales and, to the benefit of consumers, increase competition for consumers in the internal market. i would like to highlight a few of the most important points. firstly, we have tried to produce a text that is balanced, one that benefits consumers throughout the union, but also one that does not have a negative impact on businesses, and in particular on the activities of small and medium-sized enterprises in the community. secondly, i am glad that we have managed to negotiate a pragmatic text, so that those member states which already have a very high level of consumer protection on some issues are not affected by the application of mixed harmonisation. we have succeeded in introducing uniform and clear rules in specific cases, which will facilitate transactions on the internet, for example. i am also pleased that the juri committee has been able to negotiate chapter 5 on unlawful contractual clauses in a positive way. it regulates contracts which are not individually negotiated by consumers on a daily basis and are often the source of many abuses by dishonest traders. i regret, however, that despite the agreement, the text of the directive still contains some shortcomings, but i am confident that if we are committed we will be able to work on these issues at the next stage of the negotiations and achieve concrete benefits for consumers and for european businesses, because we cannot forget them either.
mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to leave. i would like to start by thanking my colleague andreas for his work in developing this project. he knows better than anyone that this was no easy task. in this work on the directive, we have often stressed how important it is for consumers themselves, but also for commerce, and in particular for electronic commerce and cross-border purchases. when consumers shop online, they want to be sure that the goods or services they order will be delivered to them and that they will be of the quality they claim. we should therefore ensure that consumer protection legislation is clear and transparent. however, we should not forget in this discussion the entrepreneurs who expect rules that are not burdensome for them. have we managed to reconcile the interests of consumers with those of businesses in the preparation of this directive? i think that almost two years of discussions have brought us closer to our goal, but not closer to our goal. i think that european consumers would benefit a lot more from maximum harmonisation of the rules. it would also be much easier for companies operating in the area of electronic commerce. however, i am pleased that we have found solutions on a number of key issues that are perfectly suited to consumer needs while reconciling the realities of doing business. i would like to take as an example the provisions relating to the 14-day period for consumers to withdraw from a contract, and i welcome the second amendment which allows the trader to make the refund conditional on the consumer providing proof of dispatch. this is a necessary solution in this directive, indicating that in certain cases we have obligations on the consumer side alongside the obligations of the trader. finally, i would like to encourage the council and the european commission to seek an ambitious agreement.
in writing. the consumer rights directive is, in my view, one of the most important pieces of legislation we are debating this semester. better access to information and greater consumer protection are particularly important for the development of the online market and for eu-wide economic growth, for example. the development of the e-market in europe is still relatively slow, compared to the united states, for example, and my country poland ranks a distant 17th among eu countries. only 23% of polish consumers shop online, and lack of trust seems to be one of the main reasons for this phenomenon. among the most controversial points in the proposal for a directive was the question of the level of harmonisation itself. i am glad that the rapporteur from the imco committee has agreed with the arguments of my group of socialists and democrats against the assumption of so-called full harmonisation adopted by the european commission, which would de facto prevent member states from adopting standards higher than those provided for by the directive. i think countries that want to maintain a higher standard should be able to do that.
in writing. i would like to thank mr andreas schwab and the other members for their work on this project. i welcome the efforts to harmonise distance shopping rules for all member states of the european union, which are designed to protect consumers and facilitate business. a compromise is clearly needed which will guarantee a high level of consumer protection and make it easier for businesses to provide services throughout the community. i believe it is appropriate to guarantee a high minimum level of consumer protection throughout the european union, with the proviso that member states will also be able to introduce more stringent rules on their own territory if they consider that the level of protection guaranteed by the eu is insufficient. however, the needs of businesses cannot be ignored, for whom the harmonisation of rules across the eu should provide real benefits both in terms of operation and cost reduction. it is therefore appropriate to develop a position which safeguards the interests of consumers as well as of businesses. increasing the security of transactions and harmonising the rules will undoubtedly improve confidence in distance purchasing and encourage more frequent purchases of products in this way.

the rapporteur. - madam president! - what are you doing? the minutes to be voted on shall be of particular importance. the european union and the united states together account for approximately 60% of the world's air traffic. opening the market to eu and us airlines on a non-discriminatory basis will offer better services to passengers and carriers, bring significant economic benefits and create new jobs. my dream is that airlines compete with each other on the basis of market rules, to the benefit of the passenger, that the passenger in transit to the united states passes through a single security checkpoint, that passengers in the european union and the united states have the same rights, and that they know those rights. does this protocol guarantee that? no, i'm not going. but i am convinced that it is a step in the right direction and will make it much easier to achieve these goals in the future. during successive rounds of negotiations between the community and the united states, the question of signing the protocol was raised several times. but eventually, i was able to accept it. this avoided a number of risks, including the most serious, the triggering of a suspension clause, which would have led to the suspension of the arrangements and the annulment of the results of the two negotiating stages. that would mean going back to the legal situation of seven years ago. this is unacceptable. the six eu member states do not have bilateral air services agreements with the united states, and the rejection of the document would mean that they would be blocked from flying from their airports to the united states. e second phase of the agreement does not achieve the ultimate objective of fully opening up the market without any restrictions on both sides, but contains a number of incentives to encourage reform, in particular following the introduction of a change in us law that will allow eu entities to take over majority stakes in us airlines, while the eu will allow us entities to do the same. i am particularly pleased to see the importance of the social dimension of the agreement. in this context, the commission should use the agreement to promote compliance with relevant international social rights legislation, in particular with the employment standards contained in the conventions of the international labour organisation, the oecd and the rome convention. this will ensure better respect for the applicable airline workers' rights. the agreement will also strengthen cooperation on environmental issues by requiring compliance and cooperation on the use of green technologies and on fuel and air traffic management. as rapporteur, i have tried to take the wider context and to present both the positive and the negative aspects of the protocol, without succumbing to the temptation to focus exclusively on the weak or strong sides of the document. i did not start my work with the a priori assumption that we must support or reject this protocol. after many meetings and discussions, i have come to the conclusion that it is much more profitable for the community to adopt the document than to reject it.
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i should like to thank the honourable members very much for their comments. of course the most complicated issue is the agreement and negotiation process with the united states. i can assure you that this is far from being the end. it is one part of the process and we are definitely continuing to negotiate with the united states but i would like to underline that the united states is a very difficult partner. as many of you mentioned, 60% of world aviation is covered by the eu and the united states. what we decide in cooperation will also define the whole framework and whole environment for aviation in the world, so the cooperation is also extremely important for the whole world. it also must be made very clear that the americans have the same parliamentary procedures: they have the us congress, which is very difficult to deal with precisely because of protectionist feeling, but we are working together and developing our relations. i will be going to washington in a few weeks’ time, and we have committed ourselves to work in five directions: first safety, second security, third technological cooperation – we signed an important agreement in budapest about interoperability of air traffic management systems which is extremely important for europe so that we do not lose our competitive advantages –, fourth the environment and fifth commerce or business. on business, as you know and as you mentioned, there are ridiculous restrictions on ownership rights. but it must also be very clear that we cannot force the united states to surrender; in writing. - i am in favour of adopting a motion for a resolution on the above matter. the treaty of lisbon increased the number of cases where parliament's consent is required for the conclusion of an international agreement. air traffic agreements are currently included in this category as they relate to a field to which the ordinary legislative procedure applies. previously, only parliament's opinion was sought on such agreements. the eu-us aviation markets together account for around 60% of global air traffic. opening the market to eu and us airlines on a non-discriminatory basis would offer passengers and carriers in air transport better services in terms of diversity and cost, bring significant economic benefits and create jobs. moreover, convergence of rules could contribute significantly to the promotion of fair competition, in particular as regards state subsidies, social and environmental requirements. at the same time, we must accept that a number of issues fall outside the scope of the agreement as amended by the protocol. the commission should therefore prepare itself to negotiate the next phase of this agreement, covering the following issues: further liberalisation of rights of way; additional opportunities for foreign investment; and the impact of environmental measures and infrastructure constraints on the use of rights of way.

mr. chairman, please! in the fight against violence against women, we are mainly talking about violence in families and in personal relationships. such violence is, of course, a great evil, and states should fight it with strong legal measures. i agree with the spirit of mrs svensson's report on this point. but i would like to draw attention to another type of violence that women often experience. it's about state violence, which is taking children away from women, which is happening more and more. there is no worse violence against a woman than the taking of her child, and sometimes it happens for the most trivial of reasons. i know of some extreme cases of child abduction in poland, including one where a family court took a mother's 10-year-old son away because the mother prayed too much. there are cases of child custody because of the poverty of the parents. instead of helping the family, they take the children to foster care or to a children's home. there are also extreme cases of child abduction by mothers in situations of parental conflict. in some cases, the scenes are dramatic, with children being taken from their mothers by police, social services, or court officials. in europe, there is a decline in the value of the family and a growing state interference in family life. this often leads to violence in the name of the law, violence that hurts parents and, above all, hurts children. taking a child from the mother and taking a child from the mother, because it works both ways, should be reserved for the last resort, where there's child abuse or violence. there's no reason to take children away because of poverty. families and women in families should be given all the help they need, but the breaking of family ties should be avoided, because this is often worse than the cure.
i am pleased that the european parliament will be adopting a report during this session which represents a multi-faceted approach to violence against women. it seems that defining violence against women in such a broad way will help to combat this negative phenomenon. there is no doubt that only integrated action at the various levels - political, social, legal and educational - can bring about tangible results. however, we are waiting for a draft directive focused solely on combating violence, which i hope the european commission will propose in the near future. i have two final remarks. and what's really important is that, finally, violence against women is seen as evil, not just from the perspective of the woman herself, or the perspective of a social unit like the family, but also increasingly from the perspective of the costs that it has on society as a whole. secondly, in debating this issue, we should not only focus on the fight against violence, but we should also focus on the dimensions of violence. we should fight stereotypes and condemn the social acceptance of violence against women and strive to change the way we educate the next generation of young people so that they recognize and practice the actual equality of women and men. i would like to congratulate mrs svenson on her report, which raises the important and socially sensitive issue of violence against women. i believe that behind today's words will also come actions and we will not only talk about violence against women, but we will act first and foremost to defend them. thank you very much. thank you.
mr. chairman, please! in the light of the comments made by my predecessors and the report by mrs svensson, it is important to stress once again that violence against women is still a part of society. one of the many reasons for this persistence is women's lower material status and economic discrimination in working life, their more difficult access to the labour market, and lower wages and social benefits. it is women who bear the consequences of motherhood and the hardships of child rearing. the social security system in many european countries is inadequate. during their working lives, and especially at retirement age, they leave women to the goodwill of their spouses and to the social security systems. this is a profoundly unjust situation and must be universally opposed. that is why it is so important to demand full equality for women in terms of time spent on motherhood and child-rearing. this is particularly relevant today, in the context of the demographic crisis in europe. actions to level the economic opportunities of women can help eliminate or reduce violence against women. the economic dependence of women on men is one of the many causes of passivity, of submission, and also of a certain acceptance of violence. it's time to put an end to this. the european parliament has a great deal of power to improve this situation, especially in countries where the situation of women is particularly difficult because of the high level of poverty. this is a very important message and i am grateful to the report's initiators for recognising this problem and taking active action to address it.
in writing. human rights and gender equality are the only priorities of the union. since violence against women is a gross violation of human rights and one of the main barriers to equal status for women and men, combating this scourge should be our main objective. the approach to violence against women varies according to national legislation. some member states, such as spain, have good legislation in this area. some of them don't have any. there are also significant differences in the approach to the criminalization of violence between member states. given the diversity of legal frameworks and the often limited impact on the enforcement of international law on combating violence, the need for clear and binding union-wide rules on the issue is becoming increasingly evident. it is necessary to summarise the different actions of the union and to integrate them into a single comprehensive strategy aimed at combating violence against women across the union. this strategy should be consistent with other international initiatives and should be based on available union programmes and best practices in the member states. the work on a common directive against violence should be completed during this parliament's term. it is necessary that no one can ever again say that in the european union even cows are better protected than women".
on paper. unfortunately, despite our efforts, violence against women, as well as violence in other areas of life, is still a major problem in europe. violent crime occurs in all countries and affects people from all walks of life. this means that the fight against this phenomenon and the assistance to victims must be multi-layered. it is important to promote family harmony and development to prevent this type of violence. in the case of crimes involving violence against women, it would be a good idea to establish a single european hotline to receive support and report such crimes. the union should aim to strengthen the penalties for violence against women, in particular for crimes of sexual violence. such crimes often leave a painful mark on a woman's psyche for years to come, making it impossible for her to function normally. it is also necessary to introduce in parallel better protection of the rights of victims in criminal proceedings. the report highlights the problem of prostitution and trafficking in women. to combat this practice effectively, a pan-european agreement is needed, involving not only eu countries but also non-eu countries.

the new architecture of public finance in the european union was based on an attempt to strengthen sound public finance and spending rules and on a completely unhealthy tendency to limit the fiscal sovereignty of the member states. i very much doubt that the euro plus countries would be able to impose public spending austerity on themselves collectively if they could not do so individually. i have no doubt that the unification of the tax base is an effective step towards a tax union which has only one objective: to eliminate tax competition in the european union. the real intentions have been revealed by french politicians, nicolas sarkozy, clementine lagarde, who have been pushing for weeks to raise tax rates in ireland under the pretext of fighting the crisis. but raising tax rates in the european union regardless of the member state is a recipe for perpetuating the crisis, not mitigating it.
madam president, i would like to touch upon three issues. first, i think that the council summit meeting brought very important and positive results, given the difficulty of the situation and the context. i welcome the formula of having an inclusive euro plus pact open to those who are not yet eurozone members, as president van rompuy said. at the same time, we are creating a european stability mechanism safety net. could we not consider that in both mechanisms in euro plus, which is an obligational commitment to observe certain rules of behaviour in macroeconomic and macro-financial policy, and also in esm. the safety net should be open so that both convergence and solidarity, which is esm, may be inclusive and not exclusive. my second remark concerns neighbourhood policy. we seem to be redesigning our neighbourhood policy. the stimulus is coming from the south, but it is important for our overall neighbourhood policy. i hope that it will be – if we read the documents by baroness ashton and mr füle – far more society-oriented, more generous towards those societies and demanding of authorities and governments. we should move away from short-sighted economic interests and base this policy on a human rights and democracy approach, moving from status quo policy to transition policy. but when we create this new paradigm it should also be applicable to the east. we should be more human rights and democracy-based and more society-oriented and less authority-oriented than we are now. my third point concerns eu-nato. in libya we have a new experience of eu and nato cooperation, which is a relationship which we do not yet fully understand. we also have an old experience in afghanistan, which is not always good. at the same time, this relationship is important. let us aim to be successful this time.
in writing. the latest european council opens a new stage - a stage of greater economic coordination and convergence in the eu and the euro area. the euro plus pact, adopted by the heads of state or government and involving the euro area countries and bulgaria, denmark, lithuania, latvia, poland and romania, offers a real chance of achieving the objectives it sets out, namely to promote competitiveness, employment, the stability of public finances and financial stability in general. it is worth noting that it does not indicate specific political or economic actions to achieve these objectives, leaving it to the individual states to choose the appropriate means. there is no doubt that the success or failure of the pact will be determined by the real commitment of the member states and the effectiveness of the monitoring of their progress. the eu can no longer afford to fail in economic coordination, as it did in the stability and growth pact. the summit also agreed to include in the treaty a provision for the establishment of a permanent european stability mechanism to be activated by common agreement of the member states in the event that it is necessary to ensure the stability of the euro area as a whole. this is a very important decision, especially in light of the recent troubles in the euro area countries. the permanent mechanism established by the treaty provides a solid safeguard against similar problems in the future, while also reducing the risk of speculative attacks on the european currency. it is also welcome that the mechanism has been opened up to non-euro area member states.
in writing. we can only tackle the crisis effectively together, without dividing the euro area into members and non-members. it is difficult to imagine building an increasingly competitive union without the participation of countries such as the united kingdom, sweden or poland, which is why we welcome the news of the adoption of the euro plus pact. at first, we had the impression that the eurozone was not only planning to reform itself, but also to reform outside the community structures, which worried meps. however, these concerns were allayed and a principled position was taken on behalf of parliament. we only regret that they have not been fully adopted by the member states, especially with regard to the european stability mechanism, which we believe should be open from the outset to non-euro area countries.

public contracts. and i would like to say a few words, as the buşoi report emphasizes, about the four projects we are undertaking with you in the public procurement. the first is the general revision of the 2004 directives to ensure the best use of public funds, to allow as many companies as possible to participate in public procurement and also to allow the purchase of high quality products and services with less bureaucracy. in concrete terms, i want to simplify procedures, make them more flexible, and see how the specific needs of small local authorities can be better taken into account, for example by making simplified procedures available to them. secondly, to facilitate access to the public market, in particular the cross-border participation of small and mediumsized enterprises. inclusion. the various objectives of the reform will now be translated into simpler and more balanced rules. we have conducted, but not completed, a very extensive consultation and economic evaluation on the ground. we have a green paper and are currently looking for the most operational proposals. it will not all be in legislation. at the same time, the commission will work on sectoral initiatives procurement, which i am preparing with my colleague potočnik, the implementation of the european plan for energy efficiency - we are working on this with mr oettinger or mrs hedegaard - and the second project is the concession. without waiting for the outcome of this long-term work to modernise the public procurement framework, i would like to see tangible progress on the question of concessions. ladies and gentlemen, concessions are playing an increasingly important role in the creation of public service infrastructure. 60% of public-private partnerships in europe are undertaken through concessions. but apart from works concessions, there is no european legislation on concessions at the moment i am speaking. and even if the general principles of the treaty apply, there is a real legal uncertainty in this area which weighs on the development of these contracts. i want to see the 24 judgments of the court of justice in recent years. i want to propose the creation of a light framework, limited to certain basic rules, which will not call into question national legislative frameworks when they are working well. it will not impose an excessive administrative burden on local authorities, particularly because of the thresholds i will be proposing. i know there have been doubts and debates in several of your groups. i am convinced, however, that by listening to everyone, if we set our goals correctly, we can avoid misunderstandings. public authorities will remain free to organise the public service themselves, but if they decide to outsource it, who can then object to a minimum of transparency and rules that ensure that there is no discrimination? for me, this is an imperative to optimize the use of public money, to reduce the practice of awarding without adequate publicity, or without an effective right of appeal, as well as certain risks of corruption. as far as companies are concerned, while we want to revive the internal market, who can oppose the idea of making it a reality in terms of concessions? i am thinking in particular of small and mediumsized enterprises which do not have the means available to large companies today to identify and secure contracts abroad if they are not published. having a minimum framework on concessions will allow for transparency, information and, therefore, easier access for smaller companies to a number of markets. it is also a question of better regulation. targeted, measured legislation is a better option that will be cheaper than trying to solve problems through the rule of offences alone. the third area - i will speak about it shortly - is the european defence market. we will work with member states on the implementation of the 2009 directive, which expires in a few weeks. the aim is to adapt compensation policies, which are often contrary to european law. and i will be organising a conference on this subject, with mr tajani, on the question of the european defence industry market, on the very premises of parliament in brussels on 23 may. finally, i would like to mention a subject which has been neglected for too long, namely the international dimension of public procurement. the objective is clear: more market access for our companies, and we are naturally prepared to offer more, too, in a spirit of reciprocity and mutual benefit. more trade will benefit all. but we have a problem today, based on this assumption, open trade and the profit that goes with it, which i would like to mention. the truth is that our major partners - the us, japan, in the gpa, china, bilaterally - do not really want to commit to opening up their markets further. and we have no real leverage to negotiate, since our own markets are already considered, almost naturally, to be open. the international commitments under the gpa and the world trade organisation, ladies and gentlemen, have not yet been transposed into european law. in this context, member states apply the rules in very different ways, and this creates distortions in the internal market. and as a result, our companies in europe today are facing an unbalanced situation - i am reminded of the case of the motorways in poland - on the one hand, foreign companies which enjoy very wide access in our country, often going much further than what the european union has negotiated, on the other hand, our own companies, which are having difficulties participating in the markets of some of our major partners. that is why we intend to propose this year, together with my colleague karel de gucht, a legislative instrument which will transpose our international obligations in the field of public procurement into european law and give us the negotiating leverage we need. we are for openness, not for naivety. the aim is to give european buyers a strong and clear legal basis to treat offers from companies from the country with which we have an agreement differently from those with which the european union has not yet agreed, and to offer more security. let me be clear: we are not talking about turning europe into a fortress, but we must place our companies in a realistic, fair, open but not naive context. i would like to take this opportunity, as you have asked me, mr president, and as your parliament has asked me, to refer to this important sector, which will be one of the 12 levers for the revival of the single market which i mentioned at the beginning of my speech, namely public procurement and the modernisation which we will propose in agreement with you in the coming weeks.

mr president, i would like to say to the commissioner that while we were working on the report on your rich document we were, just like yourself, constantly conscious that the single market is there to serve europeans. maybe this is exactly the reason why the negotiations between different political groups on the final form of the text were so difficult. i do agree with them that even if we do not fall in love with the single market, we can be very emotional about it. it is really good that the european parliament sends a clear signal today to the commission and to the council in the form of 15 priority proposals, and i am personally satisfied that we underlined the importance of the mobility of our citizens. better access to banking services; easier recognition of professional qualifications; full portability of pensions: these are the fields in which citizens need solutions in order to study, work and invest in different member states throughout their lives. europeans expect concrete actions from us for concrete needs, and we must deliver. take, for example, voice and data roaming charges. it is high time these stop hindering the mobility of europeans on this continent – our continent without internal borders. this issue is also addressed in the document we are going to vote on today. finally, the european parliament is proposing an idea to organise an annual single market forum, and this platform should enable a genuine discussion with citizens. to me, this is a crucial way of involving european citizens in the reform of the single market for its 20th anniversary, and for that event i wish all of us much success.
the single market may have seemed a pipe dream 60 years ago, but today it is a reality and a daily reality for almost 500 million europeans. of course, on the one hand we can be proud that the idea of the european union has been so wonderfully put into practice, but on the other hand we must be aware that this project will never really end, because the world is moving forward, europe is still developing, and the citizens of the european union will increasingly benefit from the opportunities offered to them by the single market. the single market act under discussion today and the results of the social consultation clearly show that the harmonisation of the eu market is not just about economic processes in the broad sense of the word, but also about legislative solutions to help ordinary citizens to benefit fully from the internal market of the union. i therefore welcome commissioner barnier's proposals, which are closely linked to the need to increase legal certainty in the area of the functioning of private international law, as they seek practical solutions to the problems arising from the mobility of citizens. these are issues that may not seem directly related to the improvement of the functioning of the free market, but which are becoming increasingly problematic for ordinary citizens and businesses operating across national borders. the more efficient functioning of the common market will, in a sense, force the whole of the european union to develop cooperation also in the field of civil and administrative law. the european market must adapt to modern solutions, and this will always present new challenges for its modernisation. i shall therefore look forward with great hope and enthusiasm to the fulfilment of the objectives of the single market act.

in writing. - the lisbon treaty introduces far-reaching changes in the common commercial policy. first, it extended this policy to include, inter alia, foreign direct investment. the second change was the decision-making procedure. the council now decides by qualified majority and parliament gains the right to co-decide. this means that the approval of our assembly will be needed both for the ratification of trade agreements and for investment matters (concerning foreign direct investment). the union must develop, within the framework of the common commercial policy, a european investment policy that meets the expectations of investors and host countries. investment policy must also take account of the european union's foreign policy priorities. in this context, the issue of regulation at international level, with particular reference to wto negotiations, also arises. the new powers conferred on the union by the treaty of lisbon also indirectly affect the competences of the european parliament, by including it on an equal footing with the council in the decision-making process in the area of foreign direct investment. a new coherent and integrated union investment policy should have a positive impact on global economic progress and development. as one of the most important economic blocs, the eu has a strong negotiating position which, through a unified policy on direct investment, can contribute to the competitiveness of the eu, its businesses and employment.

member of the commission. − madam president, i am delighted to have this opportunity to have an exchange of views with parliament on the european neighbourhood policy. in the context of the current events in the southern mediterranean, redeveloping this policy could not be more important. in fact, over the past nine months the commission has undertaken a review of the policy. i want to take this opportunity to thank members for their input into the consultation, which took responses from partner countries, eu member states, academics and civil society groups. i have read both mário david’s report on the south and marek siwiec’s report on the east and find them both significant and useful. i am pleased that our thoughts are along the same lines. you will have noticed that the results of our previous discussions on neighbourhood policy are already reflected in the communication on a partnership for democracy and shared prosperity of 8 march. now we are preparing for the wider communication on the results of the review, which is due to be published in may. a key outcome of the review is a new emphasis on differentiation of the neighbourhood policy, according to the needs and wishes of each partner country. while the policy will continue to offer engagement to all partners, every neighbour is different and has different aspirations. some partner countries want to progress as far as they can towards the european union – indeed as far as accession – but others prefer to make the most of other benefits of the neighbourhood policy. so it will deliver more for more, in a specific and differentiated way, alongside stronger political steering of our relationship with our partners. nevertheless, as both mr david and mr siwiec recommend in their reports, our shared values of democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights will be at the heart of the revised neighbourhood policy for all partner countries. they should find their expression in stronger joint commitments to the elements indispensable to democratisation. i am thinking in particular of free and fair elections, freedom of expression and association, judicial independence, the fight against corruption and security sector reform. as highlighted in both reports, the revised neighbourhood policy will also recognise and act on the importance of the civil society. non-governmental organisations have the expertise and experience to deliver democratic and market-oriented reforms from the bottom up based on shared values. a thriving civil society gets citizens involved and helps to hold governments to account so the european union will complement its relations with governments with much closer engagement with civil society. this is also important at a regional and sub-regional level where, for example, the eastern partnership civil society forum has been making good progress. the forthcoming communication will offer more detail on the approach towards the two sub-regions of our neighbourhood. it will spell out how we see the eastern partnership developing further in the wake of the summit under the polish presidency. in the south, the union for the mediterranean has the potential to make a real difference but, frankly, it has not yet done so, and must be revitalised. its promise lies in developing concrete economic projects with a focus on employment, innovations and growth. the union for the mediterranean secretariat is best placed to act as a catalyst and bring together states, international and financial institutions and private companies to work on such economic projects. i would like to mention briefly three other elements brought to light by the review, which will be key to the revised neighbourhood policy: first, the role of trade and economic integration to help advance stability and prosperity in partner countries. the most significant vehicle to achieve is the deep and comprehensive free trade area. a successful dfcta has a transformative power. regulatory reforms made by a partner country are encouraged through trade. next, the need for improved mobility between partner countries and the european union since there is no better way to promote european values than through sharing experience person to person. the neighbourhood policy will seek improvements to mobility without losing sight of security. finally, the desire expressed in the consultation by many partner countries for greater political engagement with the european union. closer and more substantial political dialogue across all areas of president of the eib. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me begin by thanking you for inviting me once again - it is becoming a real tradition - to take part in the discussion of your report on the activities of the european investment bank. i would like to thank in particular your rapporteur, mr cutaş, who had the good idea of not merely looking back but also giving directions for the future, and, if you will allow me, that is essentially what i would like to talk to you about. you say that our board of directors has set out three guidelines for the action of the european investment bank in the coming years. our action will be developed around three axes: the implementation of the europe 2020 strategy, the fight against climate change and support for the union's external policy. in the face of the financial and then economic crisis that erupted in 2008, european states provided a short-term response. these were the various national plans to ensure, first, the rescue of the banks, and then, to stimulate the recovery of the economy. and these national plans, as you know, were supported by the european economic recovery plan, adopted by the european council in december 2008. the eib has played its part in this by increasing its lending from eur 48 billion in 2007 to eur 79 billion in 2009, and by directing this injection of financial resources into the real economy towards the sectors identified as priorities by the council, in particular support for small and medium-sized enterprises, as your rapporteur has just pointed out. but after this short-term response, which has averted the worst, it is now a question of giving a longer-term response. this is the europe 2020 strategy. and the critical element of this strategy is the increase in employment and productivity, which must be articulated around what is often called the knowledge triangle: training, research and innovation. and the eib stands ready to make a significant contribution to the implementation of this strategy. in 2010 alone, it funded over 4 billion in education projects and over 7 billion in rdi projects research, development and innovation. the eib intends to increase its financing in these areas and to this end it intends to continue to implement, with the european commission, joint financing instruments, such as the rsff risk sharing finance facility for research, as such instruments provide a leverage effect to the european budget. with the same budget, the european budget can support a much larger volume of investment and, at the same time, these joint instruments alleviate the capital constraint of the eib. this means that with the same capital, the eib can grant a larger volume of loans. i cited the rsff, the risk sharing finance facility for research. that's a good example. at the end of 2010, with a budget contribution of some 390 million, with an eib capital allocation of some 700 million, it was actually possible to grant loans for more than eur 6 billion, which financed more than eur 16 billion in research investments. you can see the dual leverage effect of this type of instrument, and it is therefore clear to us that the eib's contribution to the europe 2020 strategy will be all the more effective if it can be based on pragmatic cooperation with the commission and also with other financial institutions. the second is to combat climate change and its sometimes dramatic effects. this has become a priority for the european union and thus also for the eib. the fukushima nuclear accident and the challenges it has brought about further reinforce the need for massive investment in energy savings, renewable energy and new energy technologies. in 2010, eib lending for projects that directly contribute to reducing greenhouse gas emissions amounted to almost €20 billion, or almost 30% of our total lending. of these, loans for renewable energy projects amounted to 6.2 billion, mainly for wind and solar power projects. loans for energy efficiency improvement projects amounted to 2.3 billion in 2010. they will increase in the coming years, as there is a huge potential for energy savings, especially in public buildings and housing in many european cities and towns. investments to develop urban transport, and thus reduce the harmful effects of private transport, were financed by eib loans amounting to eur 7.9 billion in 2010. and so we're going to continue that effort. we will continue to support energy savings, energy efficiency, renewable energy and, in addition, we are at the forefront of developing a methodology - inevitably complex due to technical difficulties - to more accurately assess the carbon footprint of all the projects we fund. and this particular effort is a testament to our commitment to making the fight against climate change a major priority. finally, the third point: no power can claim to conduct a foreign policy without financial support. china has understood that. it is involved in financial interventions worldwide to support its foreign policy objectives. if the european union really wants to develop a foreign policy which has any influence in the world, it must also have a financial arm. if the european union wants to, the eib can be that arm. this is one of the conclusions of the camdessus report on the eib's external mandate. it remains to be seen whether the member states, which are also the eib's shareholders, will follow up on this recommendation and make a clear choice when preparing the financial perspective for 2014-2020. that, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, is an overview of the eib's three-pronged approach for the years ahead.

the rapporteur. - i am pleased to present to the house the report on the amendment of the directive on vaccines against bluetongue, a disease which is a major threat to cattle, sheep and goat farming in many eu countries. i am pleased to do so because three years ago, in this house, in the previous term, i had the honour of presenting a report on a new animal health strategy based on the principle of 'prevention rather than cure'. today's amendment to the directive on bluetongue vaccination is a practical implementation of this principle. we are improving the prevention of the disease, we are making the animals healthier, the cost of their treatment is lower and the whole vaccination process can be better organised. the change is due to the fact that the previous 2000 directive was adapted to the conditions of that time, and in particular to the vaccines that were then available on the market. these vaccines have been and continue to be used, but with certain restrictions due to the risk of transmission of the virus from vaccinated to unvaccinated animals. this requires various restrictions on the use of vaccines, e.g. restrictions on the use of vaccines in designated areas, restrictions on the movement of animals. this is quite burdensome for the breeders and therefore the effectiveness of these vaccinations is limited. science has made progress. we have a different generation of vaccines that are being tested and can be used without fear of transmitting the virus to unvaccinated animals. they can therefore be used without the restrictions that have been imposed. the use of these vaccines will therefore be beneficial to breeders, less burdensome and probably more effective. it will be much more widely applicable. the process is very fast. the committee on agriculture has carried out its work shortly after receiving the draft legislation from the european commission and is presenting it to parliament. the idea is to be able to mass-market the new vaccines this summer. that is why these amendments, and the amendments to the report i tabled, contain a timetable for the member states' legislation to be adapted to the requirements of this directive, so that vaccination can be carried out this year and does not have to wait until next season. i would like to mention the controversy that has arisen around this report and the amendment of the directive on the obligation to have correlation tables proposed by the commission. in my report we agree that it should be mandatory to include correlation tables which contain information on how the directive is transposed into national law and which specific provisions transpose the provisions of the directive into national law. this is seen by the administrations of some member states as a kind of bureaucratic requirement, but it is necessary to look at it differently. this requirement makes european law more transparent. it is easier for citizens to check for themselves whether and how a directive has been transposed into national law. i think this is a good practice, and as far as i know, this is the first directive, or one of the first directives, to be adopted which introduces this obligation, and i think it is right. this should become a regular practice in our legislation. i thank you again for the opportunity to present this report and i feel that we are doing a good thing for the welfare of farmers and for reducing animal suffering in the eu.

in writing. - i did not support the resolution because, firstly, apart from the prohibitions, restrictions and generally expressed dislike of nuclear technologies, it does not bring anything positive. secondly, it does not indicate any way out of a completely new situation for the whole of energy policy. for example, points 19, 20 and 21 could provide new ideas and directions for thinking comprehensively about energy efficiency, especially energy efficiency from primary sources, where the greatest reserves lie, especially with regard to fossil fuels. thirdly, the radical suggestions contained in it call for a national referendum to be held in my country at the request of the left. perhaps such a referendum should be held at union level. fourthly, my country has been forced by the faulty eu regulations to stop the necessary investment in coal-fired power stations, and now the same lobby group is saying that we should stop investing in nuclear technology. so what's left? the resolution only refers to renewable energy. in my country, the full potential of these sources covers 13 - 20% of the necessary needs. sweden may be different, because it has large hydroelectric reserves, but poland is not. the fukushima case calls for a review of the entire existing energy policy of the european union.
in writing. - in april, a joint resolution was voted on the conclusions to be drawn for european nuclear safety following the accident at the nuclear power plant in japan. i voted against this resolution because, apart from the prohibitions and moratoriums on the development of nuclear energy and the suggestion of a gradual withdrawal from nuclear energy (which is unrealistic), it does not bring anything positive, it does not offer any solutions for the future of energy in general. the situation following the fukushima disaster has completely changed the philosophy of approach to the future of energy in europe and poland. in our country, the 95% coal-based energy sector has already suffered as a result of the adoption of the climate and energy package. the investments undertaken to build two nuclear power plants have also been stopped. the resolution only emphasises the importance of renewable energy, which in poland represents only 13% of the total, with a maximum of 20% of the total. moreover, the referendum on nuclear energy, which the left is suggesting, will not take place in poland until then, so the conclusions of this resolution are premature. i welcome the fact that the majority of members voted against the resolution.
in writing. − there are currently 48 least developed countries (ldcs), or one in five countries in the world. the category of ncds was created by the un general assembly in the early 1970s, over 40 years ago. since then, the number of nrm countries has doubled, with only three (botswana, maldives and cape verde) having managed to leave the group. this shows that poverty is spreading and that the measures taken so far have been ineffective. the economic crisis has further worsened the critical situation. its effects have affected the nrp to a large extent and have further exacerbated the problems there. these are mainly due to debt, high food and fuel prices and climate change. i therefore am convinced and aware of its importance, and have therefore amended the resolution on the fourth united nations conference on the least developed countries. a thorough and comprehensive analysis and diagnosis of the situation of the nis is needed, as well as concrete proposals for solutions aimed at improving the living conditions of the inhabitants of these countries in the short term and at leaving the group in the long term. as a member of the acp-eu parliamentary assembly, i would like to draw particular attention to the lack of control mechanisms for the actions undertaken. we have the political will and the desire to help, but unfortunately we do not monitor our efforts enough, and this results in little effectiveness.
in writing. − the european neighbourhood policy has brought tangible benefits to all parties since its inception. it creates a framework of cooperation that is strategically important for supporting political, social and economic reforms in our closest partners. the eastern partnership focuses on the development of democracy, good governance and stability, economic integration and convergence with eu policies. since the establishment of the epc, progress has been made in many partner countries in respect for human rights, the democratisation of public life and economic reforms. only belarus participates to a limited extent in cooperation with the eu and its continued participation in the epc should be conditional on its willingness to respect the basic principles of democracy and freedom. attention should be paid to the fight against corruption and to the electoral system and the conduct of elections in a manner consistent with international law. support should be given to the euronest parliamentary assembly, emphasising its role in strengthening democracy and developing cooperation with the eastern partnership countries.
in writing. - the european parliament resolution on the review of the european neighbourhood policy addresses the challenges that have emerged in recent months in our neighbourhood, both in its eastern and southern dimensions. these events have exposed the inadequacy of the eu's engagement with the neighbourhood to date. the ep's proposed change of paradigm from 'stability first' to 'democratization and human rights first' in eu policy is necessary. no more pretending that the political status quo, i.e. the maintenance of authoritarian regimes, is better for europe and its security. it's time to show solidarity with our neighbors. despite their differences, most of the countries in the region have one thing in common: limited or no freedom and a lack of success in modernizing. the allocation of additional, ambitious funds to build a stable eu neighbourhood seems inevitable. the foundations of the epc should therefore be continued in the form of the principle of conditionality, cooperation both bilateral and multilateral, and extended to include the pursuit of institutional integration, visa liberalisation, the opening up of the european market and the support of civil society. it is also worth recalling the position of poland, an advocate of further enlargements of the union, which two years ago called on the member states, in partnership with sweden, to strengthen the eastern dimension of the epc in the form of an eastern partnership initiative. in the face of current events, poland's role is taking on symbolic importance. poland, with its historical experience of political and economic system transformation, can be a good guide and model for both the eu's eastern and southern neighbours in current politics.
in writing. - i supported the resolution on the review of the european neighbourhood policy southern dimension. as a member of the committee on women's rights, i would like to draw particular attention to the importance of gender equality policy as an integral element of respect for human rights, which is also a fundamental principle of the european union. women's rights must be a priority in talks with countries covered by the european neighbourhood policy (enp). according to the resolution, women's rights should be included in the codification revisions (constitutional, criminal, family and all civil law codes) and taken into account in the human rights dialogue with the partner countries covered by the epc. the focus should also be on the social integration of women. we need programmes to promote women's education, to promote their employment and to increase their participation in public life. the effects of gender equality actions in the eps countries must be continuously monitored and controlled, and failures to do so must be strongly condemned and even punished. i am in favour of not strengthening the european union's relations with those third countries which do not sufficiently integrate into their political strategies issues and institutions related to civil society organisations (in particular human rights and women's organisations).
in writing. - i strongly supported the resolution on combating sexual violence in conflicts in north africa and the middle east. massive sexual violence against women is a constant feature of armed conflicts in north africa and the middle east. the united nations children's fund (unicef) cites kenya, a relatively stable country, as an example, where the pre-election violence has doubled the number of sexual violence victims in just a few days. sexual violence is becoming an epidemic. it's a tactic of war. the european union cannot remain indifferent to this matter. it is therefore essential to mainstream gender issues in the european neighbourhood policy and to put it at the heart of efforts to develop an effective and structured approach to gender equality in the countries covered by the policy. human rights, of which equality between women and men is an integral part, should be an essential element in the democratic processes of third countries. it is shocking that despite the prevalence of sexual violence in africa, governments do not make it a priority to combat it, for example in south africa. the union should focus its action on women in particular. the resolution stresses the importance of strengthening the social integration of women, promoting their employment, combating illiteracy among women and traditional harmful practices. the education of women and girls must include awareness of their rights.

on behalf of the ecr group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the common fisheries policy, based on principles that protect the environment above all, must maintain the management and development of european fisheries at a sustainable level. from an economic point of view, fisheries are extremely important, but it should be stressed that they also represent a cultural value passed on from generation to generation. the preservation of this value should therefore become the objective of the common fisheries policy. in economic terms, this is a necessary condition for maintaining economic equilibrium at a satisfactory level. in view of the drastic increase in oil prices in europe, which is contributing to the collapse of the industry, the common fisheries policy should have a mechanism to protect fishermen against uncontrolled price increases in such situations. the european union cannot afford to see another sector of the european maritime economy, after shipbuilding and shipping, migrate to the far east. it should be noted that iceland does not want to join the european union because of its fears about the cap. the reform of the cfp should therefore be stepped up considerably in order to safeguard the environment and ensure adequate protection for fishermen. the question of the need for regionalisation in the fisheries sector and for a balanced but more significant role for national governments in the cfp is once again raised. it should be stressed once again that the crisis and economic instability have led to the closure of the cap, leaving fishermen to their own devices.
we're taking up a subject we've been working on since 2008. the european parliament was already expressing its solidarity with fishermen and calling on the commission to come up with concrete proposals to alleviate the situation in the areas most dependent on fishing. statistics clearly show that since 2003, the cost of fishing in the european union has more than tripled, and the sharp increase in fuel prices has meant that fishermen now have to invest 40% more to get fresh fish to the customer as quickly as possible. the phenomenon of the sharp rise in oil prices on world markets in recent months is undoubtedly the most important cause of the sharp deterioration of the situation. the increase in oil prices has a direct impact on the income of fishermen, who operate diesel-powered boats. it's a vicious cycle. in an attempt to compensate for the increase in fuel prices, fishermen increase their catch by going out to fish further, and their boats use more fuel. there is therefore an urgent need for the european commission to take further steps and raise the de minimis ceiling, as proposed by my political group, from eur 30 000 to eur 60 000 per firm for a period of 3 years. this is a sensible proposal which, in the present situation, would provide the sector, which is in financial difficulties, with support and the conditions for social and economic development.

, in writing. india's economy is one of the fastest growing economies in the world. already today, most of india's foreign investment is located in the european union, and the tata group itself is the leader in industrial employment in the uk. given the pace of development of the country, it is recognised that the trade agreement between india and the union will be one of the most significant and demanding agreements concluded to date. the agreement will undoubtedly contribute to increasing the level of investment and exports and imports of both parties to the agreement. it will allow for a freer exchange of goods, and it will contribute to the growth of prosperity in india as well as in the countries of the community. the agreement will have an impact on the intensification of world trade, particularly in services. despite the advantages of signing the agreement, it is important to bear in mind the points on which the two parties to the agreement have different positions. the union shall not accept the movement of goods which have been produced in such a way as to damage the environment or which involve the use of child labour. the agreement we are seeking should guarantee decent jobs, diverse, growing economies and cultural diversity. the implementation of an effective decision-making system to facilitate cooperation and the training of people and organisations that help developing regions are key. however, a transparent and public debate is necessary to achieve the intended objectives.
the author. − in recent months, the japanese side has increased its interest in opening possible negotiations on a free trade agreement with the european union. the european parliament considers that non-tariff barriers should be the main issue, as has been repeatedly emphasised in the trade policy committee. the problem is not the tariffs but the many restrictive regulations and the difficulties in accessing the japanese market for eu companies. i am positive about the deepening of economic cooperation between the european union and japan, but i believe that the priority should be to eliminate the non-tariff barriers that restrict the access of eu goods to the japanese market. in this context, the article 30 provision adopted in the march european council conclusions indicates the line of action to be taken by the european union at the eu-japan summit on the opening of negotiations for a free trade agreement. the opening of these negotiations is rightly conditional on japan's willingness to address, inter alia, non-tariff barriers and restrictions on public procurement. this is therefore worth bearing in mind, especially as japan is lobbying for fear of losing competitiveness on the union market due to the expected entry into force of the union-korea free trade agreement.
member of the commission. − madam president, i should just like to touch upon two points. first, the relationship between bilateral and multilateral agreements. some members have advanced the idea that we should concentrate on the multilateral agreements rather than the bilateral ones. we do! as you know, the multilateral negotiations for the doha round are in dire straits, and we are the only big trading bloc that has been making proposals recently to try to bridge the differences between the developed and the emerging economies with respect to industrial sectors. but while we are really concentrating on the multilateral aspects of trade, on the other hand we should not neglect all our bilateral relations with important trading partners. secondly, with respect to japan, as many among you have been saying, it is really a ‘chicken and egg’ situation. do you start the negotiations and then hope that in the course of the negotiations you can resolve the non-tariff barriers that have been in place for many years, or do you rather try to do away with the majority of the non-tariff barriers as a precondition for negotiations on the free trade agreement? i think that, to a certain extent, we need that conditionality, because the real problem with japan is not so much tariffs. of course the idea would be to eliminate 100% of tariffs, which normally you would not have with a developing or an emerging economy. the real problem is with respect to non-tariff barriers. we have been proposing a list of 27 non-tariff barriers which we think are crucial for our trade relationship, but in only three cases out of the 27 is there now a solution on the table which seems to be acceptable. the japanese claim that they have solutions for all the rest too, but we cannot see a solution in the proposals that they have been making to us. so we believe that we need a scoping exercise so that we know what we are talking about. i hope that, in the course of that scoping exercise, we can do away with a number of non-tariff barriers, and that this will create the right climate for us to get down to actual free trade negotiations with japan. that is how we see it. we see it, at least partially, as a precondition that we should stick to.

member of the commission. − madam president, the regulation on transitional arrangements for bilateral investment treaties is an important legislative initiative. the lisbon treaty has entrusted the union with a new exclusive competence on foreign direct investment. the continued existence, since the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, of more than 1200 investment-related international agreements concluded by member states is not questioned under international law. however, it is incompatible, under eu law, with the new exclusive competence on foreign direct investment. at the same time, these agreements serve as a valuable source of legal protection for european investors operating abroad. because the lisbon treaty does not contain arrangements clarifying the status of bilateral agreements, we need to establish legal certainty for investors benefiting from these agreements by authorising their continued existence. while it is important to authorise existing investment agreements, it is also important to foresee the possibility of taking action in a cooperative manner to address important issues that could arise with regard to the content of the agreements and their interaction with eu investment policy. we have to reserve appropriate mechanisms for union action to permit the development and implementation of the policy at eu level. i understand that, in relation to the commission proposal, the scope for such action is the most difficult issue – for parliament and even more so for the council. so the challenge we have here is to find a solution that safeguards the principles i have just outlined and is acceptable to both parliament and the council. we realise, in this respect, that there are still some considerable gaps to be bridged between the institutions but, at the end of the day, we will have to find a compromise in the interests of the eu and of its investors. we believe that the amendments adopted by the committee on international trade constitute a basis for finding such a solution. they maintain fundamental trust in the commission’s proposal but, at the same time, seek a potential compromise. we note with satisfaction here that articles 5 and 6 would still leave the commission the power to review investment agreements and withdraw authorisation should such agreements create major problems. given the positions of the main protagonists in this process, we will all have to show some level of flexibility. the commission is ready to play its part, to be flexible and to facilitate an agreement between parliament and the council, but this cannot be at any cost. we will be vigilant on the basic principles of our proposal. the existence of the bilateral investment agreements needs to be safeguarded but, at the same time, we cannot unconditionally bless agreements if they create significant problems. the commission fully shares parliament’s sentiment that the competence on investment should be exercised primarily at eu level, and we support the objective of europeanisation of investment negotiations. however, i need to make clear that the commission will not be able to negotiate with all countries targeted for investment protection by member states. our member states have investment treaties with more than 100 countries. replacing those will be a very gradual exercise, taking years. that is why it is important to create an effective mechanism empowering the member states, under certain conditions, to continue negotiating and concluding bilateral investment agreements. such a mechanism should respect the procedures and prerogatives of the institutions involved. finally, it needs to be emphasised that we are approaching a decisive stage of the legislative process, and time is becoming a major factor. it is important because the longer the adoption of the regulation takes, the longer the limbo period lasts, with the potential to create legal uncertainty for investors. i hope that, after the vote, parliament and the council can sit down together to find an early agreement on this issue. we are ready actively to support them in that endeavour.

- mr president, i would like to thank you for your reply. i would like to express my satisfaction at the fact that the european parliament is commemorating the victims and all those affected by the chernobyl nuclear disaster, the worst nuclear disaster in history, in this plenary session. this anniversary, especially in the context of the recent events in japan, is a tragic occasion for reckoning and reflection on nuclear safety. the tragedy of that time also showed the helplessness and thoughtlessness of the then communist authorities in ukraine, who tried to hide from the world the fact and the extent of the chernobyl accident. let us recall just a few facts that illustrate the scale, scope, and magnitude of that tragedy. the explosion of the chernobyl nuclear power plant reactor contaminated some 100 000 km2 of land, 70% of which was in belarus. radioactive substances also reached scandinavia, central europe, including poland, and southern europe, including greece and italy. some 115 000 people were evacuated from areas near the reactor, and some 220 000 people from belarus, the russian federation and ukraine were resettled after 1986. the devastation of this disaster on both health and the environment is very difficult to estimate. the experts are still unable to determine the number of fatalities. the world health organization estimates that the number of cancer deaths caused by pollution from the plant explosion could be as high as 9,000. other sources estimate that about 200,000 people have already died from radiation sickness and that another 100,000 people may die in the future from cancer caused by the chernobyl disaster. according to recent studies, people in at least two ukrainian districts continue to eat contaminated food. it should be recalled that the european union, as the founder of the chernobyl shelter fund, has made the largest financial contribution to the chernobyl disaster response. on the 25th anniversary, the european commission announced that it had committed eur 110 million to stabilise and protect the environment at the chernobyl nuclear power plant. in this context, we must not forget that the approach to
