on behalf of the ecr group. 25 years after the tragic chernobyl disaster, chernobyl remains a reference point for european politics. sometimes it's very accurate, but sometimes it's completely meaningless. unlike the soviet union 30 years ago, we in the european union have very good legal tools to enforce our security standards. they are the highest of world standards, which is why it is an abuse to use chernobyl today for anti-nuclear propaganda based on common prejudice. the european nuclear industry is also being held back by another aspect: it contributes to our continued dependence on fossil fuel imports from third countries. chernobyl may also provide useful lessons. there are plans to build a series of russian nuclear power plants on our eastern border to export electricity to the countries of the european union. they are built without eu safety standards. it is worthwhile for the commission to take action to enforce its own standards not only within the union but also outside it, since the installations in the kaliningrad oblast or in belarus are oriented towards the european market. the question is whether the commission will have the strength and imagination to take action in this area.
twenty-five years after the chernobyl nuclear disaster, we are becoming increasingly aware of the tragic consequences of a nuclear disaster for human health and even for the lives of people and the environment. this is also the awareness that we have after what happened recently in fukushima. one of the main causes of the chernobyl disaster, we know for sure, was a faulty reactor design. and the question is: does the european union control what happens to the remaining soviet-era reactors, what steps is it taking in that direction to ensure their safety? there are currently over 140 nuclear power plants in the european community and over 190 on the european continent. i therefore support the decision to carry out load tests on nuclear power stations in the union. however, these tests will not be compulsory and there will be no consequences for not participating. so what are the effects of these tests for power plants that fail or do not participate? we need to set high standards for nuclear power plants so that they can gain more public trust than they have so far, as they are an important source of energy for europe. we should also develop other possible sources of energy, such as shale gas, which offers many opportunities for energy production, so that we do not build up nuclear energy unnecessarily.
two weeks ago, a quarter of a century passed since the tragic explosion at chernobyl. i remember very well the days immediately after the tragedy, when the communist regime in my country, poland, concealed the truth about the fact itself, and then about the scale of the disaster, and thousands of people were driven away without regard for their health in the may day marches, just five days after the explosion, when the radioactive cloud covered a piece of europe, also reaching the north-eastern part of my country - this is the area of poland that i have the honour to represent in the european parliament as a constituency. the issue still unresolved is the proper containment of the blast site. work on the new coating has been halted due to lack of funds and community assistance is therefore necessary to complete the work. but we can't escape the atom. nuclear energy is an excellent tool for building europe's energy independence. its further development is therefore inevitable, as evidenced by the plans to create further facilities in poland, lithuania and slovakia, which is why i support the introduction of stress tests and plant safety assessments. testing should be mandatory and carried out on a cyclical basis. international cooperation in enhancing nuclear safety should also be actively promoted, and similar stress tests should be carried out at power plants in ukraine, the territory of russia and the former soviet states.
i'm not going to let you do this. today, as we commemorate the victims of the chernobyl disaster, we also think of the victims of fukushima and of the safety of our citizens in europe. and we're discussing that, too. in europe, public concern about nuclear power has recently increased. and all the studies show that in all the countries of the european union, including my country, poland, support for nuclear power has fallen by 10-15%. it is therefore of the utmost importance that the criteria of the six-point tests announced in budapest are met, which will increase the sense of security. and, commissioner, you cannot give in to the wishes of those member states who demand more lenient criteria. this is what we are fighting for at the moment, and we are very much insisting that in the case of a crisis, as well as in the case of simple human error, we do not go for half-measures, for relaxing the criteria. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of radioactive waste. we talked about the countries that are neighbouring europe, that have nuclear power. i think that these issues should be included in the commission's communication on the external energy dimension. it is also the energy that flows from us to europe, just like gas or other energy sources, and it should be covered by eu policy. we must also work in parallel to europeanise energy policy.
, in writing. this year marks the 25th anniversary of the chernobyl nuclear disaster in ukraine. on 26 april 1986, a sudden increase in reactor power during a system test caused damage to the reactor vessel, leading to a series of explosions. according to the un, the contamination covered an area within 500 km of the power plant. some 115,000 people were evacuated from areas near the reactor, and some 220,000 people from belarus, the russian federation and ukraine were resettled after 1986. nuclear accidents happen suddenly and unexpectedly. twenty-five years ago, there was the chernobyl accident, and just this march, there was the fukushima accident. it should be noted that the disaster was caused by a failure of the cooling systems due to a power failure, and power outages are a frequent occurrence in the member states. we should certainly learn from history, but let us not become hysterical over the disaster in japan. the accident raised serious concerns about nuclear safety worldwide. all indications are that nuclear energy will remain an important source of energy in the near future, and it is therefore essential to ensure the highest possible level of safety in the energy sector.

member of the commission. − the commission has actually already responded to similar written questions from the honourable member mr ziobro on the cost of reducing greenhouse gas emissions in the european union by 2020 and on the question of carbon leakage, back in march and april 2010. the eu has managed to decouple its economic growth from its emissions. eu gdp has increased by 45% since 1990 while emissions have been reduced by 13%, and that includes 2010 figures, meaning that was after we exited the crisis. over the same period, the european union manufacturing industry grew by more than 30%. these figures show that continued growth can go hand in hand with reducing emissions. for instance, it is actually estimated that, between 2005 and 2009, 550 000 new jobs were provided by the renewable energy industry alone. firstly, with regard to carbon leakage, the commission would like to stress that in the latest amendment of the ets directive the european parliament and the council have decided to tackle this issue by allocating a higher share of free allowances for sectors and subsectors deemed to be at a significant risk of carbon leakage. the commission's analysis published back in may last year confirmed that free allocation is an effective means to address the potential risk of carbon leakage. moreover, the risks for carbon leakage have been reduced further, since now more than 80 countries, amongst which all emerging economies, are implementing the pledges they committed to in copenhagen and are implementing their domestic targets. i must say that the commission has no evidence that companies are moving their production outside the eu due to climate policy. secondly, the european commission has assessed in detail the costs and benefits of co2 emission reductions on the european economy in the framework of the climate and energy package agreed back in 2008. more recent analysis conducted in 2010 shows that the costs of meeting the 20% greenhouse gas reduction target have fallen by at least one third compared to the analysis made in 2008. now they are estimated at eur 48 billion, which represents 0.32% of the projected 2020 gdp. having said that, it should also be mentioned that some of these investments will come back in, for instance, saved oil expenditure. in developing the climate and energy package, the commission has taken due account of the different circumstances in the member states in terms of economic development, wealth and energy mix. in addition, the climate and energy package contains three specific mechanisms to balance overall costs across member states, so that efforts are shared in a fair and equitable manner.

despite the entry into force of the lisbon treaty governing the common foreign and security policy, little has changed since then. the existing diplomatic missions have been renamed, but the union has not strengthened its position as a global actor. one wonders whether it is even possible to pursue a common policy of 27 countries of the union. such conclusions are directly derived from the albertini report, which noted the lack of will on the part of the member states to pursue a common policy, and from the statements of some of the representatives of those states which gave the impression of division. similar conclusions were made in the gualtieri report, which pointed to widespread duplication of defence programmes leading to the waste of limited economic resources. the only real force is nato, which is why the voices of the left in parliament, expressed in writing in the opinion of a minority, demanding, among other things, the dissolution of nato, are dangerous and even anarchistic.

mr president, atrocities are happening in camp ashraf – atrocities that we obviously condemn and about which we are profoundly concerned – but i would like to ask lady ashton what instruments we are using apart from words? are we considering trade measures, aid measures, and other concrete and real measures, rather than persuasion, which is fruitless? regarding neighbourhood policy towards the countries on the doorstep of the union, i think this is the most important part of your portfolio, lady ashton. it is the core of foreign policy, because if we fail there we fail in overall foreign policy. the naked truth is that we are in retreat and in defensive mode in the southern neighbourhood and the eastern neighbourhood. we have been taken by surprise. lady ashton says there are storms in the neighbourhood. that is the word she used. where is our meteorological road map? time is a key factor in this policy and a scarce resource. in our neighbourhood policy we are always lagging behind events. even lady ashton’s and commissioner füle’s review of the european neighbourhood policy is delayed for the third time – and delayed in her office. our sin is inaction. foreign policy is about acts that change the course of events, not about words, series of meetings, fruitless persuasion and floods of statements. we should be using real and hard instruments to change things in libya, syria, camp ashraf and belarus. following member states and waiting for permission from foreign ministers to go ahead has become lady ashton’s doctrine and she treats it as virtue. it is the wrong approach. it condemns our foreign policy to the lowest common denominator and to always being late. we want a high representative to lead, not to follow. our debate has two weaknesses. first, we very often content ourselves with condemnation and making ineffective visa bans, which are ridiculously weak instruments. we also call for more money, to clear our conscience, but there is a lot of arab money which is not invested in arab democracy and arab prosperity.
let us stop complaining about the lack of a common european policy. in some places she is, in other places she is not. and as far as the neighbourhood policy is concerned, this common policy is. and in a unique way in north africa, new countries can support the west, because the west has no credibility. that's the credibility of those who have made revolutions in eastern european countries. and in the east, we all have business, east and west. but the old countries have money, they have the means. we need this money to carry out a common neighbourhood policy in the east and in the south, to build our credibility. and if we are talking about defence policy, what kind of defence policy is it that europe has no army? 60 european planes flying over libya: deaf and blind. there's no intelligence, these planes are not capable of carrying out their mission effectively. if the americans hadn't joined this mission in the first place, it would have been nothing. it wouldn't have any effect. and let's stop complaining about the lack of a common policy. as long as there is no common army, there will be no common security and defence policy.
, in writing. ladies and gentlemen, last week, a very important event took place. after long negotiations, we have finally succeeded in persuading our un partners to agree to a new status for the union within the organisation. this is a definite success, given the initial resistance of the general assembly. but we cannot fall into triumphalism and assume that the union will now present a united position at the united nations. the fact that the president of the european council or the high representative will be able to speak on our behalf does not mean that the member states will be able to present a common position on particularly controversial issues. the example of libya shows how deeply divided we are, even on seemingly obvious issues like the protection of civilians. it is therefore clear that without the political will of the member states, this decision will have no meaning. that is why i cannot agree with mrs ashton that the world will hear the union's clear and single voice from now on. i am rather afraid that for a long time we will be faced with a plurality of votes, where the union's united position will be weakened, not only by the permanent members of the security council, but also by the presidency seeking its place after the lisbon treaty. how does ms ashton intend to develop a unified eu voice at the un and how does she intend to build a good image of the eu in this organisation?
in writing. during the january debate on the situation in tunisia and egypt, as well as on freedom of religion, i mentioned the tragic situation of christians in arab countries, with particular emphasis on religious repression against the egyptian copts. i was paying attention to the radicalization of islam, directing its aggression against the followers of christ. today, i can see that my fears were justified. the clashes at st. menas church are just the tip of the iceberg of the tragedy of egyptian christians and the silence of international organizations. in this context, it is worth mentioning the attacks on the biszo monastery in march this year, when the egyptian army shelled a monastery full of refugees from cairo, and the activities of the extremist salafi islamic community, which were ignored by parliament and mrs ashton. in april, they carried out a series of attacks on christian sites in beni ahmad and the towns of bastil and kamadir. it is clear that the european community is still unable to develop a coherent strategy to respond to and prevent human rights violations in the asia-north africa region in the future. we should put more pressure on the egyptian authorities to protect the copts. the section on combating religious intolerance, with a particular focus on persecuted christians, within the political subcommittee of the european external action service should be strengthened.

mr. chairman, please! i agree that european foreign policy must take account of the external dimension of the european area of freedom, security and justice. i therefore welcome any action that contributes to the promotion of peace, stability and the rule of law in countries and regions in crisis. i support the commitment to the transatlantic partnership as one of the main pillars of brussels' foreign policy, aimed at creating a barrier-free market with the united states. eastern policy is particularly important from the polish point of view. the report takes account of the need for political and economic integration with the union's eastern neighbours, while calling for a coherent approach in the negotiations on a new agreement with russia, drawing attention to the rule of law and human rights issues in that country. it also stressed the need to intensify accession negotiations with turkey and to continue to involve the balkan countries in the eu accession process.
i supported the report on the common security and defence policy in europe. but i want to draw attention to the fact that this report is not just about evaluating this policy, but it is focused primarily on the future, on development. in my view, this requires more than just the various fair, accurate assessments and wise words which are abundant in this report; the common security and defence policy must be looked at in a different and serious way. i think there are three things that need to be done here. first, the union should define its common strategic interests, for example in energy security and neighbourhood policy. secondly, the union must increase its own capacity for planning and coordinating civilian and military operations as well as crisis management. finally, thirdly, a common budget for common actions should be established within the union budget.
the increasing importance of the increasing interdependence of international actors in the face of economic, environmental or energy problems determines the continuous changes in the external relations of individual countries. security issues are a policy area of particular concern to each country, requiring systematic adaptation to a changing world. the main theme of the report is the call to safeguard the union's strategic autonomy in the field of security and defence. however, it does not take into account the lack of combat experience, while calling for further efforts to expand the operational capabilities of the european union. for countries like poland, the north atlantic alliance remains the foundation of their defence policy. the strengthening of the strategic partnership between the union and nato and the requirement of enhanced mutual support for actions can significantly slow down operational decision-making procedures. all of this makes the report seem to me to be a document with an approach that is too radical, and that is why i voted against it.
in writing. − with the public and consumers of the european market in mind, we try to simplify as much as possible the rules and procedures so that they are transparent and understandable to every citizen. the same is true of the common agricultural policy, where simplification is the overriding theme in the future shape of this policy, which aims to ensure food security in europe. the harmonisation of the directive on the labelling of foodstuffs is intended to bring the provisions closer to the consumer and to make them easier to understand. at the same time, it shall be carried out in full compliance with the procedures for the adoption of acts in the union, while preserving the original content of the original provisions.
in writing. - i voted in favour of document 2010/0261 on the codification of the permissible noise levels and exhaust systems of motor vehicles. this is another example of the european commission's efforts to simplify and streamline the acquis communautaire so that it is more transparent and accessible to citizens of the community's member states. the legislative proposal harmonises the existing texts to create a more understandable and accessible legal act. the regulation approximates the laws of the member states by laying down technical standards, the purpose of which is to apply the ec type-approval procedure laid down in directive 2007/46/ec to each type of vehicle.
in writing. − the regulation adopted by the european parliament on textile fibre names and labelling of textile products is of particular importance for the textile sector in the european union. it will allow new fibres to be brought to market more quickly, and in particular will help innovative companies in the textile sector to put their research and solutions into practice. the regulation was the subject of a long debate between the european parliament and the council. parliament called for the regulation to be extended to include new elements, in particular the indication of the origin of goods, the indication of the animal origin of fibres and stricter requirements on the use of harmful substances in the manufacture of textile products. parliament succeeded in convincing the council of the need for the clear labelling of fibres of animal origin. this provision is very beneficial in particular for those consumers who suffer from allergies to leather products and for consumers who for ideological reasons do not want to buy textile products containing animal components. i hope that in the near future we will also be able to reach an agreement on the question of the indication of the origin of goods. this issue has been unresolved for too long. i think european businesses and consumers will benefit from clear rules.
in writing. - ladies and gentlemen! i fully support the decision taken today to conclude an interinstitutional agreement between the european parliament and the commission on the 'transparency register'. since 1996, parliament has been running a register for interest groups and can be a model for other institutions in this respect. the european commission only established its lobby register in 2008, while the council of the european union has not yet. a decision taken in the european parliament leads to the merging of the register of lobbyists and interest groups run separately by the two institutions mentioned above. this will help to increase transparency and, above all, make it easier for citizens to access information in one place. the creation of a common register is also beneficial for lobbyists, who only have to register once. the decision also excludes from the 'transparency register' the social partners, churches, political parties and local and regional authorities. in addition, interest groups will be recorded in the explanatory memorandum of a report or recommendation if they have been granted permission to meet with the member on a specific legislative matter. i believe this decision is an important step towards greater transparency and i look forward to the eu council joining the common register.
in writing. - brussels, which some have called the "lobbying mecca" after washington, needs proper regulation and clear rules for cooperation between decision-makers and representatives of the various interest groups. it should be recalled that lobbying understood as the representation of the interests of different social groups is an integral part of modern democratic systems. once again, meps have voiced their support for transparency. a common register of lobbyists will increase the transparency of the eu institutions. it will also distinguish between representatives of pressure groups and representatives of non-governmental and governmental organisations. there is no doubt that interest groups are a platform for exchanging information and an important channel of communication between citizens and the european union. in order to be as effective as possible and to deliver the expected results, this cooperation needs to be regulated and transparent.
in writing. ladies and gentlemen! today the european parliament adopted a resolution on eu-japan trade relations. the document draws attention to the fact that the european union and japan are very important trading partners for each other. this takes into account the provisions of the international trade organisation and the fact that japan and the eu, among others, together generated 1⁄4 of the world's gdp in 2009 and the value of trade between these regions was eur 120 billion in 2010. the document also stressed that the eu was fully open to a free trade agreement with japan, but that this would require japan to remove non-tariff barriers and remove any obstacles to the development of cooperation. it also highlighted what i consider to be a very important aspect of this cooperation, the issue of paying attention to environmental protection in the trade process and promoting climate change mitigation and the promotion of environmental and social standards. in addition, attention was drawn to the issue of the recent nuclear disaster, which has not yet been fully contained. the extent of the crisis that has already hit japan cannot therefore be fully assessed yet and there is no need to accelerate the negotiations on a free trade agreement. because what japan needs now is real aid.
in writing. - i strongly support the development of trade cooperation between the european union and japan, which should lead to the conclusion of a bilateral free trade agreement. the fact that the total value of eu-japan trade agreements in 2010 was €120 billion is a testament to the importance of the two partners to each other. japan is the eu's sixth largest trading partner, while the eu is japan's third. both sides are also important investors, with foreign direct investment amounting to eur 200 billion in 2009. it is also worth noting that the rapid economic growth of the bric countries, the economic slowdown resulting from the global financial crisis, and the urgent need to access raw materials and renewable energy are very important challenges shared by both actors, which makes the negotiations even more urgent. in their opinion on the project, both the council and the commission stated that the opening of negotiations was conditional upon japan's removal of regulatory barriers to trade, in particular non-tariff barriers, which constitute a significant barrier to access to the japanese market for european businesses. i believe that the procedures at the highest decision-making level should be accelerated, which would lead to closer trade relations between these two strategic partners.
in writing. − japan's willingness to open bilateral talks on a free trade area with the european union is an opportunity to develop closer political relations and to increase economic benefits for both the eu and japan. given that japan is only the sixth largest trading partner of the european union, the potential for japan's trade and investment cooperation with the community remains untapped. non-tariff barriers are the main obstacle that makes it very difficult for european companies to access the japanese market. as a member of the tran commission, i am convinced that the aviation industry is one in which cooperation at commercial level and in research and development would be mutually beneficial for both the european and japanese economies. i believe that the aeronautics sector can become one of the model examples of cooperation between the community and japan.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the adoption of the annual report on the main aspects of the common foreign and security policy (cfsp) in 2009. it is a well-written report of crucial importance, which discusses in detail aspects of the common foreign and security policy. i am particularly pleased that the report contains the amendment i proposed concerning georgia. i wanted to emphasise the importance of continuing and consistent political pressure on russia to implement all the provisions of the 2008 agreement, including, in particular, to allow access to the occupied territories for the eumm. i hope that high representative catherine ashton will consider our recommendations.
in writing. − recent developments in north africa and asia highlight the need to strengthen the european union's foreign policy and the alliances in which it participates. the continued threat of terrorist attacks indicates the need to strengthen european security standards. however, some of the provisions proposed in the report by mr roberto gualtieri are unacceptable. they are at odds with the strategy of international alliances that has been built up to date, based mainly on the leading role of the north atlantic alliance. the proposed strengthening of the european defence agency would not actually mean strengthening eu security, but only the development of another bureaucratic monster incapable of carrying out the tasks assigned to it. who would decide on the use of european armed forces? whose interests would her units pursue? what voice would the new european states have? would the seat of the eao change? institutional concerns also arise: would the development of the eeas lead to a reduction in the armies of some european countries and would it conflict with the remit and objectives of the european external action service? as previous reports have shown, despite the considerable financial burden and the very good logistics and management, european forces are not doing well in simple police missions in kosovo and bosnia. let's think about how to improve their performance before we want to elevate their responsibilities to military action.
in writing. ladies and gentlemen! the european parliament adopted a resolution on the role of the european union in multilateral organisations. the general principle adopted is to strengthen the eu's role in the multilateral system. through agreements and joint action, the european union is becoming a model for the functioning of a world order based on international law. the need for the eu to work with the prime regions and to play an active part in shaping the international environment was therefore underlined. in addition, cooperation between member states and a common position, including on budgetary savings and cuts, is necessary. as regards the eu's role in the un system, the eu and its member states are called upon to step up their role and strengthen their position (change in support for the un, particularly in terms of policy and humanitarian assistance and conflict resolution). in cooperation with international financial institutions, the eu must find a solution to the external economic and financial representation problem that limits the eu's influence. on the eu's role in multilateral security organisations, it was felt that the rules that allow the eu to use nato assets should be improved. the eu-osce agreement should consider the eu taking on greater responsibility and more effective action in pursuit of common objectives (joint dialogue, joint action and coordination, etc.).
in writing. - the international situation has been changing rapidly in recent times. the growing economic importance of asia, revolutionary movements in africa, the increased threat of terrorism, the need to build common, sustainable european raw materials strategies and the increasing prevalence of human rights violations are just some of the problems facing eu diplomacy today. as practice shows, in many cases it is helpless. the european union's foreign policy seems to be ill-conceived and poorly coordinated. moreover, the idea of a common sustainable european policy often fails to meet the interests of the largest countries of the so-called 'old' union. the absence of a geographical equality rule for the recruitment of the european external action service is a perfect illustration of this. this system needs to change. that is why i did not support the report by mrs maria muñiz de urquiza. i believe that it indicates the important conditions that the union and the member states must fulfil in order to be able to better fulfil the tasks set out in the lisbon treaty. but we should not seek to replace nato with a new eu army, but rather focus on a proper division of responsibilities in times of international crises. the eu could play a role in humanitarian aid, with the north atlantic alliance coordinating military aid. such a division of tasks could also allow for a strengthening of cooperation with the eu's most important trade and military partner, the united states of america.
a law that is too complex, too unclear, too rigorous, too unchangeable is clearly not conducive to development or progress, and that is why, as coordinator of the legal affairs committee, i would like to draw particular attention to the importance in the legislative process of respecting the principle of inclusion in the impact assessment, both ex ante and post ante, a test for small and medium-sized enterprises which, already at the stage of legislative enactment, makes it possible to identify and eliminate the obstacles that new legislation may pose to a sector which is, after all, the driving force of the european economy. similarly, the 'think small first' or 'only once' approaches, or the limitation of the overly rigorous transposition of eu directives into national law, of course by the member states' authorities, lead to a significant reduction in the administrative burden on the sme sector. both the work of the stoiber group and the european commission's review of the small business act confirm that administrative hurdles and excessive burdens of controls often hamper, and sometimes even prevent, the further development of small businesses that have the potential to generate new jobs. i therefore consider it appropriate to ask whether the analysis of the reduction of the administrative burden to 25% promised by the commission is already available. i also agree with the conclusions that these principles should be the guiding principles for both the eu institutions and the member states when creating new legislation or revising existing legislation. it is worrying that the implementation of the small business act faces many obstacles in the member states, although - as examples from some countries show - the implementation of these rules is producing positive results. finally, i would also like to draw attention to the importance of the work already under way on european contract law and the work being undertaken in the legal affairs committee on the creation of a european patent protection system. good regulation in this area will certainly give a direct boost to the development of innovation, especially in the area of the operation and development of small and medium-sized enterprises.
the ongoing work on the revision of the small business act should focus in particular on the establishment of a european private company statute, thereby facilitating cross-border operations of economic operators on the union market. although the time to start a business has decreased in recent months, an analysis by the european commission shows that more than half of the member states still do not meet the requirement of being able to start a business within three days. in addition, most member states still do not assess the impact of future legislative and administrative initiatives on smes. they don't fully apply the only once rule either. the list of countries where business can be definitively closed during the year has remained unchanged over the past two years. i therefore suggest that the european commission should be even more involved in the efforts to ensure that member states implement these provisions. in addition, i believe that further action under the small business act should also include improving the availability of finance, access to venture capital markets, the development of single points of contact in the member states to facilitate administrative procedures. it is worth noting that in order to reach the 75% employment target under strategy 2020, it is necessary to support smes, which, due to the economic crisis, instead of generating jobs, are facing a number of additional costs.
, in writing. micro, small and medium-sized enterprises play a central and most important role in the development of the european economy, are a major source of employment and have a fundamental impact on the development of european competitiveness and innovation. we can say with full responsibility that we will not achieve the europe 2020 objectives without supporting smes and making it easier for them to take full advantage of the single market. the solutions provided for in the small business act, such as reducing red tape, improving access to finance and facilitating market entry, are particularly important and, in my view, effective measures to create the best possible conditions for the development of smes. however, the effectiveness of these solutions may be jeopardised by problems with their implementation at member state level. i therefore hope that member states which have not yet fully implemented these measures will do their utmost to complete this process as soon as possible.
mr president, our duty is to look for the best solutions to cope with the crisis, to which end the learning process is of great value. my feeling is that we have learned why things went wrong and how we got ourselves into the difficult situation we are in today, but my feeling is also that now we are less open to drawing lessons from the evolving reality. in this context, i would like to raise two issues. first, we can see great similarities between member states with regard to public debts and deficit ratios, while at the same time, for the same member states, there are substantial differences between the risk premiums paid on their sovereign debt. in my view this is clear proof that factors other than sovereign debt enter into the picture and influence markets. among other things, it is foreign debt or excessive external imbalances on which markets have focused, and this clearly means that in responding to the situation we must go beyond fiscal adjustment. the second issue is related to the fact that those economies that are the most strongly affected by the crisis have to cope with a combination of high risk premiums and severe austerity measures. this double challenge makes achieving debt sustainability practically impossible. if we reject debt restructuring then we need a better balance between punishment and assistance and the design of response packages which would make it possible to avoid pushing countries further into a debt trap.
in the context of the current economic crisis in europe, employment agencies have a particularly important role to play. so it is worthwhile to take a closer look at the effectiveness of their activities. there is no doubt that these agencies should help europeans to acquire skills that they can use in a rapidly changing and increasingly competitive labour market. they should therefore take measures which, first, will increase flexibility in the european labour market through, for example, the mutual recognition of workers' qualifications between member states. secondly, the agencies should actively participate in the development of such programmes which take into account the economic and social challenges facing the european union, including the demographic crisis and the overburdening of the pension system. finally, they should carry out studies that highlight the real problems facing the european labour market. in conclusion, the main focus of the employment agencies should be to help the citizens of the european union in the light of the economic and demographic crisis.
mr. chairman, please! as co-rapporteur on cooperation in vocational education and training, i follow the activities of the european centre for the development of vocational training with particular attention. linking vocational training to the needs of citizens and the labour market is one of the key elements of increasing employment and increasing the competitiveness of the european union. the role of cedefop cannot therefore be underestimated. the 2010 report has confirmed my belief in the effectiveness of cedefop. this is demonstrated, among other things, by the steadily increasing number of people using its publications and the europass portal. however, i believe it is important to increase cedefop's involvement in structural actions for vocational training, including the introduction of a system for evaluating the effectiveness of training. i also think the agency has a great potential to make an attractive offer.
i think that agencies that are effective in the field of labour market, in the field of employment, are extremely important. of course, we have to account for the agencies' performance. let us remember that one third of the citizens of the european union have no vocational qualifications. the issues of monitoring the employment sector, labour market potential and vocational training are a vast body of knowledge that cannot be measured today by a single member state. we should therefore be able to judge the performance of the agencies, but we should also be aware that the performance of these agencies can have an incredible impact on the labour market and on the linking of vocational training with jobs and future professions, which are becoming scarce in the european union today. we have to import a lot of narrowly specialized jobs: doctors, nurses. these are the problems facing the european union, and we should appreciate the effectiveness of these agencies.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on regional development. − mr president, i would say to the commissioner that, in recent years, innovation has become a symbol of a policy instrument that can fix all our problems. this means that there are huge expectations and that we must deliver. of course, for a successful implementation of ideas, governance matters very strongly and a governance framework for innovation must be based today on pragmatism and must be delivered with a sense of urgency, and also must be at the service of the policy content. europe, we all agree, has to innovate or it will lose out to competitors. every link in the european innovation chain must be strengthened and innovation policy must be focused towards challenges. that is what i understand the innovation union is offering. today we run the risk that, not only companies, but also governments might decrease investment in innovation. that is the logic of the crisis and the logic of national budget cuts. eu policy responses and eu budgetary instruments must move firmly against that logic. in europe, innovation is not just a concept that can be limited to specific innovation centres. it needs to be applied across the entire european territory. europe is simply too small to afford an innovation deficit anywhere on its territory. research and innovation are clearly not the same thing and we agree with you very clearly. governance for innovation should therefore do more than just support research and development policy. promoting innovation-led growth is not about increasing excellence in r&d infrastructure, important as they are, it is first and foremost about mobilising talents and mobilising new ideas. governance for innovation must mean establishing new partnerships enabling efficient innovation systems that mobilise intellectual and entrepreneurial capacities, detecting also sleeping innovators – of which we have many in europe – through a business environment that is conducive to innovation, and particularly for smes, covering all sectors of the economy. to conclude, let me say that we do not yet have a fully-fledged european model for innovation, but what is clear is that it must be rooted in a well-orchestrated, concrete, strong and joint public/private effort. i trust that the innovation union will take us all the way forward towards such a model.
madam president! of course, we are all for innovation, especially in science, industry, and i say this not only as a politician, but also as a university worker, because before i became a politician, i was a university lecturer. but it's just that, actually, we've had this happen a couple of times in this room, and we're losing this innovation race to countries like the united states and the far east. it therefore asks that our cooperation in innovation be extended to non-european countries. i am very pleased that my amendment (it has paragraph 167 here) was accepted, which calls for cooperation with the eastern partnership countries, and i hope that paragraph 71 will be interpreted in the same way, which, while it refers to the mediterranean countries, should be extended to all the countries of the european neighbourhood policy.
in my speech in november here in strasbourg, i pointed out the great disparity between the old and the new countries of the european union in the financial support for the research and development sector. in the long term, this leads to significant disparities in the development of individual european community countries and to the ill-deservedly named 'brain drain' phenomenon, which is mistakenly referred to in the report as intellectual mobility. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to promote the use of renewable energy sources, such as the renewable energy programme, the renewable energy research programme and the renewable energy research programme. it is also worth encouraging individual governments to increase the budget allocated annually to research, as well as to establish a minimum percentage threshold of the budget that must be used for such projects. it is also crucial to finance innovation in the sme sector. we should put a lot of emphasis on that.
member of the commission. − madam president, i would like to thank all the members who took part in the debate. i think everybody here agrees that we need to improve the conditions for innovation. most of the speakers talked about jobs. that is what innovation union is all about. it is about taking the very basic blue-sky research that we do so well in the european union, and translating it all the way to the marketplace so that we provide the jobs here, and they are not provided abroad. a number of speakers raised the role of the regions. this is really important and we need to develop synergies between research and innovation funding, on the one hand, and structural funds, on the other. indeed, ms merkies underlines that point in her report. all the regions of europe should play to their strengths. i will go in a couple of weeks’ time to debrecen, in hungary, to the ‘week of innovative regions of europe’ conference, where all the regions will come together to talk about the , in writing. innovation, competitiveness, sustainability, creativity, efficiency - these are all beautiful words that fit perfectly into the trends in politics, the economy and the labour market. but are there concrete actions, real projects, behind them? such words certainly make a positive impression on the listener, help to promote the ideals presented and win over followers. but let us not forget that behind these slogans there must be practical actions, legislative decisions and laws that actually help to achieve the objectives of the eu 2020 strategy. the potential of europe and europeans is immense, and it is our task to create the right conditions for its full exploitation.
, in writing. as a member of the committee on culture and education, i support the innovation union initiative. i would like to emphasise the role of education, vocational training and social research (to combat poverty and social exclusion) in this initiative. it is important to simplify the administrative procedures for the submission of applications for eu research and innovation programmes in order to increase the participation of enterprises and scientific institutions. simplified procedures will also ensure a more efficient and effective use of public funds and reduce administrative burdens. innovation policy should go hand in hand with training, vocational training and labour market policies. the new products and services are intended to increase employment and to help forecast future trends and skills requirements in the labour market. given that women represent only 30% of european researchers and only 13% of the heads of european research institutions, i call for the innovation union initiative to include further guidelines for a more balanced representation of women and men in scientific disciplines. i also call for their effective implementation by the member states.

, in writing. ladies and gentlemen! the cultural dimension of the eu's external action is an important and much-needed one. in general, european culture is perceived in the world as attractive and desirable. it is more difficult to get people to accept european values. working in the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly, i have experienced many cultural differences and their effects. as europeans, we regularly strive to promote values and principles that are fundamental and indispensable to us. and quite often, this is misunderstood by our partners. some of them see this as a form of cultural imperialism. that is why it is so difficult to convince our partners that the values promoted by the european union are not an attempt to impose our way of thinking on others. our efforts to promote our ideals, for example, in the field of human rights, are simply motivated by a moral imperative. we respect difference and diversity, but we can't give up on the principles we've come to believe are fundamental. we will not accept discrimination, we will not give up the protection of human life and dignity. the union is united and consistent on this issue.
, in writing. support for the mobility of young people, especially from the eastern partnership countries and the union for the mediterranean, is particularly important in the context of recent developments in belarus and north africa. the democratic transition processes now under way in egypt and tunisia can be strengthened by eu efforts to educate their citizens in the spirit of democracy and respect for the rule of law and human rights. educated citizens are the greatest enemy of dictators and totalitarian regimes. the experience of eu member states can be used to organise such programmes. for example, in poland there is a programme named after konstantin kalinowski, which is implemented by the studium europy wschodniej of the university of warsaw, among others, an international institution that enables students from the east and the balkans to study in poland. the union should also step up efforts to establish an eastern partnership university, modelled on the euro-mediterranean university in slovenia. the eu should support initiatives by young and capable people to promote its policies. a good example of this is the eastbook.eu portal, whose founders are already informing thousands of internet users daily about events in the eastern partnership countries and the progress of the programme. the eu should also support study trips of young people from member states to neighbouring countries. it helps to break down cultural barriers. the eurobus initiative , an annual tour of ukraine by young people from eu countries, is commendable.
, in writing. fellow students and colleagues! the adoption last june of the eu's new strategy 'europe 2020' is intended to help the eu emerge from the economic crisis and develop further. this is also an important step towards maintaining and even increasing the mobility of young people. one of the priorities of the europe 2020 strategy is 'youth on the move', an initiative to improve the performance of education systems and facilitate the entry of young people into the labour market. this objective is to be achieved by developing the idea of youth exchanges and the acquisition of new skills by young people. statistics show that as many as 15% of young people are now leaving school early, thus acquiring qualifications that do not meet the needs of the labour market. in addition, only about one third of the population has a university degree, a much lower percentage than in the united states or japan, for example. one of the major challenges facing the european union is therefore to focus particular attention and funding on these two problems. however, the situation will not improve unless both the commission and the member states implement the guidelines of the europe 2020 strategy. youth mobility is one of the keys to europe's future development and if we aspire to be the world's most innovative economy, we cannot ignore investing in human capital, especially young people.
, in writing. in a time of economic crisis, when some member states are cutting back on investment in education and training, i am pleased that parliament is adopting a report on the 'youth on the move' programme today. in recent years, young people have been the ones most affected by the crisis. the unemployment rate among young people in the eu has exceeded 20%, twice that of adults, and in some member states it is as high as 40%. budget cuts have a direct impact on the prospects and development opportunities of young people. the knowledge and skills of young people are essential for achieving smart and sustainable development. the 'youth on the move' programme, the flagship initiative of the 'europe 2020' strategy, should aim to make higher education in europe more attractive, to improve the quality of education and to increase the mobility of students and staff. this initiative enables young people to acquire the knowledge, skills and competences they need in their work and in their lives. these priorities and objectives will not be fully realised and achieved unless the eu provides long-term financial support in its budget. that is why it is so important that this programme receives a high level of funding, while at the same time not forgetting the importance of its continued promotion and a proper information policy.
, in writing. the ep calls for concrete action: the european commission to recognise the creative sector as one of the most productive parts of the eu economy and thus give its development absolute priority. to this end, we want to increase the possibility of financing the creative sector from the eu budget as a pillar of smart growth. it is possible to create synergies between eu cultural support programmes, such as culture 2007-13, with existing eu research programmes (such as the eu's 8th framework programme for technological development), or to expand the scope for spending money from existing funds (such as the european social fund). in parallel, we recommend encouraging the emergence of new innovative financial instruments (bank guarantees, repayable advances and smart loans) that would make it easier for creators and creative smes to launch their ventures. money, of course, is not everything. we call for, among other things, the strengthening of cooperation between the cultural and creative sectors and european universities, the increase in the number of specialist training courses for young people and the mobility of all cultural creators and people. to this end, we intend to create a multilingual online platform that would serve to exchange experiences between creators and, consequently, to create an even closer network of links between all those for whom the development of the creative industries in europe is important.

european programmes to support young people need unquestionable support. the people who make up the future of our continent are also the most vulnerable. we must ensure that they have access to proper education, cultural resources and, above all, the opportunity to learn foreign languages and the freedom to choose their place of education. not everyone has the money or the means to provide for themselves. the positive results of many youth programmes, such as erasmus and leonardo da vinci, demonstrate that this is a worthwhile investment. the greatest need for support is among young people in rural areas, who often have no financial means to start their studies and no opportunities to start work outside of farming in their area of residence.
i am very pleased that the 'youth on the move' initiative is an integral part of the europe 2020 strategy. i am also pleased that the report voted on today has recognised the importance of non-formal education, understood as education through participation in youth organisations, ngos and through volunteering. i believe that non-formal education helps young people to become active citizens, teaches teamwork, helps to develop individual interests and, very importantly, gives better chances of finding a job.
madam president! children are our future. they are the ones who will create a future european society with a conscience, which is why it is so important to start early. we need to instill positive values and proper moral standards in our children from an early age. education should be based on good, solid foundations and be delivered by appropriately trained and prepared teachers. we need to work towards equality of opportunity so that every child, whether they come from the city or the countryside, whether they come from a rich or a poor family, has access to early learning. in the process of equal opportunities, we should pay particular attention to rural environments, where children have much less access to educational and cultural facilities.
faster growth, productivity, efficiency and increased competitiveness are the best mechanisms to combat economic problems. to achieve these objectives, joint action on innovation is needed. it is important to focus on the creativity of citizens, for example by giving workers the freedom to come up with ideas for improving the working process. consumption is also a driver of innovation, and the iphone applications developed by european consumers are a concrete example of how citizens' creativity and their desire to use modern technologies are combined. an important element of the innovation union is the strengthening of the knowledge base by bringing together businesses, research institutions and citizens. this will require the full involvement of public and local authorities. the fundamental objective of innovation is to maintain a high level of prosperity in europe. i hope that the proposed joint actions will help to support the innovation process and contribute to economic stability. i therefore support this report.
i voted for the report by the innovation union. innovation is, of course, the key to europe's development. however, i believe that it is absolutely fundamental to promote innovation, particularly in the small and medium-sized enterprises sector, especially in the new member states of the european union, which are far behind in this respect. it is in this sector - as it appears from numerous analyses - that the future competitiveness of the european economy vis-à-vis other major world economies will be decided. and it is worth remembering as research conducted by ernst & young shows that three quarters of the applications for research and purchase of new technologies submitted by small businesses in europe are unfortunately rejected by banks. the financing is a serious problem and we should therefore encourage the member states to support small and medium-sized enterprises in this area. without this support, they will not be able to cope with the increasing competition in the global economy.
i supported an interesting and comprehensive report on the transformation of europe after the global crisis. i did so in the hope that the direction proposed in the report would reduce the growing disparities in the development of individual countries in the union and that it would weaken the so-called 'brain drain', which the report, i think, too politely calls intellectual mobility. to ensure europe's sustainable development, we must therefore devote more resources to developing innovation and research projects in the new countries of the european union. governments should be encouraged to establish a minimum percentage threshold of the budget that must be spent on a research and development project, in addition to increasing the budget allocated annually to research. however, the emphasis on r & d should not in any way limit the current priorities of the european union, such as the common agricultural policy or cohesion policy, in the future budgetary agenda. they are doing their job well.
the cultural heritage of european countries is a value in itself. although culturally diverse, the member states already have a global brand that attracts citizens from other countries who are ready to benefit from the cultural heritage. the political and economic power of the european union can be enhanced by promoting its identity and cultural value. new technologies play an important role in the field of culture, and they also promote the realisation of fundamental human rights. particularly in countries that are enslaved by censorship, civic activity and access to information is maintained through the network. the union must therefore promote internet freedom on the global stage, making a significant contribution to the cultural development and awareness of closed societies. the young generation also needs a coherent mobility strategy to increase its development in the fields of science and culture. i support cultural diplomacy, and the work of parliamentary delegations can also contribute to this. that is why i voted for this report.
the statements and comments in the report are extremely valuable and timely. i would like to refer in particular to the statements which indicate that the european union is committed to taking action worldwide to promote respect for freedom of speech, freedom of the press and free access to audiovisual media. it is also very timely to call on the european commission to promote internet freedom worldwide in the face of the threats we are reading and hearing about more and more. while i am pleased to see that we are remembering these values which are fundamental to us as europeans, i must admit that i voted with some sadness on this report. i am aware that we sometimes forget these fundamental values in the world, and we forget that they are also being violated in some of the member states of the european union. an example of this is what is happening in poland with journalists who are critical of the government. they are being removed en masse from public media, and government officials are trying to liquidate the independent, private daily newspaper "rzeczpospolita", which is the second largest major daily in poland, critical, to say the least, of the government's line. this too must be opposed.
i supported an interesting report on the cultural dimension of the european union's external action. how can we not support the record of the eu's actions around the world to respect freedom of speech, freedom of the press, free access to audiovisual media, etc. however, i have the impression that we care too much about the situation outside the union and not enough about the standards within the union, for example in poland, because it was in poland that the mass dismissal of journalists and the liquidation of programs owned by them, which were united by a common criticism of the current reality, began after the current ruling coalition gained power in the public media. and for example, people like jacek sobala, anita gargas, jacek karnowski or wojciech leszczyński were fired from their jobs. joanna lichocka, tomasz sakiewicz, rafał ziemkiewicz, jan pospieszalski, grzegorz górny, tomasz terlikowski, bronisław wildstein, wojciech cejrowski - these are just some of the many examples of journalists who have been deprived of their programs. the suppression of freedom of speech in poland is a disgrace to the entire european union.

in writing. − i supported the report on improving european education and training systems. i'm in favor of extending all youth education programs. in addition to youth on the move, financial and political support should be provided for programmes such as erasmus, leonardo da vinci, comenius, grundtvig, youth in action and marie curie. these programmes have been very successful in the union. they involve a large number of young people from different backgrounds (the number of polish students who left for erasmus between 1998 and 2010 was 93 807), and they contribute to developing their potential and to creating a strong european civil society. these are very efficient programmes with very low unit costs and high utilisation rates. promoting youth mobility requires overcoming practical barriers. around one third of erasmus students experienced difficulties due to the uncertainty of the study abroad system and the lack of coherence, continuity between the subjects of study in the home country and abroad. the aim should be to ensure that both time and qualifications acquired in other eu countries are recognised. other issues that need to be addressed include obtaining visas, medical documents in different languages and transferring grants while abroad. disabled people face even greater obstacles to mobility than healthy people. additional mechanisms should be put in place to ensure a level playing field.
in writing. - i supported the report on early childhood education in the eu. i would like to draw particular attention to three points. first, the early years of childhood are crucial to a child's mental, emotional, and physical development. therefore, member states need to take into account a range of different issues affecting child development, such as health, migration, gender equality and employment, when developing comprehensive strategies and action programmes. secondly, the local level should develop implementation programmes that take account of the different living conditions and needs in early childhood education and care. they must also have sufficient autonomy to be able to implement children's programmes independently and creatively. another issue is the improvement of the quality of early childhood education and care services. this is where the development of mechanisms for evaluating and monitoring service delivery and compliance should start. my final point is about universal access to child care. according to the ministry of education, there are 8,400 public and 1,600 private kindergartens in poland, and there are about 1,6 million children aged 3-6 years. so the nursery school is only able to accommodate 40 percent of them. in poland, there are 352 day-care centres, and only 2% of the youngest children use them. this problem is one of the main causes of high unemployment among women.
in writing. − despite the openness of the eu's public procurement market, access to third countries' public procurement markets remains largely restricted. in this situation, european companies have no chance of competing on a global level in public procurement. for example, in 2009, the chinese authorities adopted a system of accreditation for local innovative products, which further restricted the access of international companies to the chinese market. but it's not just the chinese market that's a problem, it's also the highly developed economies like the united states, japan and canada, which are all using protectionist policies. i therefore support the call for the principle of reciprocity in access to public procurement markets, contained in the resolution voted today and which i supported in the opinion i prepared for the committee on international trade. however, i would like the european commission's future proposal on the principle of reciprocity to contribute primarily to the opening up of third country procurement markets, rather than merely restricting access to public procurement markets in the european union for third country companies, which could have a negative impact on competitiveness on the eu market.

in writing. − as a member of the culture and education committee delegation to sarajevo, i support the city's candidacy for european capital of culture in 2014. sarajevo deserves a chance to show its enormous potential. his multiculturalism is unique. sarajevo is surrounded by an atmosphere of multiculturalism and europeanism. it is the only city in the world where you can find temples of five religions in one square kilometer: there are mosques, a roman catholic cathedral, an orthodox church, a synagogue and an evangelical church. the bosnians, on the other hand, are known for their warmth and hospitality. i recently read the memoirs of a polish exchange student in sarajevo who had not met any foreign exchange student there who didn't like her. since the end of the war in 1995, sarajevo has also been rebuilt, mainly with the financial support of the european union. sarajevo is looking to its european future with great enthusiasm. he wants to demonstrate his enormous potential and to encourage europeans to join him. there's no doubt this city deserves that chance, and we should support it.
in writing. - sarajevo has a very important place in the historical consciousness of europeans. i support the granting of the title of european capital of culture to this city, by way of exception, in 2014. the initiative, which has been promoting the richness and diversity of european cultures for over 25 years, will also contribute to the city's tourist and economic revival. sarajevo has witnessed important historical events, and was heavily damaged as a result of the war in the 1990s. it was also the site of the massacre that started world war i. the centenary of that event is in 2014. the award of the title of european capital of culture at this time would not only have an impact on cultural regeneration and the improvement of the city's image abroad, but also on the commemoration of important aspects of european history and identity.
the dramatic events in sri lanka, as described in a un report, illustrate the kind of problems that armed conflict can lead to. what happened there is further proof that resolving differences through violence, through armed means, generates further gigantic problems. the concept of a just war has been debated in europe for centuries. what is especially painful is the fact that in the modern world, even a war that is theoretically just inevitably brings innocent and unjustified victims. it's happening no matter what we define as a just war. in the case of sri lanka, there is a growing body of evidence that this war was not fair to either side. the winner isn't always right, even though he's always trying to prove he's right. if there is to be a reconciliation, as the sri lankan government claims, it must be based on the truth of what happened during the fight against the tamil tigers. there will be no true reconciliation without the exposure of war crimes, no matter which side committed them. there will be no reconciliation if the parties consider their sins taboo, not to be talked about.

increasing innovation in the european union is one of the key elements of economic development, especially in times of crisis. this aspect has been very well emphasized by the rapporteur. unfortunately, however, some important points have been presented in what seems to be too general a way. first, however, it is worth noting that relatively little money is allocated to innovation in the new countries of the european union. it is almost as if there is a great disparity and disproportion between the old and the new countries of the european union. the report mentions it in only one sentence. their modest contribution is negatively perceived and has a negative impact on the sustainable development of the community and its cohesion. it is worth mentioning here that despite the €86 billion allocated to research in the 2007-2013 funding period, this situation is not changing, and therefore the cohesion fund allocations for innovation in the next financial perspective should take greater account of this factor of balanced allocation of funds to both the old and the new countries of the european union. this innovation is also an opportunity for these new european countries, and science and modern technologies should also be developed there in a coherent way for the benefit of europe as a whole. it is also worth noting that research funding problems are largely in the sme sector. the tightening of monetary policy resulting from the financial and economic crisis has limited the provision of credit that is necessary for long-term investments linked to innovation. this must be taken into account in order to facilitate the access of smes to credit for these purposes. it is also worth mentioning the simplification of administrative procedures in this respect.
i thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. the main thing i would like to stress is the simplification of the rules and procedures applicable to programmes supporting research and innovation activities and the need to identify the reasons for the under-representation of the new countries in the european union. the future framework programme must respond to current needs so that each country can develop its research area, research activities and innovation by designing common financial instruments which, if well managed, would allow the focus of action on market and societal needs. enabling associations, enterprises, in particular micro-enterprises, to participate in the future framework programme as clusters, national or regional networks of technology platforms is a necessary task. at the same time, i would like to emphasise that the continuing diversity of innovation levels across the eu regions requires particular attention when formulating common strategic frameworks for research and innovation funding. it is worth noting the synergy of actions at european, national and regional levels, in addition to introducing common administrative and financial regulations and forcing the harmonisation of rules and conditions for participation in the different programmes towards the creation of a common and transparent system. i hope that the conclusions drawn from the evaluation process of the seventh framework programme will form the basis for further work on the next one, the eighth.
as i listen to today's evaluation of the seventh framework programme, i would like to take this opportunity to draw attention to the preparations for the next, the eighth programme. we already have a green paper on this subject which makes almost no mention of the need for research to be applied in other areas, such as fisheries. unfortunately, the evolution of direct research funding in this sector is very worrying. we started with funds that were gradually reduced in successive programmes, and these drastic cuts led to the fact that in the seventh programme marine research was completely eliminated as a specific funding objective. in the next framework programme, this situation must change so that we are able to meet the objectives of the reformed common fisheries policy. fisheries face many challenges and research and scientific support are powerful tools for further sustainable development of the sector. that is why it is so important to allocate adequate resources to this purpose. thank you, sir.
