consistency to bring europe together, and it is still working today. this unification is not just about the accession of individual countries, but also has a deeper dimension, thanks to which citizens of the european union with such different histories, with such a heavy baggage of history and their own experience, feel in europe and in the european union as in their political home. it was the decision of the european parliament to entrust the office of president of the parliament to a pole that, among other things, caused the division into the so-called old and new europe within the european union to finally lose its meaning and cease to be relevant. i have something in my memory that's probably gone down in history, but to me it's a living memory. i mean decisions taken by the european parliament that gave faith in europe, gave a sense of europe to all those who for many years could only dream of europe. i remember how today, when the great dream of the poles also about europe, which was solidarity, was broken by the introduction of martial law in poland and the european parliament a few dozen hours later gave a very clear sign that it remembered those who did not have a chance to live in freedom. i also remember that many years later, when we regained, together with half of europe, the independence of our countries and the freedom of our citizens, but we were in an absolute economic collapse, linked, among other things, to a gigantic debt, it was from the european parliament that the strongest signal was sent in favour of a radical reduction of debt, which allowed poland and many other countries to get back on their feet. it was a decision that was a testament to the highest level of european solidarity. it was a decision that allowed tens of millions of europeans to emerge from an economic and civilizational crisis that lasted a dozen years, a crisis that was incomparably deeper than what we now call the crisis. what happened then, thanks also to the european parliament, thanks to all those who believed in the sense of solidarity as the foundation of a united europe, is today, i think, a great lesson for those who do not believe that a united europe, a europe that believes in its own strength, will find a remedy for the crisis of our time as well. i would like to repeat once again for those who do not remember: the crisis we are facing today, for all those europeans who have had to live in poverty and slavery for several decades, is a challenge that is important, but not final and incomparable to the one we have emerged from thanks to the solidarity of all europe. i would therefore like to get straight to the point and describe what i believe is most important not only for the next six months, that is, for the polish presidency, but also for the permanent task, the permanent challenge for the whole of europe. this is the simplest question, not some complicated philosophy: is the response to the crisis, both the temporary one, related to the financial crisis, the situation of some european countries, especially in the south of europe, the response to also this deeper crisis, the crisis of trust in europe, the crisis of a global dimension, is the response to be leaving europe, reducing what is european and common, or is the response to be what we have tested over the decades and what has worked well. (cheers and applause) the experience of europe as a community, but also the personal experience of each of us, tells us that the best response of europeans, the best invention of europeans is a united europe. i would like to stress very strongly, as i have said many times before many of you in this chamber, that this is not a speech just for the inauguration of the presidency today: united europe, its institutions, its budget, its objectives are not the source of the crisis. we know very well where the sources of the current financial crisis are, and it would be a false response, the worst possible, if we believed those who say: we will reduce europe and this will be our response to the crisis. history shows that when europeans believed that the answer to threats was to increase nationalism, statism, protectionism, it invariably ended in disaster. today we are not facing the same threats as in the past, but historical awareness, knowledge of the history of europe since its foundation, makes us believe in this recipe, which is solidarity between nations, solidarity between people, the willingness to help each other when others need it, solidarity understood not as charity, but as cooperation for the common good, where sometimes someone has to give more, so that whoever needs help sometime in the future can give back what he has received. (cheers and applause) today, we sometimes hear that the best response to the financial crisis, or the crisis caused by the events in north africa and the increase in illegal immigration, is to increase barriers within europe. i would like to say that the discussion on schengen is a basic, very strong illustration of the dilemma facing europe today. from our point of view, it is in europe's interest to protect these fundamental - i think - rights of european citizens, which include freedom of movement within the european union (thank you) and this is a value that we should absolutely protect. it does not conflict with our conviction that the external borders of the european union should be well guarded. that is why we are building the community, also when we are enlarging it, so that at the same time within the community we can allow the maximum of freedom for each member of that community. this community will be safe if we can keep its external borders well guarded. we can and should expand these frontiers, but it is not the way to protect our community to create barriers within the community. that's a false answer, and that's why (applause) it's going to be such an important task to strengthen frontex not just during these six months. i understand that everyone is worried about the immigration situation, but they are looking for this fake recipe. we must understand them, but at the same time we must take action to prevent europe from re-establishing internal barriers. in the context of the crisis, we also sometimes talk about what to do with one of the most important tools of the european community, which is undoubtedly the european budget. sometimes we question the value of strengthening european institutions. it seems to me that it is extremely important today that we take an open, unhypocritical approach to this dilemma. i am convinced that the answer to the crisis is more europe, there is more european integration (applause), and that requires strong european institutions. i believe this deeply, but this belief is also underpinned by the experience of a whole generation of millions of europeans once on the other side of the old iron curtain. our experience tells us that more europe - which does not mean more ideology, more false philosophy - is a very practical decision. more europe means spending european money wisely, european institutions capable of making decisions, more european policies, more european leadership. without taking up this challenge, we will be increasingly helpless in the face of the global dimensions of the crisis. our experience also tells us that more europe means more freedom, more prosperity, more practical solidarity, more security, in the individual experience of the world. is not a united europe the answer to our experience of the first and second world wars? is not a united europe the best invention here in europe that protects us from ourselves? in our history, we've also created threats to ourselves. an integrated europe of free citizens is also a europe that is secure from within but also from outside threats. (cheers and applause) i know that not everyone shares this view, although i am convinced that everyone, whether they are deeply religious europeans or sceptics, share in common the value system on which a united europe is founded. you can criticize this or that aspect of europe as an institution, but nobody in this room is questioning the meaning of freedom, human rights, democracy, freedom of speech, freedom of religion. and let's just say that this is the place on earth where, even if things don't go our way, the core values that we all agree on are the best protected in the world. it cannot be, and i am deeply convinced that there is growing doubt about its meaning here in europe, and outside europe, as it was 10, 20 years ago, millions of people long to be able to live in the same political, civic, social, economic conditions in which we europeans live. sometimes we stop believing that this is the best place on earth, but everyone outside the european union knows that this is the best place on earth. (cheers and applause) it's not an ideology. so much of our debate is about illegal immigration, which we obviously have to deal with, but let's also note that the direction of this immigration has been the same for decades. never from the european union to the outside, always from the outside to the european union. the people, by their decisions, by their escapes from places where they are either in slavery or poverty or misery, show us every day that europe is truly the best place on earth, that nobody has ever invented anything better. and it's not because god insisted that people here have a better life than people in other parts of the world. the manna does not fall from the sky here, it is better here, because we have persevered in this fundamental fidelity to the fundamental values on which a united europe is based. and remembering where europe's roots are is also a very important foundation for our thinking about the crisis today. we talk about greece a lot. greece is associated by some only with financial problems, with a breach of the rules of financial governance. first of all, let's not look for a scapegoat. let us ask ourselves: were all the others really true to the principles they had set for themselves in their search for ways to combat the crisis? secondly, let us also remember that greece in our european consciousness is not a painful but in fact quite trivial financial problem. i don't disdain them, but they're banal in character. greece is also the experience that taught people and politicians, warring city-states, two and a half millennia ago, what solidarity means in the face of global threat. we are all from there, we would not be in this room, there would be no europe, if once upon a time people, distracted by petty interests, had not met one day and said: we can and must be together when such a challenge arises. so for me, greece is much more pericles than today's demonstrations over budget cuts. i say this because an effective fight against the crisis must be equipped with such historical memory that we know what we are really defending. polish priorities, or rather european priorities for the polish presidency, are part of our conviction that the more europe we have, the less crisis we will have (a europe understood as a guarantor of the values i have mentioned). and that's why we're looking for a europe that's safe in several dimensions. that is why our priority will be to make europe safe, including in the obvious sense of europe's military security. it is high time to start a debate on how europe can respond in a coordinated way to future threats. we are talking about a europe that is secure in terms of energy, food and raw materials. security is the key to understanding the phenomenon of europe. there is a second priority which i very much believe in, the clear progress we want to make in the single market, including the growing market on the internet. freedom, including the removal of further barriers that restrict the development of the free market, can be, as it has been in the past, the source of growth for europe. if europe is not only security but also prosperity, then we must believe anew that the sources of prosperity have always been the same: free enterprise for people, minimum barriers, courage in decision-making, the primacy of the individual over the institution, the primacy of the market over the state, a level playing field for everyone in the economy. and that is why the single market and its development will be our second priority. there is a third thing we want to focus a lot of energy on: open europe. if we can - and i believe we can - build a europe that is safe, well protected, without internal barriers, then we need not fear opening up this europe to others. the next six months are also a breakthrough in negotiations with those who aspire to be in europe. it is a europe open to those who may never be part of our community, but who share the essential values of our community and have shown this in recent months. i'm talking about europe's southern neighbors. the eastern partnership, the completion of the accession process for croatia by signing the treaty, the association agreement with ukraine, and the wise and thoughtful support for those who want democracy and freedom in north africa are tasks which, if done well, can also strengthen the european union itself. the vision we're going to propose is a very practical vision. we want more europe, not just in europe but also on its periphery, if by europe we mean the value system we agreed upon when we founded the european union. i realize that the presidency is only six months, i have no exaggerated ideas about the tools at the disposal of the presidency, i know the lisbon treaty, i do not overestimate the role of individuals in history, although these roles are not to be underestimated. despite the modest tools at the presidency's disposal, despite the time of crisis we are feeling so acutely, i am convinced that we will contribute a lot of polish enthusiasm, polish energy, polish optimism, which has allowed us to get through the crisis quite safely, because we really believe in europe and we want to work with you (applause), by doing these practical tasks, to bring about a reopening of the investment chapter in europe, so that we all believe in europe again. i know it's possible, and i'll be at your service, all of you, for the next six months. i'm looking forward to a good working relationship. thank you, sir.

president of the commission. − mr president, i will make some brief remarks, summarising a debate that i believe was very interesting. first of all, prime minister tusk, you have seen a remarkable consensus from the main political forces of this parliament – what i consider to be the pro-european, responsible forces – supporting your speech and your vision. at the same time, it is interesting that we heard more than usually aggressive remarks from the eurosceptic or europhobe fringes. remarks were made here today which were very close to racism; we also heard xenophobic messages and some expressions of naked, shameless nationalism. why should this be? i think the reason is the following. some of those eurosceptics and europhobes were expecting the enlargement of the european union to mean disintegration, and now they are very disappointed to see poland, a new member of the union, saying not only that we need to enlarge but also that we need to deepen europe, and to listen to your commitment to, and your conviction in, the european project. so, prime minister tusk, congratulations. today you have disappointed the eurosceptics and europhobes – that is one of the outcomes of this debate. (applause) what basically is their message, if they have one, apart from ‘no’? for simply saying ‘no’ to anything constructive is the simplest demagogic message of all populism. their message is that, although they are not necessarily against europe and they believe in european cooperation, they do not need the european institutions, the commission or the european parliament. what they say we need is an internal market: we need a single market. so they say ‘yes’ to the freedom of circulation of goods but ‘no’ to the circulation of people – as if it were possible in europe to have a market without these indispensable principles of freedom. we know well, from the experience we now have – and you know well, prime minister, because we have worked very closely on some difficult issues – that without strong institutions in europe, without a strong commission, a strong european court of justice and a strong european parliament, even the single market will be at risk. the temptation will be present to break the single market, to have internal protectionism, and to return to the naked nationalism that made a disaster of europe’s past. that is why it is important today to reaffirm, as you have reaffirmed, our values. those values are, of course, about an internal single market and about opening our borders, but they are also about solidarity and cohesion, because without solidarity a union cannot exist. some of the eurosceptics say that they are for europe but that they are against the european union. what an interesting nuance! if you go to washington, moscow or beijing, you will find they do not make that distinction: it is europe or it is the european union. it is basically the same thing. if the european union fails, all of europe will be put at risk. that is why we need a strong european union to protect our interests and to protect our values. prime minister tusk, the message you conveyed to this parliament today was a message of confidence in our common future in europe and in the world. we are grateful to you for that and we want to encourage you to have a successful presidency of the council. the commission will support your work because i know that is the way we can build a better future for all europeans. in writing. − in the age of the internet, the question of the protection of personal data is one of the most crucial. consumers expect to know who is using their data and how, and sometimes wish to enjoy ‘the right to be forgotten’ if they do not allow companies to take advantage of their personal data. this is the purpose of the commission’s communication on a ‘comprehensive approach to personal data protection in the eu’, which was followed by an own-initiative report in the parliament. the commission is proposing to revise current legislation on data protection and adjust it to the fast-moving technological and globalised environment created by the use of the internet. against this background, the voss report identifies challenges in the commission revision and calls to the establishment of a harmonized law on data protection that consolidates the diverse rules across the member states. another scoop of this report relates to the geographical coverage on the data protection legislation. accordingly, european companies who operate within and outside europe, as well as international companies who process european citizens’ data, will apply european data protection law. i believe the voss report is a desirable step in guaranteeing further protection of the personal data of eu citizens, therefore i voted in favour of it.
in writing. − the new regulation on food information is a very important instrument for consumers, who will be able to make more informed food purchasing decisions thanks to the new rules. the new rules will make labels more legible. this will no doubt make it easier for consumers to choose the foods they need in their diet. under the new rules, the energy content, fat, saturated fat, carbohydrate, sugar, protein and salt must be clearly indicated on the packaging. the content of the ingredients listed must be given per 100 grams or per 100 ml. in addition, the content of these ingredients may be converted per portion of the product. the labels will also have to contain information on allergenic substances. this is particularly important because of the increasing prevalence of allergies. i hope that with the new regulations, consumers will pay more attention to what they buy. however, i believe that consumers also need information campaigns on the new rules, and in particular on how to read some of the graphic motifs that often appear on food products.

in writing. − the european parliament has just adopted the report by rodi kratsy-tsagaropoulou on women and business leadership, which addresses issues such as promoting corporate social responsibility and women's participation in the workplace. it is worth noting that equality between women and men is one of the main principles of the european union. there are now clear differences in the employment of women, especially in senior positions. women, in the same roles as men, earn less, and looking at the employment statistics for management positions, there is a clear gender imbalance. while the data show that men dominate the top positions on company boards, women are increasingly bravely seeking prestigious, well-paid positions. i am personally in favour of any action to remove these barriers and that is why i voted in favour of the report.
in writing. - i have improved the resolution on women and business management. as a member of the committee on women and equalities, i would like to draw your attention to two issues in particular: 1. significant disparities in the participation of women and men in decision-making bodies. 89% of the members of management and supervisory boards in europe are men. in poland, according to eurostat research, in the third quarter of 2010, women accounted for only 37% of all managers and senior officials in our country. the proportion of women on boards of listed companies and supervisory boards is even lower (around 12% in 2009). in view of these sad statistics, i call on companies and member states (in line with paragraph 1 of the resolution) to take voluntary and rapid action to increase the participation of women at the highest levels. otherwise, i support the commission's proposal to propose eu legislation on this matter. 2. the gender pay gap in management. in poland, according to the national wage survey, men's average pay was over 33% higher than women's. in management positions, the difference was about 25%. the resolution voted on today calls on the member states to take urgent action on this matter. i hope that the polish presidency, during which we are adopting this report, will work towards a solution to this extremely important issue.

in writing. − the economic crisis that has disrupted the european union in recent years has affected not only the financial sphere but also the social sphere. reduced employment, falling incomes and rising prices are problems for every european. the threat to the capital stability of many enterprises has led to the liquidation of many plants and companies, and public debts in some countries have been and continue to be the cause of strikes and demonstrations. that is why the work of the special parliamentary crisis committee is so important. the development of austerity programmes, the development of agreements and the initiation of cooperation with national parliaments, and the coordination of crisis management mechanisms are the commission's main achievements. any action to counter the effects of the crisis to rebalance the market, reduce unemployment and ensure sustainable development is absolutely worth supporting.

vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. − mr president, honourable members, thank you very much again for this agenda item. i think it is important that we take time to reflect on the upcoming russian elections. may i also thank parliament for the resolutions on russia. your resolution of 9 june on the opening day of our most recent eu-russia summit had real impact. of course, russia is a partner with whom i work on a large number of foreign policy issues, but today i want to just focus with you on the upcoming elections. i think a number of decisions have been taken recently in moscow which give us some ideas as to what we can expect in december for the duma elections, and in march 2012 for the presidential poll. russia is already in pre-election mode, with new party alliances and increasing debate. there are some encouraging signs: president medvedev is calling for economic and political modernisation, and finance minister kudrin insists on free and fair elections. at the same time, political pluralism still faces obstacles. as honourable members will be aware, on 22 june, the russian ministry of justice refused to register the new liberal opposition people’s freedom party (parnas). parliament here is of course fully aware of this case; one of the party’s leaders, mr kasyanov, has spoken here several times, and i met briefly with him today in strasbourg. the main reason given for the refusal to register this party was that a few minors, young people and people who were dead had been found among the party’s 46 000 members. another of the party’s leaders, mr ryzhkov, has rejected these claims as false or groundless. but, even if you exclude those people, he would say that the party would still have the required 45 000 members. honourable members know that the earlier political party, the republican party of russia, met a similar fate in 2007, when authorities ordered its dissolution. on 12 april 2011 this year, the european court of human rights in strasbourg ruled that this dissolution was in violation of article 11 of the european convention on human rights. as far as i am aware, the authorities have not yet acted upon this judgment. parnas seems to have been denied registration on the basis of this very same and unchanged law. the court also noted that minimum party membership requirements in russia are the highest in europe. the court was not persuaded that these requirements are necessary, and stressed that small minority groups must also have an opportunity to participate in elections. it said that frequently-changing membership requirements, linked with regular checks, had imposed a disproportionate burden on political parties in russia. i think that ruling should give the russian leadership pause for thought. at the eu-russia summit, we again emphasised the need for political pluralism. president medvedev acknowledges that a focus on too much stability results in stagnation. two weeks ago, he introduced a bill which would lower the threshold for parties to enter the duma from the current 7% to 5% – but, of course, this only applies to the duma elections in 2016. we know that the purpose of democratic elections is to give voters a real choice, and a sense that their vote matters for the outcome. our main contribution is to offer election observation; consultations between russia and osce/odihr are ongoing. russia seems keen to cooperate, and to avoid a repeat of the situation we saw in 2007, when it did not admit any long-term observers. long-term observation is important, in particular to be able to evaluate whether there is fair access to television and other media during the campaign. we received encouraging signals at the summit, and i look forward to a request being sent from moscow to the osce. i am also sure that many honourable members would be interested in participating in this observation. let me close with a few remarks about other human rights and rule of law issues in russia. i believe our partnership for modernisation opens new opportunities for cooperation in this field, and i welcome the joint project with the council of europe on reforming the appeal system for civil and criminal court cases in russia. i also welcome the opening of new forms of dialogue with civil society, in particular the creation of an eu-russia civil society forum. likewise, i welcome president medvedev’s decision to examine the khodorkovsky-lebedev and magnitsky cases. the conclusions of the magnitsky case were presented yesterday, while those on the khodorkovsky and lebedev cases will take more time. let me restate that in their cases, the second verdict was disappointing. to conclude, russia remains an essential partner for the eu and a challenging one. i think there is an interesting debate going on within the country about the modernisation of society and economy, and changing attitudes and expectations will materialise and shape the new realities. the nine months ahead will be very important for russia’s future development. we believe the democratic process must come from within russia. we will continue to build our engagement, we will continue to build on our common interests and we will continue to stand firmly behind our values.

the author. the circumstances in which the indian court found the suspect davinder pal singh guilty of his crimes are not debatable as we recognize that india is a democratic country which has granted the accused the right to a fair trial. the issue at stake is whether to sentence him to death, which has long been a subject of controversy and debate among countries around the world. the european union countries have abolished the death penalty, considering it to be contrary to the values of universal human rights and dignity. the union also continues to work towards the universal abolition of the death penalty in accordance with the resolutions adopted by the united nations general assembly in december 2007, 2008 and 2010, which explicitly call on all states that continue to use the death penalty to take steps to abolish it. in the case of the convicted man davinder pala singh, we europeans can only try to appeal to india, a sovereign and democratic country and an important strategic partner of the union, to refrain from executing this convict and others in the future.

mr. chairman, please! the raw materials policy due to the uneven distribution of resources in the world is prone to monopolisation. this may involve unjustified economic or political demands. the sovereign management and efficient exploitation of the union's raw material resources by the member states is therefore necessary. the extraction of primary raw materials requires energy: in other words, the energy equivalent of the raw materials can be determined as one of the measures of the efficiency of their use. fiscal incentives for raw material production should be the domain of local authorities, responsible for water, land and geological structures. their efficient use allows for the full application of the principle of subsidiarity and a better use of public funds. the union's strategic partnership policy with the russian federation is becoming an important element in improving the balance of not only energy resources. the secondary raw material sourcing through recycling and material substitution is a large reserve which requires a rational investment in research and innovation. the development trend of the union materials engineering is a wider substitution of energy-intensive raw materials and materials by those that meet the criteria of use with lower energy consumption. examples include the use of wooden structures in individual buildings and the use of high-quality ceramics with high resistance to fracture to replace metals in machine construction. an ambitious energy and climate policy cannot be achieved without access to raw materials for materials with special physical and chemical properties, such as rare earths for super magnets or copper, which is a good conductor of heat and electricity.
mr. chairman, please! i thank our commissioner tajani and the rapporteur who have devoted a great deal of time to this really excellent report. today we are dealing with a very important issue: the resources that europe and the world need. we are talking about an effective strategy that will set new directions for both consumption and the sustainable use of our raw materials. natural resources are now the basis of all economies, both global and european, and they affect the quality of our lives. that is why we must ensure that the model of consumption and production that we have today is also of quality for future generations, so that we do not just use and give little to our successors. the high consumption of raw materials also blocks european economies as competitive, as low-carbon and as modern. that's why it's so important to deal with waste, which in large quantities contains very valuable raw materials. the transition to a green economy will require significant investment, but it will also require changes at the socio-economic level. integrated action is also needed in the fields of development of modern technologies, energy, industry and environmental protection. policies and strategies must be geared to reducing emissions of pollutants into the atmosphere in the near future. so it's important that we develop a strategy that is a legacy that we inherited from our fathers and that we pass on to our next generation.

in writing. the oil rig disaster in the gulf of mexico was a terrible memory. it turns out that the great ecological risks on the shelves are rising disproportionately as the difficulty of extracting hydrocarbons from wells in the deeper seas increases. this requires new solutions to better monitor drilling conditions to ensure that uncontrolled oil spills at the bottom of the sea are immediately cut off when pressure is increased. drilling companies must obtain a license from the countries in which they operate. the technical possibilities of 'cutting off' in the event of a sudden pressure jump in the well and full environmental and weather monitoring of the platform operation must be presented at each time. fire safety is necessary, as well as technical and financial security in the event of an emergency. the european union should support scientific research that will enable innovative technical solutions to improve the reliability of offshore drilling platforms.
in writing. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. fellow workers! i know from experience what it's like to be a female entrepreneur, because i ran my own business before i got into politics. i therefore vote with great enthusiasm in favour of the report on promoting female entrepreneurship. we need women in business, and in small and medium-sized enterprises especially. there are many young, well-educated women who are unfortunately unemployed in the labour market. it seems that for some of them, going into business for themselves would be a very good alternative. we need to encourage and help women to take the first steps. they need help in particular in the form of information on potential sources of finance for smes, grants, preferential loans, and the possibilities of using the european progress microfinance instrument. equally important is the training and career counselling for women who lack practical knowledge of how to navigate the legal system, how to find investors, how to create viable business plans. to naturally increase women's interest in self-employment, entrepreneurship should be taught from an early age in schools, which will not only increase the market share of women entrepreneurs but also help to combat the stereotypes that discriminate against women as unable to run their own businesses.
in writing. a group of women whom we call in official documents diplomatically approaching retirement age, or more media-specifically 50+, the polish writer olga tokarczuk once called invisible in society. i am therefore very pleased that next year the 'invisible' will become visible through the european year of active ageing and solidarity between generations. the employment rate of women aged 55 and over in europe is currently too low for the union to achieve the 75% employment target for women and men that we set in the europe 2020 strategy. we're not going to do that if we don't increase the employment of women. in poland, the ministry of labour and social policy is implementing the 'solidarity of generations' programme. it is a government package to increase the employment of people over 50 in our country. it is shocking that in the labour market, women many years younger than men are often considered "old".
in writing. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i have read the draft resolution on the situation of women of pre-retirement age and i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on her report. this is a very important issue, because an increasing number of women over 50 are facing the double problem of age and gender discrimination. increasingly, these are being found in isolated elderly populations. in the light of the facts and statistics presented by the rapporteur, the fact that 2012 has been designated as the european year for active ageing and solidarity between generations should be all the more appreciated. in poland, too, measures are being taken to improve the qualifications of women and enable them to start an active life in old age. in many cities, training is provided for mature women, including computer training, accounting training, and career counselling. given that the proportion of people aged over 65 will increase from 17,4% in 2010 to 30% in 2060, such efforts need to be further intensified, thus enabling every woman to improve her skills and lead an active lifestyle.
in writing. in line with the europe 2020 approach, tackling poverty, discrimination and ageing societies is one of the most important social objectives, while avoiding or reducing intergenerational tensions. this is why it is so important to introduce concrete, long-term solutions in the field of the labour market and the pension system. in many eu countries, this will involve considerable change. the widespread discrimination on grounds of age and sex has meant that only one in three women of pre-retirement age can count on working, often part-time and for a lower salary. often, their good health, willingness and especially their qualifications and skills would allow them to work full-time for many years to come. the rapporteur rightly draws attention to the need for continuing training and the creation of opportunities to acquire new skills in order to remain in the labour market. action is needed to promote flexible forms of employment, which will enable women to reconcile their professional and personal lives. the biggest challenge is to change the attitude of employers towards older people and to end the compulsory retirement age. and let's remember that older people are the most valued, and as research shows, the most loyal employees. especially in the face of the problems of paying benefits guaranteed to citizens in many eu countries, we should see the potential of the 50+ generation.
vice-president of the commission. − madam president, i would like to thank the rapporteur. she has presented a very comprehensive report on something which i believe could be a wonderful alternative to court cases. access to justice is a cornerstone of the european area of justice, but mediation offers an important alternative to going to court in a cross-border dispute, as well as helping us reach to amicable settlements. as the rapporteur so rightly says, it saves time and money and also spares the parties involved in family cases the additional trauma of going to court. ms mccarthy’s report provides a political assessment of the way in which some member states have implemented the provisions of the directive. i agree with the rapporteur that we have to aim for a strict application of the provisions. i am pleased that, through this report, more member states will probably go for a smooth application. the rapporteur is correct that not all member states have put in place measures to transpose the directive. nine countries have not yet notified the national measures needed to fulfil the implementation of the directive. that is why, in july this year, the commission began infringement proceedings by sending letters of formal notice to these nine countries. they have two months to reply. we will follow up these nine cases and also follow up the way in which the other member states have already implemented the directive. we will check the conformity of national implementation. in 2012, i intend to present a communication on the way this directive has been implemented. it will focus on the effect of the directive with regard to the promotion of mediation. i absolutely agree with parliament that it is not enough merely to have a directive: you must make people aware that this possibility exists. i would like to add that nothing in the directive should prevent member states from applying similar provisions to internal mediation processes at home. it is not intended only for cross-border cases – where it is obligatory – but also for national purposes. i would like to thank ms mccarthy, her collaborators and teams and the other parliamentarians very much. the proposal which is on the table is a great help in pushing for mediation to become more popular and more widely taken up.
on behalf of the s&d group. cross-border mediation in legal disputes can only be effective if member states implement the relevant legislation at national level, as the european commission reiterated on 20 august this year, as the implementation of eu mediation rules has not yet been implemented everywhere, despite the deadline of 21 may this year. by promoting and enabling access to alternative justice options in citizens' daily lives, we are providing them with an effective and low-cost tool. the latest studies funded by the european commission estimate that the amount of time lost as a result of not using mediation in disputes is between 331 and 446 days across the union, with the associated additional legal costs per case reaching a ceiling of more than eur 13,5 thousand. in poland, mediation in civil matters was already introduced into the national legal system in july 2005 by the amendment of the code of civil procedure, which is consistent with the directive in terms of the main objectives, method and need to introduce a separate institution of mediation into procedural law. unfortunately, statistics from my country show that mediation in court cases represents only a small percentage of the total number of proceedings. in civil cases, it is estimated that on average only 20 to 40 mediations are carried out per year. the lack of adequate public education and promotion of this relatively new form of justice is hindering its development. most citizens are not aware of mediation and simply do not use it. therefore, in the interest of citizens, member states should intensively develop programmes promoting this form of dispute resolution. the benefits of mediation, both in terms of financial costs and in terms of reducing the burden on the justice system and saving time, are invaluable. finally, i would like to congratulate rapporteur mccarthy on a job well done.
madam president, commissioner, minister, i have to ask you to stop this. i share the rapporteur's and the commission's view that frontex's activities should be based on the principle of solidarity, even if it is mandatory. i am thinking, among other things, of the organisation of european border guards and the transfer of technical resources from the various member states. it is also necessary to cooperate with europol or eurojust and other agencies, as well as to increase activities in countries with poorly functioning asylum systems. in summarising the agency's activities to date and planning its activities for the future, it is necessary to take into account its responsibility for the protection of the union's external borders, but also for the respect of fundamental rights. every effort should be made to enable the agency to fulfil its tasks properly.

in writing. - dual-use products are the result of scientific and technical achievements, the fruits of civilization. the idea behind such products is usually to improve the quality of life, as in the case of chemical and medical products, or to make everyday work and communication easier, for example, as in the case of information technology. however, if misused, they can pose a serious threat to health and life. therefore, the control of exports of dual-use items outside the eu should be as thorough as possible and the standards for its implementation should be as high and rigorous in all member states. inaccuracies in inspection, lack of information on final customers and final use of products can lead to disaster.
in writing. − a vote was held on the amendment of council regulation (ec) no 428/2009 establishing a community system for the control of exports, transfer, brokering and transit of dual-use items. i have supported the complex idea because i believe that control of these products is necessary to prevent the spread of biological, chemical and, most importantly, nuclear weapons. i believe that the european union should speak with one voice and that its position should be supported by the european parliament. in addition, coordination at the level of the european union and its role in the international arena should be improved. in order to achieve those objectives, it is necessary to ensure that member states and the commission establish a system for the collection, transmission and storage of notifications. the commission should also be required to inform the european parliament of the operation of the system and to request an annual report from the coordination group.
in writing. − consumers' demands on the european union market are constantly increasing, not only for the quality of food products, but also for their variety. the agreement between the european union and the swiss confederation will certainly provide greater access to regional products for european union citizens and will also contribute to improving their quality. i believe that this agreement will strengthen trade relations between the two countries and increase the competitiveness of exported products, mainly from the agricultural sector of the european union, by increasing the protection of geographical indications and designations of origin. increased competitiveness and an increase in the quality of exported agricultural products will contribute to the stable and sustainable development of rural areas.
in writing. − the trade agreement with the kingdom of norway should be developed to mutual benefit and the gradual reduction of restrictions on the exchange of agricultural goods. the inclusion in the negotiations of products of a special nature which are important for agricultural production (such as meat or dairy products) is a most welcome initiative which allows the establishment of quotas and customs duties appropriate to market conditions. of course, we cannot predict today what concrete results this agreement will bring in a dozen or so years or decades. however, the progressive liberalisation of agricultural trade with norway has so far resulted in increased exports of agricultural products to the eu, which gives reason for optimism about the future.
in writing. − the audit policy report is a response to the european commission's green paper on the broad audit activity in europe. from the beginning of this report, i was convinced that the far-reaching reduction in the activities of the so-called big four audit firms could also have negative effects on the industry as a whole. i am glad that it has not gone in the direction of witch-hunting and finding the culprits of the current financial crisis. i believe that it is far more constructive to seek new and improve existing auditing standards than to blame the failure of global financial markets primarily on the activities of audit firms. i am also pleased that the report reflects the demands of the audit industry, which is not always flattering and which itself feels the need to make some changes. we should continue to insist on the independence of those who carry out audits of the financial situation of companies, which is a challenge not only for auditors but also for the supervisory boards of the companies audited. i would also like to emphasise that the report provides a balanced and balanced assessment of the activities of audit firms, while also highlighting the opportunities for the smaller firms in this sector to develop more fully and participate more in the market and to increase their competitiveness.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the report as it touches upon one of the most significant social problems europe is facing today – the ageing population. low birth rate on one side, and growing healthy long-lived pensioners on the other, may create a problem for us with a view to ensuring sustainable pensions in the future. to prevent such a catastrophic scenario, the report examines the proportions of older women in the labour market, and suggests that maintaining their employment, instead of enforcing compulsory retirement, could prove to be a remedy to many economic and social problems. i am very much in favour of such a strategy. while many citizens today view the ageing population as a burden on society, i believe that proper management and integration of older labour can certainly prove the opposite.
in writing. − most eu countries are facing not only the problem of an ageing population but also the increasing unemployment of women over 50. the occupational position of these women on the labour market is much less favourable than that of men of the same age, which often results in early retirement. providing older women with better access to education, care and addressing the negative perception of their labour market opportunities could lead to a significant increase in their labour market participation. a number of options can be considered to avoid the situation where older women are faced with the consequences of pension benefits for having given up their professional activities to provide unpaid care. i also welcome the inclusion in the document of the issue of women in caring roles. in the context of the many thousands of polish women working in this profession illegally in other eu countries or, having given up their professional careers, doing it without pay in their own homes, action to prevent their future poverty and social exclusion is necessary.
in writing. - europe is in a difficult demographic situation. this is particularly true of the ageing of the population and the decline in population. unfortunately, the pension system and the labour market suffer. we should therefore pay more attention to the benefits of employing people who are approaching retirement age. there are many benefits to this. above all, a senior employee has a wealth of knowledge and experience, and he or she feels very satisfied because he or she can feel appreciated and needed. sadly, older people are often discouraged from working or even sent into early retirement. more should therefore be done to activate them. women are particularly vulnerable, as their potential is often under-exploited. in later life, they take on the role of caregivers for grandchildren or the elderly, thus excluding them from the labour market. in order to make better use of the advantages of women as workers, they should be allowed to remain in the labour market as long as possible. this requires special programmes to support older women to be able to work freely in the labour market, to the benefit of society as a whole.
in writing. − on 13 september 2011, a vote was held on the situation of women of pre-retirement age. it was adopted by a majority of votes. i supported the motion for a resolution because i believe that older people are an invaluable source of cultural, professional and social wealth. the 2020 strategy aims to reduce poverty and increase employment to 75%, but the employment rate for women aged 55-64 is only 37.8% and for men 54.8%. i think that we should create training and develop the skills of older women, which will help them find work. it should be noted that women's careers are often interrupted or curtailed and their earnings are much lower than men's. women are at high risk of poverty, exclusion and social exclusion because their working lives are much shorter. women are often not active in the workforce because of their domestic duties, and therefore have no chance of receiving pension benefits later on. the right changes in approach to the problem of ageing can have a positive impact on economic and social policies.
in writing. - i supported the report on the situation of women approaching retirement age. age is the most common reason for not getting a job these days. graduates are too young, too inexperienced, and the rest of the population is usually too old. the situation of the elderly is particularly difficult. people approaching 50 years of age have limited chances of finding employment on the polish labour market. at the end of december 2009, 391 672 people over 50 years of age were registered with polish employment offices. this represents 20.7% of the total unemployed. older women are particularly vulnerable. this group is characterised by low levels of employment. more than half of women of pre-retirement age remain outside the labour market. given that by 2020 people over 60 will represent more than 26% of the population, reintegrating older people into the labour market is one of the key tasks in the professional activation of disadvantaged groups in employment. i therefore wanted to draw particular attention to paragraph 10 of the report, in which parliament calls on the commission and the member states to create the conditions for older women to remain in the labour market or to re-enter it, and to help them to fulfil their professional potential and to respect their rights. at the same time, measures should be introduced to encourage employers to improve equal opportunities policies in order to eliminate discriminatory attitudes towards older women.
in writing. − it is not often that, despite the different models adopted in national systems, we can commend member states for implementing an eu directive. mediation as an institution is already widely recognised in national legislation, but we need to ensure that the letter of the law is alive and has a wide practical application. i believe that the current efforts of both the member states and the eu institutions should be directed towards promoting the mediation instrument among european citizens and businesses, as they are often unaware of the possibility of using mediation, do not fully understand its principles and fear that the outcome of such negotiations will not be legally binding. therefore, a campaign for mediation should emphasise that it is a fast, cheap and professional way of resolving disputes. the position and perception of the mediator is crucial. he must be a person of public trust, his neutrality and independence must be confirmed by the creation of codes of ethics and provisions in the law. the quality of mediation itself should also be based on the consolidation of good practices and standards, which, as the report shows, are already beginning to yield good results and confirm the assumption that mediation can be effective and, beyond the obvious benefit to the parties, can relieve the burden of overcrowded courts in the future.
in writing. − the eu's raw materials strategy is designed to ensure that europe has stable supplies of key raw materials for european industry, such as copper, at a time when the raw materials market is becoming increasingly competitive and raw materials, in particular rare earths, are available in few, often undemocratic, countries. in an increasingly globalised world, europe must take steps to ensure the security of its raw materials. this can be done by making better use of indigenous raw materials and, where this is not possible, security should be sought through appropriate international agreements. i believe that this report is a step in the right direction, but it must be followed by concrete action.

on behalf of the s&d group. as previous rapporteur on better lawmaking, subsidiarity and proportionality last year, i paid particular attention to the issue of transparency and citizens' understanding of legislation and to ex post evaluation, i.e. the careful monitoring of what happens to eu law after it has been adopted. i therefore support the report's demands to assess the impact of legislation, to correct its irregularities and to replicate successful initiatives, to focus on simplifying eu legislation and to refrain from drawing up legislation unless it is needed in a specific situation. however, i am still opposed to the rapporteur's proposed 'one in, one out' rule, which provides that new legislation can only be introduced if some previous legal arrangements are removed. it's just not practical. the reduction of administrative burdens and the simplification of the law must not lead to a lowering of the standards provided for in the applicable legislation. i believe that more action and ambition are needed if the target of reducing administrative burdens by 25% by 2012 is to be achieved. it is also worth remembering the regulation on the european citizens' initiative, which entered into force on 1 april 2011 and thus opened up the possibility for ordinary citizens to participate in the creation of better legislation. we need to take all of this into account if we want to see real change and improvement in the way we make good and understandable legislation. finally, i would like to congratulate and thank the rapporteur for a job well done.
ladies and gentlemen! when we talk about better lawmaking, we must first of all remember that it all starts here, in the eu institutions, and therefore also in the european parliament. we can and of course should draw the attention of the member states to delays, incorrect or complicated supplementary provisions in the implementation of individual directives or the imposition in national legislation of requirements which are more restrictive than those actually contained in community regulations. but first, we need to look at the parts of the legislative process that we can improve ourselves to make the law that comes out of this house better. the smart regulation that mr karim talks about in his report is no longer just clear and legible legislation, it is legislation that is based on rigorous and independent impact assessments that are consulted with all stakeholders. the situation of smes operating on the union market is a particularly striking and frequently cited example. the importance of these small businesses for the development of the common market and the european economy cannot be overstated. yet it is these individuals, these entities, that continue to suffer from a degree of legislative ignorance, continue to face excessive costs and administrative burdens, and continue to be too rarely considered in the legislative process, despite the call of the small business act. we're still discussing the financial crisis that is plaguing europe. however, it seems that this is the last moment to stop just discussing the need to improve the legal environment for smes and micro-enterprises, and to put these rules into practice. we all make mistakes, but let's learn from our mistakes.

member of the commission. − madam president, given the strange and precarious conditions which many people are living and working under, it is not surprising that homelessness is increasingly in the homelessness existed before, and the crisis just aggravated this situation in a number of member states. there is, however, also a growing understanding of what is needed to tackle it. the member states need to continue developing national or regional plans for action to deal with homelessness along the lines identified in the 2010 joint report on social protection and social inclusion. of course, the member states are responsible for much of what needs doing, but the eu can encourage and support the member states in their efforts – for example, by helping to improve our understanding tackle homelessness. the european regional development fund provides funding for social housing for marginalised communities, and should continue to do so in the future. the european social fund provides support for the social and labour market reintegration of homeless people. we are currently drawing up the post-2013 financial framework. in this connection, gearing cohesion policy funding to meeting the europe 2020 headline targets, including for reducing poverty, is vital. the european consensus conference identified possible avenues and we are following them – for example, improving knowledge and monitoring, applying housing-led approaches, and promoting innovation and experimentation. similarly, parliament’s declaration of 16 december 2010 on an eu homelessness strategy highlights a number of priorities, including the need for better statistics. the commission is actively engaged in work at eu level. preventing and tackling homelessness is an important aspect of work to tackle social exclusion and poverty under the europe 2020 strategy. it is also a key area of work under the european platform against poverty and social exclusion, which covers areas highlighted at the consensus conference. we have just commissioned a new study on the links between homelessness and migration. we are continuing our work on homelessness indicators in conjunction with the social protection committee. we have promoted social innovation based on housing-led approaches which we would like to see applied more widely. what matters now is putting all our energy and resources into carrying out the tasks identified at eu level so we get results quickly, rather than introducing new procedures or steering structures in the form of high-level groups or committees. last month, i met key stakeholders to talk about how to step up our work on homelessness and what framework would help ensure that enough attention and energy are put into doing what is needed. this dialogue continues and will also be followed up by action.

madam president! the problem of homelessness remains unsolved in europe. the characteristics of the homeless population are also changing. the stereotypical homeless person used to be a middle-aged man, but now young women, victims of violence and immigrants are increasingly homeless. the most visible and extreme form of homelessness is street homelessness, although it can take other forms as well. this phenomenon has a negative impact on entire societies and, despite the efforts of the member states, action at union level is necessary. not only do member states have different definitions of homelessness, but they also use different methods of collecting and presenting data. therefore, in order to create a common framework for the union to support and monitor the member states' efforts to develop strategies to combat homelessness, it is necessary to address these problems. that is why i would like to ask the commission a few questions today. the european consensus conference on homelessness last december divided the causes of homelessness into many categories, which arise from different backgrounds. in its work on the strategy, will the commission propose solutions that take account of the different circumstances that lead people to homelessness? does the commission intend to involve ngos in the work on the strategy? how would the commission like to involve ngos in the fight against homelessness beyond the activities they already carry out as part of their statutory tasks? how does the commission intend to measure the effectiveness of the strategy once it is in place, given that the situation of homeless people varies across the member states?
madam president! one of the five objectives of the new eu strategy europe 2020 is to lift 20 million people out of poverty in the european union. the 2009 poverty figures are alarming: 113 million people are at risk of poverty and social exclusion. this situation is so worrying that it may worsen due to the economic and financial crisis. homelessness is a very drastic form of poverty, and worse, it's hereditary, making it harder to fight and prevent. i welcome all the work of the european parliament, which has placed particular emphasis on combating this phenomenon. the initiatives so far have set out clearly defined demands for the prevention and eradication of homelessness, including the elimination of street homelessness by 2015 and the fight against its causes through adequate housing and social policies. the success of the strategy to tackle homelessness at european level will depend on how the commission fulfils its role of mobilising member states as soon as possible to develop effective and comprehensive strategies to tackle and respond to homelessness. the success of the project will also depend to a large extent on the openness to working with people affected by homelessness, ngos and other social partners. the creation of an effective policy against homelessness is therefore dependent on interinstitutional cooperation and the proper and effective implementation of existing legal acts. only a common political vision and the commitment of the european union and the member states can contribute to the full achievement of the europe 2020 objectives.
in writing. ladies and gentlemen! homelessness is a serious problem. we should be using best practices in the fight against homelessness. we must do this because human dignity and its protection is one of the fundamental values of the european union. fortunately, we have many examples of successful work with the homeless. it should not only be done by ngos, but perhaps above all by local authorities. in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, local authorities should not and cannot avoid this problem. i therefore encourage local authorities, including in my home town of poznań, to treat the issue of homelessness with due care and seriousness. after all, the goal of all politics, at all levels, is to serve the common good, to serve the people. and who is more in need of public assistance than someone who, for whatever reason, is on the street? let's keep that in mind. thank you very much. thank you.
