the next item is the report drawn up by mrs deborah serracchiani, on behalf of the committee on transport and tourism, on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the creation of a single european railway area (recast) (com (2010) 0475 - c7-0268/2010 - 2010/0253 (cod)) (a7-0367/2011).
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur and her colleagues for all their good and very intensive work and welcome the progress made by this parliament to reach a compromise on this complex piece of legislation. the commission will present its work programme for 2012 tomorrow. i have already confirmed on several occasions my intention to propose further substantial reform in the rail sector next year. let me be clear at the outset that i do not seek change for change’s sake, but rather because we need to strengthen rail to ensure it offers attractive services, capable of playing a substantial role in the transport of the future. but rail will only fulfil its potential if rail companies are innovative, cost-efficient and forward-looking. although the commission has been seeking this for the past two decades, change has been very slow. so next year’s package will revitalise the process, with proposals to open domestic passenger markets and review related public service obligation rules, with further structural change to ensure fair competitive conditions for newcomers and a refinement of the rules on standards and certification of rolling stock to make the approvals process quicker and more cost-effective. completion of work on the current proposal, the recast, is a precondition for the 2012 package. i am fully aware that discussions in both council and parliament proved to be difficult and subject to intense lobbying from various stakeholders. they demonstrated that rail remains a conservative sector. in some cases, some of the principles and rules already agreed ten years ago have been challenged in an attempt to undermine ongoing infringement procedures. let us be clear: the status quo – or even worse, backward steps – is not an option! a large majority of the 133 amendments adopted by the committee on transport (tran) are acceptable to the commission, even though in some cases subject to certain redrafting. however, let me draw your attention to the fact that some specific amendments voted in tran and others now tabled to the plenary would substantially weaken the commission proposal. these amendments would be a step backward compared to the text agreed by council and even compared to existing law, which is not acceptable for the commission. let me insist on some of these: first, the issue of separation between infrastructure managers and railway undertakings will be subject to new proposals at the end of 2012 and therefore all amendments in relation to articles 6 and 7 are premature. the new provisions on separation of accounts are contrary to the principle of financial transparency and (at least as drafted) extremely difficult for the regulators to control. the result would be that state money paid to support the infrastructure could instead leak to an incumbent train operator, giving it an unfair competitive advantage – and at the same time diminishing the funds available for investment by infrastructure managers. secondly, debt write-off by member states can only relate to so-called historical debt incurred before market opening. thirdly, the recast proposal does not modify the fundamental principles of infrastructure charging; it simply clarifies how these principles must be applied. new exemptions to infrastructure charging cannot be justified by any objective criteria. fourthly, national regulators must have the possibility to fulfil their oversight functions, including for cross-border traffic, and prevent problems. fifthly, experience shows that the competence of national regulators must be extended. however, some amendments would restrict their interventions to cases of discrimination and impede interventions to correct other undesirable distortions of the market. sixthly, amendments 126 and 127 are problematic. the first would undermine the direct cost charging principle; the second would put an unnecessary administrative burden on infrastructure managers. seventhly, amendments restricting or removing powers for the commission to adopt delegated or implementing acts often relate to non-essential elements. we need to make technical adjustments which practically should not be done in co-decision. i also need to draw your attention to the 2001 interinstitutional agreement on recasting. this agreement establishes a discipline to guarantee interinstitutional equilibrium, the right of initiative of the commission and the right to make use of recasting as a key instrument for better law-making. thank you for your attention.
we'll discuss that in a moment. it is a remark which concerns the merits of our case. our discussions are designed to address these issues.
i welcome the view expressed by the rapporteur, debora serracchiani, and by saïd el khadraoui, who assess the delays in the creation of a common economic area for rail transport in europe. we have examples of countries, including my own country, where the railway is rapidly deteriorating: technically, operationally and organizationally. i therefore welcome the commission's initiative to make rail more european. it is important that railways in the union have good access to their eastern neighbours, which have a wider track gauge and a different railway edge. there is an amendment by a group of meps to facilitate this integration by separating one section of the broad gauge railway from russia and ukraine to katowice in poland. the aim is to remove only certain articles from the regulation. i ask you to support this amendment.
i would like to congratulate congresswoman serracchiani on a very good job. for the past few months, the transformation of the first rail package has been the main and perhaps the most difficult dossier in the committee on transport and tourism. the agreement reached by the commission, through a series of compromise amendments, reflects the determination of all political groups. we all want to travel by rail in comfortable conditions, to travel safely and as quickly as possible, and to be able to buy a single ticket for connections provided by different operators at the same ticket office when travelling to the station. we are determined to achieve this goal. but we must remember and be careful not to make any mistakes. in the pursuit of free competition in the railway market, we must bear in mind that in some member states there are self-financing railway lines which do not connect to the national and european network, which are of purely industrial importance and whose width is different from the dominant one. the need to apply to those detached lines all the provisions of the directive, including unbundling, would impose disproportionate and irrational burdens and would distort and misrepresent the purpose for which they were built. i therefore ask you to support amendment no 135 tabled by myself, mr marcinkiewicz, the ecr group, and signed by several dozen donkeys from various political groups and different member states, when we vote on wednesday.
madam president! the railway package adopted in 2001 was intended to integrate the railway sector and make it more attractive than other modes of transport. unfortunately, despite the passing of 10 years, despite the favourable conditions, the european rail sector has not been able to develop. while road transport is growing and moving across borders is not a problem, rail freight as well as rail passenger transport faces many legal, technical and political obstacles. this shows how difficult it is to create a single railway area and a better, more passenger-friendly and simplified rail policy. however, we must bear in mind that any solution to this problem must take account of the different systems of governance of the sector in the various countries of the european union and the different levels of development and quality of the railway infrastructure. at the same time, we cannot afford to waste the huge potential of this sector, which unfortunately is not being exploited properly.
in writing. in the context of tomorrow's vote on the revision of the first railway package, i wanted to highlight some important aspects that could play a key role in the future of rail in the eu. in some member states there are some lines with a different track gauge from the basic track gauge, which are a relic of the old post-soviet system, where these lines are not part of the national and union railway system. this type of line was deliberately built for regional needs, taking into account the transport of goods from third countries. the length of the line and the traffic on it usually do not play any role in the train-per-kilometre ratio when considering national transport. member states should therefore be able to exclude from the application of the directive those lines and the carriers operating them. so, with the help of congressman arthur rule, i've introduced amendment 135, which is the one that solves the problem i mentioned.
madam president! the free movement of people and workers within the european union is one of the key benefits of integration. in the period following the economic and financial crisis, we should particularly support the mobility of european union citizens, so that we can respond more quickly and effectively to the demands of the labour markets in the member states. despite the fact that freedom of movement and of employment in the member states has long been a core value of the union, citizens still face many barriers and obstacles resulting from the different national conditions and legislative arrangements. currently, only 2% of union citizens work in a member state other than their own. the willingness to work in another country is about 20%, which shows us that we are dealing with untapped potential. the recognition of professional qualifications remains one of the barriers to freedom of movement within the union. this requires an urgent revision of the current directives, but also the appropriate and rapid implementation of the new rules in the member states. the new rules should be based on simplified procedures, good information, a reduction in the number of regulated professions and the introduction of greater automation in the recognition of professional qualifications. only in this way will we encourage greater mobility and guarantee the fundamental right to work freely in the european union. the issue of recognition of professional qualifications is only one element of the long-term and comprehensive strategy for mobility that europe needs to ensure sustainable growth. the elimination of all existing legal and administrative obstacles to the free movement of workers should be a priority for the commission, the council and the european parliament in the coming months.
madam president! i would like to congratulate the rapporteur very much because today's debate on the recognition of professional qualifications is meeting the expectations of the people of the european union. enabling citizens to have their qualifications recognised in a member state other than the one in which they obtained their professional qualifications and the benefits of a competitive european internal market are important factors in stimulating economic growth and creating new jobs in the european union. if we are talking about the free movement of people and goods, if we are talking about the internal market, then today's report showing the need for the european commission to prepare the relevant legislation is an important support for thousands of young people who want to work in another country of the european union. we can only hope, especially for all the citizens of the european union, that the necessary legal solutions will be implemented as soon as possible. the commissioner's question is: how long will it take for the citizens of europe to implement these relevant rules?
in writing. facilitating the free movement of skilled workers across the european union is not just a right enshrined in the treaties as a result of the nature of the single market. this is primarily an economic need that must be addressed as soon as possible, given that we will need as many as 16 million highly skilled workers by the end of 2020. in order for the mobility of these workers to really bring about economic recovery, we must make it easier for them to take up employment and set up their own businesses in a country of their choice, where their knowledge and skills are needed. to this end, national rules that create unnecessary barriers and obstacles should be reviewed. in my view, although i realise that this would be complicated, harmonising vocational training legislation at eu level could be a good solution. it is also important that relevant information is easily accessible to interested parties. i therefore call on the european commission to consolidate the information sources already available so that people wishing to set up a business in a country other than their own can have access to the necessary documents and information on the relevant sectoral authorities in their own language.

almost halfway through the current term of the european parliament, we should have the courage to ask ourselves where europe is heading, to what extent we are achieving the ambitious goals of the europe 2020 strategy, and whether we see any real prospect of getting out of the prolonged financial crisis affecting many member states of the union. we must remember that in times of instability and when people feel threatened by the inability to meet basic needs, populist movements often emerge with extreme slogans of change. we must not underestimate the "movement of the outraged", which for now has the form of an idealistic opposition of young people without real prospects for creative development and decent work, but in the future it may become the seed of a serious political force, but what kind of face? we cannot ignore the irresponsibility of some politicians who have forced their lives on credit, their lives at the expense of future generations, making unrealistic promises in exchange for maintaining power, even using the hiding or modifying of the real situation. even the brussels administration, famous for its meticulousness, failed to control the individual member states effectively, accepting the dangerous increase in budget deficits and debt.
demographic change is a problem for many countries and regions. in europe, we have low natural growth, a high percentage of people, mostly young people, migrating from rural areas to large, wealthy cities. the author of the report considers that structural policy in particular has to face the serious challenges of demographic change and identifies six priorities in this regard. i'll focus on three. first, the structural funds must be better adapted to the challenges of demographic change. the breakdown of the structural funds by region should take into account demographic indicators. secondly, as regards infrastructure, the rapporteur sees a serious challenge for both rural and urban areas. the outflow of the population and the isolation of the elderly should be prevented. urban planning also needs to be adapted accordingly. cities and municipalities must be attractive to their inhabitants, including through child and family-friendly infrastructure and good local public transport. one of the main factors in addressing the demographic challenge is the increase in the number of women in employment. we must also combat youth unemployment.
i welcome the vote today on the report on the european platform against poverty and social exclusion. i hope that the common legal basis will contribute to better coordination and increase the effectiveness of the measures to combat poverty and help those most in need. especially in difficult times of crisis, which will most affect the poorest people, often without savings and without greater prospects, we must focus our attention on those who are in the most difficult situation. in the search for budgetary savings, national governments tend to reduce spending on social assistance, which further aggravates the situation of these people. the report by frédéric daerden is particularly relevant in its proposal to create a basket of basic goods and services that would be available to everyone. this would guarantee the minimum necessary for each person and would allow for a dignified existence. at the same time, such a project must be accompanied by measures to create jobs, including for low-skilled people, and an appropriate social housing policy. the goals we set for ourselves in the europe 2020 strategy are ambitious but achievable. if we follow the theory, written on paper, with the actual actions of our governments, in cooperation with social organizations, we have a chance to reduce the number of people who are left on the margins of society.

in writing. - ladies and gentlemen! i fully support the initiative to update the bankruptcy regulation of 29 may 2000. since its entry into force, a lot has changed, with 15 new countries joining the union and the phenomenon of company groupings becoming extremely intense. from today's perspective, the solutions proposed in the regulation of 11 years ago seem anachronistic. particular attention should be paid to the need to establish a clear definition of the debtor's centre of main interest (comi) in order to correctly identify the jurisdiction for insolvency proceedings. the misinterpretation of the term comi is a source of confusion in the bankruptcy of foreign companies. the location of the comi determines the jurisdiction of the court to open insolvency proceedings. the main factor determining location is the identification of the place where the debtor's business is managed and whether it is recognisable as a place of business for third parties. here difficulties may arise (when a foreign court) declares the bankruptcy of a company from another country, and considers that this company has a comi in another member state because the company is controlled by a company in that member state. the european court of justice tried to resolve this dilemma in a judgment of 2 may 2006 (europood ifsc limited), but unfortunately this did not resolve the problem completely, which confirms the need for a clearer definition. i also stress the need to interpret the regulation in line with directive 2008/94/ec on the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of a company. member states should not undermine the rights of workers in insolvency proceedings. i support the proposal to introduce a creditors' ranking in which priority would be given to employees with at least minimum standards of protection, regardless of the different national legal definitions.

in writing. 2012 is the european year of older people's activity and solidarity between generations. the commission's programme must include a strategy for active ageing. the number of older people will increase markedly in all eu member states over the coming decades. by 2050, the number of people over 65 is projected to increase by 70% and those over 80 by 170%. the elderly, as a growing social group, have relatively low incomes. many of them are among the 16% of the eu population who live below the poverty line, have difficulty finding employment and housing, and have limited access to basic services, especially health and social services. according to the gus, there are about 6.4 million elderly people in poland, which represents about 17% of the country's population. by 2035, this group is projected to represent some 27% of the total population. at the same time, the average number of people of working age in the eu is projected to decline. this creates two main challenges and objectives for the commission's work in 2012: adapting healthcare to the needs of an ageing population and ensuring that it is as long-lasting and effective as possible.

period until 2015. official development assistance will continue to play a key role also as a complement to and catalyst for other sources of financing. however, it is not limited to development the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the joint parliamentary assembly is an important element of democratic cooperation with the acp countries. due to the regularity and quality of its work, it has managed to establish itself as an indispensable actor in north-south cooperation. we want the european union's cooperation with the acp to be a partnership, and this assembly is succeeding in doing so. our partners are the akp mps. two meetings of the joint parliamentary assembly took place in 2010: the 19th session in adopted. in the same year, a regional meeting was also held in seychelles. in addition, a working group on the assembly's working methods was set up in 2010 to strengthen its political role and improve the efficiency of its activities. the commissioner responsible for development, mr piebalgs, was present. the co-presidents of the acp-eu council also attended the first meeting, but only the acp council was represented in kinshasa. the absence of the council of the european union from the question time was regrettable and the assembly decided to convey its regrets to catherine ashton, while urging her to avoid a similar situation at future sessions. i am glad that this matter has been resolved and at the next assembly in lomé, notabene next week, with mrs ashton's agreement the council will be represented by minister stanowski. the assembly's standing committees met four times: twice during plenary sessions and twice in brussels between sessions. i would remind you that the committee's main task is to draw up reports which are then adopted by the plenary. in addition, committees are responsible for following up resolutions by interviewing the european commission officials responsible for the field. it also provides an opportunity for a deeper dialogue on the follow-up to resolutions adopted. the economic development, finance and trade committee has been given the additional task of checking regional strategy papers for the acp regions. this committee appointed co-rapporteurs for each regional strategy paper, and the proposals for these documents were adopted at the tenerife meeting. the european commission submits national and regional strategic documents to parliamentary scrutiny, both here in the european parliament and in the parliaments of the acp states. the development committee and the joint parliamentary assembly should monitor the situation in this regard and ensure that this parliamentary oversight tool is used properly. the assembly also plays an important role in monitoring the negotiations on economic partnership agreements. the hearings with the main negotiators from both sides, meetings with business and civil society representatives and the dialogue between meps and those from the global south have helped to make the process more transparent and to better address local issues. in 2010, the european commission and the acp states negotiated a second revision of the cotonou partnership agreement. the revision envisages an increased role for the parliamentary assembly in the scrutiny of the other institutions, as well as the regionalisation of the acp group as a result of the economic partnership agreements (epas) process. the joint parliamentary assembly should follow these developments closely, as their consequences will determine the future of the assembly itself. these are the elements i have tried to include in my report. thank you very much. thank you.

mr president, it is telling and symbolic that this debate, which is supposed to be on economic governance, is on the eurozone in the absence of the president of the council. are we already in the two-tier europe? do we need, as pervenche berès proposes, a separate parliament for the eurozone? the present crisis is not a crisis of the euro as a currency – it is a healthy currency. it is a crisis of excessive indebtedness. dividing lines, if unavoidable although deplorable, should not go between the 17 and the 10. they do appear, de facto, between macroeconomically healthy and unhealthy countries. it would be fatal to institutionalise a smaller club within the bigger club. that would lead to unravelling and undoing the reunification of the continent, creating disunion in place of the union. for those left outside, it would be unfair and unacceptable to be ‘sort of’ expelled and then obliged to re-enter, for the second time, the true, so-called core europe. a split union will not work. a spread union will not work, but will further disintegrate creating divergent levels of solidarity. a split union would make the crisis deeper. the only answer is more convergence and more community method. we should say no to this two-speed europe. many non-eurozone member states are much more in the de facto first speed when it comes to growth, fiscal discipline and reform – my country poland included – than some eurozone member countries. moreover, they are, with two exceptions, committed and obliged – no derogation, as you said – to join the eurozone. should that lead to institutionalising a ‘euro- and economically healthy member states’ group also? certainly not. that would be against our principles of unity and solidarity. the answer is centrifugal euro plus. it equals 23 at least. eurozone summits, president van rompuy, should precede – not follow – eu summits.
mr. chairman, please! i think that there is something missing in this debate that would make us more trustworthy with the citizens of the european union. what am i talking about? well, we talk about the crisis in europe, but we talk about it as if it fell from the sky, as if it were part of some natural disaster, and yet you can trace the successive elements of mistakes that were made and that led to the crisis that we have today. if we want this crisis to be a new beginning, a better start for europe, then for the sake of our credibility, we must be honest about what parts of our design have failed. and that does not mean euroscepticism, it does not mean denying the european union. on the contrary, admitting mistakes will only enhance your credibility. i hope that this crisis will be an opportunity to build a europe that is more. but the question is: what does 'more europe' mean? does that mean more bureaucracy, more regulation and therefore less competition, does that mean more europe with a larger free and common market?
i listened with great interest to both president barroso's speeches and those made on behalf of the council by mr van rompuy and president juncker. i would like to say first of all that there seems to be a consensus in this house on one thing, namely that the proposed solutions which we are adopting, which are of a preventive and coordinating nature, with regard to credit rating agencies and short they address the root of the problem and solve problems for the future. we really need more ambitious actions and this base is just a prelude to that. the key today is to strive for real convergence, because only under such conditions can economic and monetary union develop effectively in the long term. community regulations must promote real convergence, otherwise we will simply drift, unable to develop and compete on world markets. convergence is first and foremost a common market, which guarantees our competitiveness on the world market. one point directed to mr van rompuy, if the president will allow it: the euro is not the property of the eurozone countries. the euro is a value that is important to all of us. the impact of the euro and its stability on the economies of member states which benefit, let me remind you, from a temporary derogation is often no less important, or just as important, as for the euro area countries. that's why we have to make decisions about this together. we must take them, mr president, by the community method, with all the countries. this is because, although the community method does not work very quickly and often breaks down on the particularism of the member countries, the intergovernmental method has built us a euro zone without a common fiscal policy, without a common tax policy. it is the intergovernmental method that has built us an imperfect, or far from perfect, monetary system. the community method, on the other hand, guarantees that if we adopt certain rules, they will apply to all of us, not just the weakest. because today we can ask ourselves, if we had a weak government in germany or in paris, for example, would we be able to change it through outside pressure? or not? thank you very much, sir.
in writing. in the context of the deepening crisis, which europe is experiencing today in particular, the overriding objective should be to take joint action to stabilise european economies and to better coordinate anti-crisis measures. discussions on how to do this effectively are often accompanied by concerns that the introduction of new economic governance rules in the eu could lead to a two-speed union. they are not without foundation, but the fact is that we already have two communities: the one that brings together the countries with the common currency, the euro, and the more political one, made up of all 27 member states. it is clear to me that countries with a single currency must have the instruments to conduct a common fiscal and monetary policy, and the means to enforce discipline in both areas. accession to the euro area entails shared responsibility for the single currency. it is therefore clear to me that membership of the euro area must be linked to acceptance of the rules of common economic governance. for your own good and for the good of all.

in writing. the eu is responsible for only 11% of the world's co2 emissions. over the last dozen years, we've been reducing our greenhouse gas emissions every year while expanding our renewable energy sector. the costs of such changes are enormous for us, as scientists from the e. kwiatkowski institute have calculated. in poland alone, a 20% reduction in emissions means a loss of about 5% of jobs in heavy industry and energy caused by the relocation or closure of plants. we didn't look to other international actors when we decided on the next limits, whereas in recent years the us, china, india and brazil have not only not reduced their emissions, but they've actually increased them. now it's finally time to realize that even if europe, hypothetically, stopped emitting greenhouse gases, it still wouldn't make a difference to the world's climate. today, the warming process can only stop a 50% decline in emissions in china and india. i cannot understand the wording of this resolution that encourages an increase in the emission limit above 20%. that's why i voted against it.

in writing. internet service providers are service companies, just like water and gas suppliers. companies like this shouldn't tell me that the water in the kitchen will run faster than the water in the bathroom, or that the light in the bedroom will be half as bright as the light in the hallway. the supplier is responsible for the operation of the pipes and cables, and the consumer is responsible for deciding whether to use them. the content of the internet should be equitable and equally accessible. the role of the supplier here is to impose a financial burden on the user in a manner appropriate to the way in which he has used the services. if the supplier wants to offer an unlimited tariff plan and the consumer is willing to pay for it, then everything is fine. however, this unlimited plan must actually have no limitations. we all know that from time to time, we may experience a power outage or a water outage as a result of an accident or maintenance. sometimes the internet is slower than usual. but this should be the exception, not the rule. internet services and content security must be unbreakable. just as it is in europe, we cannot afford two-speed internet.

on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur for a job well done. the integrated maritime policy is an action that concerns many areas of the european union's economy. it is also a cultural heritage area and a part of the social consciousness. the report is of such importance that it needs special attention from the european commission. the lack of clear and comprehensive regulations on the maritime economy in the european union is one of the reasons for the collapse of the industry. you have to ask yourself: why are most of the ships built outside the european union? why do companies register their vessels outside the eu? why is it that the job of a sailor or a fisherman is so completely unattractive? there are many more questions to be answered if we are to take the maritime economy seriously. in the absence of good and friendly law, another industry will be lost to the far eastern countries that have created a favorable environment for the development of the maritime industry. this is a blow to the innovation economy, because the maritime industry is the source of innovation, and that is the european union's motto. in my country, poland, the european commission's decision has led the government to close down the shipbuilding industry, leaving no alternative, and the construction of the nordstream gas pipeline, in contravention of international conventions, has completely blocked the development of polish ports. as a member of parliament and a former seafarer, i call on the commission to take a responsible approach to the problem of the maritime economy.

member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank all the speakers. let me start by giving you some clarification on recreational fisheries. recreational fisheries is not, i repeat not, an eu competence. so the european commission is not responsible, and the national governments have to tackle all these problems. so please, do not come back again and again here to recreational fisheries. the commission’s only responsibility is to ensure, when we are talking about recreational fisheries, that the product cannot be sold. everything else comes under the competence of national governments. let me now turn to our main point. this report was broadly supported and deserves it, because it is a good report, is well-balanced and also refers to all the relevant issues. however, i would like to answer some of your remarks and would mainly like to raise two points. i would like to try to convince you that we are improving, and i would like to convey to you this positive message. we have done a lot since this iuu regulation was put in force. we have achieved much and sometimes we have solved some problems. that has to be recognised. for example, you have mentioned our obligation to be responsible in our waters. well, we have been responsible. the commission is doing its job. i should mention the last case of the use of drift nets in the mediterranean. the national governments have been pushed and been obliged to take all the necessary measures, and we are going further on this case. secondly, mr romeva rueda referred to a spanish enterprise. well, i can tell you that we have had some news today: the owner of that enterprise himself was sanctioned by a court in las palmas, and now he is facing a prison sentence because of fishing illegally in the antarctic. so we are improving here, and not only on paper as somebody said. regarding international cooperation, we have done much in the last year. let me just give you some figures. to date, the commission has finalised ten evaluation missions to panama, belize, sri lanka, mauritania, thailand, china, guinea-conakry, senegal, korea and indonesia. so we have done a lot of work. referring to other countries and our cooperation, i would like also to mention that since july 2011 we have gone through 120 procedures of requests to flag states because their vessels have fished illegally. up to now, the flag states concerned have put sanctions on 19 vessels. we are talking about belize, china – 13 vessels were punished by the chinese authorities themselves – the comoros, guinea and others. we are doing a lot, bearing in mind our limited resources, but i do agree that we have to do more and i really rely on you in order to take that exercise further.
in writing. the report by ms lövin shows how serious the problem of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing is. to understand this, it is enough to compare the 6.4 million tonnes of fish caught by the european union countries in a year with the estimated, i stress, bottom forks of illegal fishing, which is worth 11 million tonnes a year, almost twice the annual catch of the entire european union. in my view, eu countries should not only fight against iuu but also take practical preventive measures, including harmonising legislation to the extent that enforcement bodies can effectively act to eliminate iuu. almost half of the eu population is directly or indirectly linked to fishing in general, economically or socially, and improving the situation in this sector would be a major catalyst for economic growth. cooperation with non-eu countries is an important aspect of fisheries support. despite the eu's strong position in the fisheries sector, i believe that cooperation with countries such as japan, china and the united states is very important for the effective implementation of the regulation. the iuu phenomenon knows no borders and should be controlled and then eliminated in accordance with the theme of this report, i.e. international cooperation worldwide.

on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i have had the pleasure of being a member of the legal affairs committee of the european parliament for over seven years. during that time, we've handled dozens of cases involving the possible waiver or defense of the mp's immunity. i would like to remind all my colleagues very clearly - because bernhard rapkay has spoken about this, and i want to make it even clearer - that the european parliament is the parliament which stands out among the european parliaments in that it has a very precise framework for dealing with the question of parliamentary immunity. it is expressly stated that parliamentary immunity can be invoked only if the act for which the person is to be brought to justice in his own country is connected with the performance of his mandate as a member of the european parliament. i, while maintaining my full sympathy for mr uspaskich and his activities, including in the european parliament, want to say clearly that after a long debate in the ppe group we have come to the conclusion that our sympathies are one thing and the letter of the law another. we must therefore continue with the line we have been presenting for many years: if the act is not in the least connected with the exercise of the mandate of a member of the european parliament, there is no possibility for the european parliament to defend immunity. bernhard rapkay has outlined the whole story that has already been raised about this case, i just want to remind you once again that the european parliament lifted mr uspaskich's immunity over a year ago. today we can only say whether that decision was right or wrong. the ppe group believes that this decision of parliament should not be changed.

obligations themselves serve to ensure that all citizens are able to take full advantage of membership and this has a direct bearing on the credibility of the whole enlargement policy. it is something determination on the road to fulfilling the accession criteria. we hope this event on 9 december will give a new momentum to the european perspective of the western balkans as a whole, provided that all countries concerned persevere on the path of reform.

in writing. the ongoing debt crisis has shown that the current european economic governance system is not effective in preventing crises from occurring and spreading. the european semester is a cycle of peer reviews of eu countries' budgetary plans, which allows for the use of economic policy surveillance in the eu to prevent the emergence of major fiscal and structural problems. the first european semester was inaugurated on 1 january 2011 and, as experience has shown, this procedure needs to be improved. in most cases, the council has softened the commission's recommendations to member states, which may in future hinder effective economic coordination. this also demonstrates the superiority of the community method over the intergovernmental method in this area. in future, therefore, the role of parliament should be strengthened at the expense of the council when further regulations are drawn up, since this would make the shape of final recommendations independent of national political interests. the position of parliament can be strengthened, inter alia, by institutionalising the so-called economic dialogue, in particular by setting up a special parliamentary committee on the european semester. in the context of such a committee, meps could, among other things, ask the council to justify changes to the commission's recommendations and invite finance ministers from countries that have not implemented the recommendations to attend meetings. the explicit involvement of parliament will enhance the democratic legitimacy of the whole procedure, as well as the integrity of european law and the transparency of the institutional structure.

in writing. the need to review the 2009-2013 hiv/aids response plan in the european union and neighbouring countries is linked to the rapid progress in research into the nature of the disease and its treatment. a new antiviral medicine was registered in may 2011. it is necessary to review the objectives and the means and amount of funding for further research. as in any field, prevention is the most effective. since hiv remains asymptomatic for a long period (about 10 years on average), systematic screening is necessary. we also need effective information and education campaigns. they should be addressed primarily to the most vulnerable groups. in poland, for example, about 50 percent of hiv infections are among people between 20 and 29 years of age. people with hiv and aids face not only the disease but also discrimination and stigma, and often lack of funds for treatment. intolerance leads to poor access to employment and poverty, which in turn increases the risk of disease and closes the vicious circle. as nelson mandela said, "it's not aids that's the killer, but stigma, discrimination and ostracism are the real killers". on the occasion of world aids day, december 1, i appeal for understanding and institutional support for all those who are sick.

member of the commission. − mr president, we are discussing the very modest budget for 2012, below 1% of eu gni, despite growing responsibilities under the lisbon treaty and despite growing challenges which deserve a common answer. although this budget is nominally growing, it is not growing in real terms – in real terms it is decreasing. and we are not asking on behalf of the commission or on behalf of parliament; here we are starting savings. 94% of what we are asking for is for the operational expenditure of a different nature from that which is in the national budgets. therefore i have to respond to some speakers who notoriously accuse us of growing while others are making cuts. this is simply not true; this is true of only about four countries, which are easy to guess – greece, ireland, spain and portugal, which are decreasing. the other national budgets of the european union are growing, including the uk and the dutch budgets. despite all the savings, we have some obligations to make payments from the european budget. this is all the same, with the big difference that the european budget is always in equilibrium and cannot be blamed for the mismanagement of fiscal policy at the national level. this is mainly about investment, as clearly explained, for example, by anne jensen or mr vaughan from wales, in the name of the stakeholders of the budget. i am sorry to repeat this on so many occasions but some members of the parliament have the habit of making a critical point and leaving before they receive the answer.
acting president of the council. - mr president! - what are you doing? of course, we can debate for a long time about the amount of commitment appropriations, the amount of payment appropriations and there will always be a group of people who are not satisfied. the same applies to national budgets, where some people are always unhappy that the resources for a given priority have not been taken resources. but for me, there are two very important messages from this year's budgetary procedure that i think are worth highlighting at this point and are worth remembering. firstly, this year's budgetary procedure has confirmed that it is still possible to discuss and solve very difficult issues in the european union using only the community method. this is a very important message. we have followed exactly the lisbon treaty in reaching this agreement. no other extra-institutional action was required. it's a value we should be pursuing right now. we have set an example for the whole of the european union that the community method still works. the second very important message is that despite the criticism of amending budget no 6 to this year's budget, its adoption proves that the mr president, i welcome the substance of the agreement reached, a binding commitment to macrofinancial debt brakes and fiscal rigours, and strengthening the firewall and firepower of the esm. the question is, are those instruments sufficient? this remains an open question. i welcome the wide, inclusive front of – hopefully – 26 member states. it is not 17 plus, it is 27 minus. we should preserve the unity of the union and avoid a two-speed europe at all costs. the dividing line, unfortunately, is between those willing and those unwilling, not between eurozone and non-eurozone. we are all in the same boat. it is a crisis of excessive debt, not a crisis of the euro currency. i am extremely concerned by the method chosen, i.e. an intergovernmental agreement. the third-best option was chosen and the lowest common denominator applied. it has one key deficiency: it is outside the single institutional framework of the eu treaty and its institutions. it has three deficiencies. it is weaker in terms of enforcement – no ec, no ecj; it is weaker in terms of democratic scrutiny legitimacy – no european parliament; and it weakens the community method as such. we have to try to remedy the shortcomings of this imperfect compromise. the european parliament should be invited to be associated with the agreement, because in future it will be part of the acquis. we should provide for the repatriation and transposition of this fiscal union agreement into the eu legal order and treaties and institutions. the rights of the european parliament in this new agreement should be guaranteed and safeguarded.

way that is fully compatible with european union law. this issue raises important legal and institutional matters. i have been frank in making some of these points to you. i think it is possible to do it, but it requires efforts on all sides. this is what the commission is determined to do while always trying to be constructive. i think it is possible to come to an agreement that is fully european council and in the formal summit, namely that i think this parliament should be associated with the present efforts for finding that solution. i am ready to work with you to that end. an issue that came up very often in the debate today was the position of the united kingdom. it is important to put the uk relationship with the rest of the european union in its proper context. emotions are what they are but i think, as some of you have mentioned, that it is important to see how we can get out of a situation that was indeed unfortunate. i welcome the statement made yesterday by prime fighting climate change and the development agenda. i sincerely believe that we have a joint interest to agree, and to agree among all of us. i think that it is in all of our interests to have a united kingdom government that fully engages with the other member states and the european institutions. indeed, it is the european institutions that are the best guarantee that the interests of all member states, including the uk, will be fully respected. it is precisely through european institutions and in full respect of the community method that we can avoid any kind of split, any kind of directorium, or any kind of derivation that will be negative for the overall interests of the union and each one of its member states. i therefore hope that we can work constructively with the uk government to make sure that the fiscal compact now agreed dovetails neatly with the european union treaties so that the interests of all member states and european institutions, including this parliament, are respected. regarding the evaluation of the results, i was extremely prudent on purpose. i tried to avoid adjectives as much as i could. the reality is that by now we have all learned that the solution to this crisis – as i have mentioned very often – is not a sprint, it is a marathon. when i use the expression ‘marathon’ i am not just thinking about the greek situation. one can lose confidence in one day, but to recover confidence takes much longer. so what we need now in the euro area, and in the european union, is a commitment to sustainability, to persistence, to rigour, to discipline and to convergence over time. there will be no panacea. there is no silver bullet. in these matters there are no miracles. i think it is also important that we show everybody, including our partners, that we are committed to a solution and that we will work consistently, coherently and over time to reach that solution. as some of you said – and in fact i also made the point in my introductory remarks – the issue of budget discipline and addressing the problems of debt is an important one, but it is not the whole problem. we have in europe, and in the euro area, a problem of sovereign debt. this sovereign debt is partly the cause of the crisis, but it is partly also the result of the crisis. the crisis started with the subprime problems when in fact there was a problem in terms of the evaluation of risk by markets and investors. we have both a sovereign debt crisis and a financial crisis at the same time, but at the origin of these different crises we have a problem in europe of competitiveness. we are losing our position to many of our competitors in the world. that is why we need the reforms to enhance our competitiveness and to liberate the potential for growth. that is why in fact what we have discussed in this summit is only part of the solution because it addresses only part of the problem. we need fiscal discipline. we need of course to be rigorous in terms of having a debt sustainability path, but we also need measures for growth. i made this point very clearly. we need growth in europe. that is why i think we now have an agenda. we have the eu 2020 agenda and we have other initiatives to address this major problem of growth. without creating confidence globally that europe is able to restore growth, i believe we cannot get out of this current crisis. this is our position. this is the position that the commission has sustained over time and we are ready to work with you and of course with all the institutions in that direction, as i said earlier, to build a europe of stability but also a europe of growth, a europe of responsibility but also a europe of solidarity. this is our commitment and we will go on working for this, hopefully with all the member states and in full respect of the principles that made our union what it is today, after all a union of free, democratic societies committed to the very strong values of the rule of law, justice, freedom and solidarity. president of the european council. - mr president, first of all, as regards the overall assessment of the results of this european council, i think we must be consistent in our analysis. we cannot say at the same time that the financial markets are partly responsible for the present crisis and the difficulties we have to overcome and at the same time say that we are waiting for the reaction of the financial markets to evaluate the decisions taken at political level at the european summits. as the president of the commission has just said, ladies and gentlemen, there is unfortunately no miracle cure, not at all. trust can only be restored step by step. the crisis of trust has been too deep for any change to happen overnight. we do not always have all the facts and i will not go into that. but the fact that some member states have not carried out the plans they were asked to do creates mistrust. the fact that some member states have waited far too long to act - we experienced this again this summer - creates a crisis of confidence which cannot be resolved at union level. the member states therefore have a very great responsibility. there are also crises of trust that are completely unnecessary. on 21 july we decided to make our rescue instrument, the efsf, more flexible, more effective. and the markets believed that the measures taken and the measures decided could never be passed by the parliaments of the 17 member states of the euro area. we did it anyway. set in and never left. so there is no miracle solution. there are many things that we cannot control, which explains the situation we find ourselves in. the third point to consider is that many of you in writing. – the outcomes of the recent eu summit of 8-9 december 2011 are partly satisfying. on the one hand i am pleased leaders took a firm decision to apply new fiscal rules to eu member states for tackling the euro area crisis. on the other hand, i deplore the fact that this agreement failed to include all 27 eu member states. in the new situation, reflected by the uk’s veto, many questions remain to be answered; for example what is the role of parliament in the new situation? what parts of the new eu treaty will apply, and to whom? how will the uk’s veto affect future discussions on plans to introduce eu-wide taxes? these questions must be resolved in order to end confusion and restore trust in the euro currency. so long as we do not have concrete answers speculators, who have played their share in provoking the euro crisis, continue making money by betting on the future of the euro area and the future of the eu. i remain hopeful that solutions can be found to these problems within the eu common framework, so as to avoid new divisions between eu member states and to preserve integration and trust – two essential features for the future of our union.
ladies and gentlemen! last week's european council was once again called the meeting of the last chance. analysts and journalists have been telling us all along that this is the last moment to make a decision to save the single currency. looking at the agreement from this perspective, one can feel disappointed. however, the compromise reached should be welcomed, as it can help member states to rebuild their public finances and thus save the single currency. the main shortcoming is that the proposed changes will not be incorporated into the treaties but will be adopted by intergovernmental agreement. the question arises as to what role the community institutions will play in the context of the fiscal union that is being established. we must do everything possible to keep the community institutions strong, for they alone safeguard the principles of solidarity and equality of nations. we cannot allow ourselves to be in a situation where we save the euro and lose the union. we must not forget that only the acquis communautaire and the institutions of the union guarantee the equal position of all the member states. despite the shortcomings of the agreement reached, he should be pleased that the agreed intergovernmental agreement is not limited to the euro area but is open to the other eu members. the six non-euro countries, including poland, decided to deepen their integration and once again showed that they are responsible for the whole community and that they want a europe that is strong at home.
in writing. the conclusions of the last european council are consistent with the demands repeated in this chamber since the beginning of the crisis and partly reinforce the economic governance instruments contained in the so-called six-pack. it is no longer in doubt among us that debt and budget deficits are a major threat to the stability of the functioning of monetary union and should be subject to a stricter control procedure at community level. the assumptions set out in the european council conclusions are to be seen as moving in the right direction, but not enough. the entry into force of these provisions will take place at the earliest in one year, which does not correspond to the need for rapid reform of the structures of the european union. the increase in the automaticity of sanctions, the requirement of ex ante control of national budgetary drafts, the strengthening of the imf rescue programme and the faster ratification of the esm treaty are all good ideas that are hardly unfair in the long term. however, the main source of uncertainty about the effectiveness of the fiscal pact is the unclear legal nature of the future agreement, including the definition of its position in the hierarchy of community law and, consequently, the extent to which it will be possible to benefit from the support of the european institutions. it is also concerned, above all, that the community method of regulation has been abandoned in favour of the intergovernmental method. the european institutions have therefore made another declaration to the financial markets on fiscal adjustment, leaving unanswered the question of the differences in competitiveness between euro area countries.

madam president! i abstained from the vote. the specific obligations on member states in relation to the administrative processing of residence and work applications can be extremely costly. in a situation where we are trying to save money, it does not seem right to impose new responsibilities leading to the creation of additional offices. nor, in my view, is there any need to harmonise the procedures for such applications throughout the community, particularly as the markets of the member states are not subject to harmonisation either. the regulations in force in the countries of the union perfectly reflect the need in these matters. i therefore also do not think it necessary to harmonise the rights of workers from outside the union. these issues are already regulated in some detail by european law. any social benefits should be activated at the legislative level of the individual countries, taking into account their interests.
madam president! the removal of various types of obstacles to international trade will help the european economy to develop. it is in the interest of union businesses, particularly in their relations with key partners, to reduce non-tariff barriers between them. i agree that this should be a clear trade policy priority in the europe 2020 strategy. at the same time, regulations that are beneficial to public health, such as those related to agriculture or to gmos, must be respected. i welcome the commission's commitment to take active action to reduce the constraints caused by non-tariff barriers and to facilitate access to foreign markets for european companies. the commission's activities in international cooperation fora such as the oecd and the wto should also be used in this regard. it also appears necessary to carry out regular information campaigns among union businesses on the elimination of barriers and changing trade restrictions in order to make international trade more efficient. that is why i support the report.
in writing. − i have voted in favour of resolution a7-0408/2011 on the right to information in criminal proceedings. this vital piece of legislation has taken two readings to come to the proper formula for european citizens. the resolution provides a common minimum standard with regard to the right to information in criminal proceedings throughout the european union. if correctly implemented, it will improve the rights of suspects and accused persons by ensuring that they receive information about their rights in their own language. we have developed this legislation to prevent citizens who are travelling in other member states from being unaware of what they are being accused of and thus allowing them a better opportunity to properly defend themselves. all citizens of the union are granted fundamental rights regardless of what member state they are in and should always have access to the proper information in their own language through all legal proceedings.
in writing. - ladies and gentlemen! i am pleased that the report presented here makes improvements to the process of creating better eu law, a process in which i have been personally involved for many years. in 2007, the european commission identified 42 regulations in 13 priority areas, representing some eur 115-130 billion in administrative costs. this was the basis for the action programme approved in march 2007 to reduce the administrative burden on european businesses by 25% by 2012. in addition, the european economic recovery plan called on member states and the eu to take immediate steps to reduce the administrative burden on smes and micro-enterprises. on 29 february 2009, the commission prepared a proposal to amend directive 78/660/eec on the annual accounts of certain types of companies. it was just the beginning of the improvements. today we need new solutions, and the ones proposed by the rapporteur, which introduce exceptions for micro-enterprises in accordance with the 'think small first' principle, are very appropriate. they should be justified by the fact that 93% of micro-entities in europe are not engaged in cross-border activities and therefore accounting harmonisation is not needed at their level. the remaining 7% are only able to produce such reports if their trading partners require it. i support the compromise amendment to article 1 proposed by the rapporteur which would exclude the exception of a micro-enterprise acquiring more than 10% of its overall profits from cross-border activities. they are good news for the 5.2 million or so micro-enterprises across the eu and a step in the right direction towards creating better and more citizen-friendly eu law.
in writing. - i would like to express my full support for the european parliament's recommendation for a second reading on the annual accounts of certain types of companies as regards micro-entities, which was voted on today. i would therefore like to thank the rapporteur and the polish presidency for their hard work and to congratulate them on reaching a compromise which is a clear step towards building a legal environment favourable to the activities of the smallest economic operators in the eu internal market. the increase in the annual net turnover and balance sheet total criteria will significantly increase the number of undertakings that can benefit from exemptions from certain accounting obligations. in the long run, this will lead to a reduction in the administrative burden for these entities, which will certainly translate into increased employment opportunities, focus on investment and the development of micro-enterprises. such action by parliament and the council is to be fully welcomed, especially in times of economic crisis.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because i believe that financial assistance to member states where the use of eu funds is threatened by a lack of national resources, which is in turn caused by the financial crisis in europe, requires community intervention and assistance. the use of european funds is an important task for the countries of the union, but the lack of internal resources in the member states can jeopardise the implementation of programmes concerning the structural funds, the cohesion funds, the eafrd and the european fisheries fund. these actions will help countries with financial problems to implement these programmes. i believe that in this situation, an increase in the co-financing rate by the european union will make a positive contribution to the implementation of projects and thus have a positive impact on the economic recovery in these countries.

vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. − mr president, can i begin by also thanking mr lisek for his report. as i said last night when i saw him, i come from the european defence agency where they too would wish me to express their thanks for the work that he has done. there is no debate about the common security and defence policy (csdp) this year that can ignore the financial crisis which has led to a wave of defence cuts across the european union. this has resulted in both the increased focus on pooling and sharing of military capabilities and in the current staff shortfalls we are experiencing in important csdp missions and operations. but the demand for the eu to do more and better is getting stronger. we need to be able to respond to the complex threats of today – crises from cyber-threats, energy security and others – and we need to assume our global responsibilities whilst showing real value for money. to deliver value for money we need csdp action to be based on coherent and effective strategies and a truly comprehensive approach and equipped with the right capabilities, as was restated in the foreign affairs council on 1 december. the budgetary constraints force us to save, but they are also a driver of closer collaboration; whether on pooling and sharing of defence assets, joint programming of development aid, or solidarity in the evacuation of european nationals from scenes of conflict or disaster. the message is clear: doing better with less. the 1 december foreign affairs council endorsed my call to maximise synergies and strengthen cooperation – complementing instead of duplicating each other. i am committed to ensuring that the actions by the external action service, the commission and the eu member states reinforce rather than compete with each other. at the meeting of 1 december, we also agreed that the eu needs to improve its operations by more clearly identifying needs and acting with clear objectives and clear exit strategies. the european parliament, alongside national parliaments and governments, plays an important role in ensuring the democratic oversight of eu foreign, security and defence policy, as recognised in my declaration on political accountability. i want to focus for a moment on some important achievements during the course of this year. at the level of structures, we have established the external action service and it is now equipped to deal with crises better, faster and smarter. when the service was launched in january 2011, the arab spring required our immediate response. in light of this experience, we have set up the crisis management board and crisis platform, which also dealt effectively with crisis situations in ivory coast, libya and the horn of africa. these structures are central to our capacity to respond, and maintain their direct reporting line to me while working closely with the rest of the service. we have also improved the early warning capacity through the situation room and the conflict prevention group and we are currently exploring how to strengthen the security policy expertise in eu delegations. all of this has been achieved using and restructuring the existing resources and improving their flexibility and efficiency rather than by seeking other expensive and complex solutions. we are turning a comprehensive approach into comprehensive action and i believe the external action service is uniquely placed for this. we can join up all of the instruments of the european union and cover conflict prevention, development and conflict resolution. we are putting this to full use in the horn of africa and in the southern neighbourhood. some people try and say that we are facing some sort of fatigue on csdp, yet this year has been a year of intensive work on this area, with concrete results, and ending with comprehensive and, i believe, forward-looking council conclusions. on military capabilities, the 30 november european defence agency steering board delivered concrete member states’ commitments in specific projects, including in areas where the libya crisis showed our shortfalls. this is a good first step towards more substantial achievements next spring, also in view of the nato chicago summit which i will attend. but as indicated by the honourable member mr lisek’s report, there is no alternative to cooperation in this area. multinational cooperation must become the rule rather than the exception in order to preserve and develop europe’s defence capabilities. i agree with what mr lisek says: pooling and sharing is a means of delivering enhanced capabilities and of offsetting defence budgets cuts. as the head of the european defence agency, i will continue to make every effort to facilitate cooperation among and between member states and to increase the global competitiveness and efficiency of the european defence industry. in july, i presented a comprehensive report on csdp. it set out the parameters for further work, both in terms of hardware – our military and civilian capabilities – and software – how we plan and conduct operations and engage with our partners. the foreign affairs council on 1 december welcomed my work to strengthen the csdp. member states’ initiatives, such as the weimar initiative and subsequent contributions, have provided an added impetus to work. i am pleased too that we found a pragmatic way forward on the issue of the planning and conduct of csdp operations. we are now beginning planning for the activation of the operations centre for the horn of africa operations by the next foreign affairs council in january. this will allow us to test this tool, with a view to strengthening civilian-military synergies and again to draw lessons for the future. i believe that we have achieved a lot of progress in working with our partners. in the area of security and defence, the relationship with nato is essential. it is recognised in the lisbon treaty, which is the first of the eu treaties to explicitly refer to nato. the breadth of eu instruments can be usefully combined with the depth of nato’s role on defence. the two organisations can and should reinforce each other’s work. i have worked hard to establish a good, close working relationship with nato secretary-general rasmussen, to bring the eu and nato closer through a pragmatic step-by-step approach, while maintaining the overall objective of a true organisation-to-organisation relationship. the libya crisis again showed clear need for this. we work hand in hand in many theatres, and we owe it to our people in the field. i am also pleased to confirm that on capabilities in particular – whether labelled pooling and sharing or smart defence – we have now achieved an unprecedented level of cooperation. the un remains, of course, a longstanding partner, and we are turning this partnership into reality: in theatres where both are or could be engaged, in afghanistan, somalia, kosovo and libya, and through our strategic dialogue. i have also personally engaged on security and defence with our strategic partners, not least regarding areas like the horn of africa or in libya. i signed a framework agreement with the united states of america in june on their participation in csdp civilian missions and already 60 us citizens under eu chain of command are operating in kosovo and afghanistan. i also want to foster closer cooperation with other partner countries, including contributors and the neighbours to the south and to the east. i would like to end my remarks with the possible way forward. i think we have to further operationalise the comprehensive approach, by better linking our conflict prevention, mediation, development and conflict resolution activities. csdp has a vital role to play in addressing forms of organised crime, such as trafficking of drugs, of weapons and of course of people. these are directly linked to conflict. for example, the security threats in the sahel also relate to the influx of weapons and militias as a result of changes in libya. on this the combination of all of the european union’s tools in a coherent strategy is absolutely essential. we have to pay constant attention to force generation and capabilities. the council undertook to make every effort to address this challenge and i will examine innovative ways to improve force generation in order to make proposals in the first half of 2012. force generation, by the way, means getting the right people in the right place. work on military capabilities should continue towards a systematic pooling and sharing, not only as an answer to financial constraints but also as means of enhanced operational effectiveness in the long term. we also have to enhance the effectiveness of missions and operations. the eu should act through csdp missions and operations to add value, on the basis of identified needs, with clear objectives and exit strategies to deliver and sustain results. as long as we can deliver on the existing missions, i am always ready to take forward work on possible new missions – in particular in regions of such strategic importance to europe’s security such as the sahel and libya. the common security and defence policy can only be as effective and ambitious as we let it be. it relies on collective political will and ambition to act. it also means that the cfsp budget should be able to respond to the financial aspects of force generation. and i personally believe - that the area of security and defence, even in such a turbulent and difficult period for european finances, must not be neglected. in the report, i presented some ways to optimize spending, to show how we can spend the resources we have - in writing. two aspects are particularly important in the human rights debate: equality and social exclusion. human rights and equality: the idea of equality before the law is the daughter of the french revolution. today, it is recognized as a basic human right. although the law guarantees equality between women and men, its implementation in the eu is ineffective. in the european union, gender equality is only on paper. in reality, women are discriminated against socially, economically and politically. discrimination also affects minorities (sexual, ethnic, religious, racial), the disabled, the poor and the elderly. there is a widespread feeling of inequality and discrimination in europe. the only group that's not discriminated against are young, healthy, wealthy men. in poland, additionally, the catholic faith. human rights and exclusion: second generation human rights include economic, social and cultural rights. they provide what is called social security. since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, the union has aimed to combat social exclusion and discrimination. the question arises whether these rights in the eu constitute a guarantee against exclusion. the problem of exclusion affects 79 million people, or 16% of europeans, whose fundamental rights are constantly violated. in 2010, the union allocated eur 26 million to combat poverty and social exclusion. what have been the results? is the union capable of dealing with such a permanent violation of human rights?
