the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? today is a very happy day for all those who have spent the whole year wondering how europe should shape its relations with its close neighbours. we have a report ready, which was prepared in a very special year. it was a year when from all over the world, one big slogan was heard: change, change, change. a call for democracy, a call for a better life, a call for the values that are so close to the european union. the european neighbourhood policy was once designed as a consolation prize for those who are close but will never be in the european union. both those who are close to us, such as those across the mediterranean, and those who live in the east, who were once part of the soviet empire. everything has changed in the meantime, first of all the attitude of the people living in these countries, but also the attitude of the european union towards these countries. we understood that the politics of empty gestures, the politics of hypocrisy, the politics of maintaining relations with regimes that have managed to be stable, but that stability turned out to be illusory, just doesn't make sense. investing in fiction, investing in dictatorships, has proven to be completely unnecessary. this year, a powerful voice has been heard from the people of north africa, who are demanding freedom, democracy, who want to fight for values. earlier, a few years ago, the same voice was heard from the maidan in kiev. millions of ukrainians came out to maidan and demanded the same thing that people in africa are demanding today. so what is this new neighbourhood policy being developed by the european commission (and here is great respect for the work of commissioner füle, who is sitting in a seat reserved for the commission)? it is above all an integral policy towards the east and north africa. why is it integral? when it comes to freedom, democracy, tolerance, there is no geographical division, people are (we believe this deeply) the same. they want to live with dignity in ukraine, azerbaijan, tunisia and egypt. this new policy is based on values that are dear to us, it's based on the struggle for democracy, for freedom. it gives a chance to people who want to fight for those values. sometimes this fight will be long. this is a policy that is people-oriented. we want to create the foundation of this new policy, of this new relationship, first of all by building the conviction of the public - through contacts with ngos, with the elites, with the media - that we want to give these people a chance to convince themselves and their loved ones that this is the way to look at it and the way to look at the european union as an institution that supports these values. we assume that the pace of change will be determined by the countries themselves. we're talking about the fact that the whole concept of benchmarks is, you do whatever you want, and we'll help you. the principle of 'more for more', as mário david rightly said, also means 'less for less'. you can take from someone to add to someone. so today is the big day. everything that is important to us, to the european union, to the countries that have gained their freedom, becomes an offer to those who live near us. we can complain and say that there is still a lot to do in the east and in north africa, that we are dissatisfied with the situation in azerbaijan, in armenia, that we can improve the policy in georgia and in ukraine, that we can say that moldova is making progress, and that there is still a lot to do in egypt and tunisia, but it is important that we make sure that things are going in the right direction. mario, thank you for your cooperation, we wrote this report together. i thank the commissioner for the important content of his communication. thank you to all who helped us, the members of parliament, to put these wise words into words.

acting president of the council. - thank you very much, mr president! ladies and gentlemen! it's been six months since we met at the beginning of the polish presidency. i declared then the great attachment of the poles, and myself, to the idea of a united europe. i have declared my commitment to the european community, knowing that we are assuming the presidency in a time of great crisis. not only a financial crisis, but - as we already predicted then - also a crisis of confidence, and today - i think it is necessary to say this strongly - perhaps also a systemic and political crisis. our presidency - although we were a country making our debut in this presidency, and perhaps that is why - was a presidency of people determined to do their european jobs to the best of our ability. we have brought not only goodwill but also the work and skills of hundreds of young poles who have worked here in strasbourg, brussels, warsaw and many other places in europe into this presidency, and we have undertaken - with awareness of our capabilities - the tasks that are the routine responsibility of any presidency, including legislative tasks. i'm not going to go through everything we've done in the last six months. i've heard a lot of warm words in the last few days about our commitment and our effectiveness. it may sound immodest, but i think the poles deserve these words precisely because they worked with such faith in the sense of a common europe on these challenges that fell to the polish presidency. whether it was the work on the six-pack, the accession of croatia, the eastern partnership, energy security or other legislative acts such as the common european patent, we have succeeded in bringing our commitments to the final stage, in completing our work. mainly because the polish presidency was led by people who really take europe as a community seriously and who - despite the crisis, or perhaps i should say it differently: precisely because we have a crisis, also a crisis of confidence - wanted to show that the responsibilities and commitment of the european should be even more pronounced and determined at a time like this. i would like to turn this summary into one of the serious political reflections that have emerged from the experience of the polish presidency over the last six months. but i am convinced that you too share the same thoughts and the same need to give a name to what is happening in europe today. because despite the satisfaction i get from the work i do, i cannot say that europe at the end of 2011 is a more united europe than it was six months ago, a year ago or five years ago. i cannot say today, as i leave the polish presidency, that we have jointly avoided what is perhaps the most serious crisis in the history of a united europe, which is afflicting our continent. i'll say the opposite. today, we have to say this very openly to ourselves: we are at a crossroads. we have a very serious choice to make: during this crisis, in search of ways and means of overcoming it, will we follow the community's way, will we seek a european way out of the crisis, or will we follow the path of national and state egos, selfishly seeking a way out for each individual and considering the community as a ballast and not as the best way for europeans to overcome the crisis? i want to remind you that the real sources of the crisis, the financial crisis, are not the community institutions. it was not the european parliament, not the european commission, not the other community institutions that created the financial crisis. it is not european integration that is the source of the financial crisis and, therefore, of the political crisis. these six months have shown us with all their force that it is exactly the opposite - that this crisis is fed by, and is fattened by, the threat of the community's collapse, that if today we cannot say that we have overcome the crisis, it is because europe has not always behaved like a community in the face of this crisis. (applause) why are we talking about a political crisis today? because too many people in europe, too many politicians in europe want to convince us and want to convince europe that the way out of the crisis is to move away from community action. i want to say that in my and the polish presidency's opinion, it is a sign of a certain disease. this current crisis is violating that sense of community. if we hear in europe today that the foundations of the community need to be revised, it is clearly a sign that the crisis is in our hearts too, not just in our banks. the last european council summit showed very clearly that some are looking for tools to not only save the euro but also to strengthen the community in the long term, but that there are others who believe that the way to save the euro or the financial situation of the states and institutions is to loosen the community and ultimately destroy it. i'm not accusing anyone, because they're equals. everyone may have his own view of the future of europe, but we cannot hide the fact that today, somewhere under the surface, the debate is not about the future of the euro but about the future of the community. at the last european council we took decisions which are only the first step. i have been trying to convince everyone, both in brussels and in my own country, that if we are not fully satisfied with this summit, it is because we have taken only one step, that we still lack the full determination to take the next steps quickly and decisively within the community and for the community. when i hear some comments - i am sure they are made in good faith, and i do not blame anyone for the ill will - filled with the satisfaction that britain is an island again, that the english channel is wider than it was a few weeks ago, i must say frankly that i do not understand that satisfaction. (laughter) we cannot accept the decisions of politicians in one country or another, but we cannot publicly celebrate the fact that we are witnessing the growing distance between the member states, in this case between the united kingdom and the european community. but i also want to say that there were other comments, too, like that one capital city won against other capitals. we know that europe needs strong political leadership not only for this crisis, but also for the future. at the last european council and over the last six months, i have witnessed this as yet unnamed but great european debate: will the political leadership of europe be the result of ruthless competition between nation states, and will this competition result in the domination of one or two or three capitals over the others, or will the political leadership of europe be community leadership for the benefit of the community as a whole? it is very important that we can conclude each subsequent meeting with the conviction that the community is winning against selfishness, and not that someone is winning against someone in this disintegrating community. (applause) i also want to say, after these six months, that europe needs a common conscience. we can't point fingers today and say, "oh, that's where the crisis is coming from", or, "oh, that poor country in the south is causing all of our problems". we also need to share responsibility for the future. northern europe, which prides itself on its discipline, must also begin to understand better the need for solidarity. and the south of europe must understand that shared responsibility also means more discipline. we must also make it very clear that the source of the crisis, not only financial but also political, is the breach of our mutual obligations, including those arising from the treaties, and that these breaches are not a matter of recent months. let each one make his own examination of conscience. let each of us reflect on when he started to break the maastricht treaty. let each one of us consider whether he is ready to cherish the schengen arrangements. (applause) we - those of us who are in favour of a truly integrated community europe - must say very clearly to ourselves today that we need more determination to protect the foundations of europe, not constant debate about the revision of the foundations of europe. i would therefore like to conclude the polish presidency by also appealing to all european leaders without exception to make this effort to strengthen the community, starting with themselves, and not to seek methods of disintegration, exclusion or division in europe. so today, let's say it again: we are for integration, against disintegration. (laughter) we are against the division of europe into better and worse, and we are for the growing political unity of europe. we are for responsibility, shared responsibility against selfish irresponsibility. we are against exclusion because the community must rely on solidarity even when sometimes one person is worse off and another is better off. we need real political leadership, because europe deserves to make decisions quickly, not only about the current financial crisis, but also about the future. the crisis has proved to be a great test of the community's ability to function. we need to start a serious conversation about greater political efficiency in europe. there will be other crises, other conflicts in the future. this crisis has shown us - and it's really good that it has - that europe as a community doesn't always react quickly, because there is a lack of trust - on this fundamental foundation - in the institutions we have set up. this leadership cannot be the leadership of one, two or three of the most powerful states, nor can it be the leadership of technocrats, because they have no democratic mandate. this leadership must be political, it must have a democratic mandate, it must be accepted by all in order to be able to enforce the obligations of all. it must be leadership based on european institutions. (laughter) i want to say that just as we need quick decisions in the coming hours, days and weeks to save the euro and stabilise the euro area, we also need an honest, robust debate on the new political order of europe. today not everyone accepts the community order and we cannot continue to deceive ourselves today we cannot enforce the rules we ourselves once established. today, when we're comfortable, we're avoiding treaty obligations. so let's be honest: we need a very deep, serious debate on the political structure of europe that will give europe a community leadership. so the motto of our presidency, 'more europe in europe', has a political dimension too. i believe that the european parliament is that place, and do not let it take away from you this obvious historical and political mandate. this is the place that should become the constitution for europe. nothing will be the same as it was before the crisis. (laughter) the status quo ante bellum is not an option. europe will certainly be different after this crisis. it's just a question of whether it's going to be broken or more integrated. she's not gonna be the same. that is why the european parliament - because you have a democratic mandate - should, i think, take on this great commitment, this great challenge - should become such a modern constituent for this newly emerging europe. because we are seeing a new europe emerge. let us do everything we can to make europe united, not divided. this deep reflection can't be a decoration, like it was in the past. we had groups of sages, we had task forces, committees. everyone knew that this reflection had to be made for the future. but the seeds of a new order have not been planted, and the crisis has shown this with all its clarity, with all its power. it is not about thousands and tens of thousands of new laws, it is about restoring the balance between what is national and what is community, about rebuilding trust on the basis of a few, a dozen or so clear principles - principles that we all accept, and principles that we can enforce against those who want to break them. this is a key task, i believe, also for the european parliament as the modern constituent body that will build the foundations of a new political order. it's not about scaring each other, the crisis scares people enough. but if we fail to do this, future generations will curse not only the crisis, but us as well. today we will fight for the future of europe, or tomorrow we will mourn for it. thank you, sir. above all, a political one. there is just, as prime minister tusk mentioned, a problem of confidence and of trust. let me highlight some of the concrete points we worked on throughout the presidency. first, a strong europe: a more stable europe that can withstand all kinds of weather. a europe that can learn from its own mistakes and can also address its weaknesses, building its recovery on sound and sustainable foundations. we have laid the foundations on which any further reforms will be built. the adoption of the legislative package on strengthening economic governance – the ‘six-pack’ – has significantly reinforced the stability and growth pact. it puts more emphasis on debt limitations and extends the commission’s surveillance to macroeconomic imbalances. now we need to combine words with actions so that we can reinforce this stability culture. yesterday the ‘six-pack’ entered into force. it will put the commission at the heart of ensuring fiscal discipline, in line with the position of this parliament. we will accept this increased responsibility knowing that its democratic legitimacy derives precisely from this house. to complete this set of tools, we have come up with two article 136 proposals on further strengthening economic governance, and more proposals will come to bring the new fiscal compact as much as possible into our existing union framework. a strong europe is also a europe that is able to recreate the conditions for growth and job creation; as i said yesterday during the debate, we need stability but we also need growth. that is why our 2012 annual growth survey puts a strong emphasis on the need for implementation of growth-enhancing actions, and i welcome the support for our fast-track programme for measures with a significant impact on growth and jobs. this includes the proposals on the single market act. during the polish presidency we have taken key decisions to prepare the relaunch of economic growth, through the development and strengthening of the single market, notably on the e-economy. i would also like to mention the very good progress made in the negotiations on the unitary patent, which showed the energy and constructive approach needed. i call on the member states quickly to resolve among themselves the one outstanding issue: the seat of the litigation court under the intergovernmental agreement.growth is also about green growth, energy security and the fight against climate change, and we are moving forward on all these fronts. the commission has already tabled proposals on completing the internal energy market, boosting energy efficiency, enhancing the coherence and coordination of our external energy policy and improving nuclear safety. let me emphasise in particular the commitment of poland to reinforcing the external dimension of the energy policy that has been adopted by the energy council. on the fight against climate change, durban was certainly not a perfect agreement, but in the difficult circumstances we can say that it achieved some important results; in spite of all the scepticism it was possible to make progress, with all major emitters agreeing for the first time to have a new comprehensive and binding legal instrument, which will include limits on co2 emissions. this was only possible because of the leadership from the european union, and i am particularly proud of the role that the commission has played in this matter. we will now continue our efforts with our international partners to flesh out a new global climate agreement involving all countries as quickly as possible, and we will no doubt have a strong partner in this parliament. the polish presidency has also put a lot of energy into defending a united europe, and you have just heard the inspiring words of prime minister tusk. together with the commission, the polish presidency has been a strong advocate of the preservation of the coherence and the integrity of the european union. what we need is more integration, not fragmentation. what we need is to consolidate our acquis and not to weaken what we have achieved over the last 60 years. what we need to do is to tap the full potential of the single market, not to damage it. what we need is more union, not a désunion.(applause) this is exactly what the community method guarantees. it enables us to join forces in the general interest. it reinforces our solidarity and our cohesion. let me tell you very frankly that it was not insignificant that the discussions about the reinforcement of the euro area took place during the polish presidency, because poland, whilst supporting very clearly a stronger economic governance of the eurozone, was also making clear that this stronger governance of the eurozone must not be to the detriment of the overall objectives of our union. this was particularly important. i want to say the same thing regarding the next presidency. we are, i hope, going to continue to conclude the negotiations for this new fiscal compact during the danish presidency of the council. with the very constructive position taken by the prime minister of denmark, i am hopeful that we can conclude these negotiations with a stronger euro area and stronger governance but, at the same time, also with a stronger union, because that is exactly what we need. the last point i would like to make before concluding is about open europe: united but also open europe. since the early days of european integration, our openness to the world and our attractiveness to our neighbours and to newcomers has always been one of our greatest strengths. over these last six months we have done a lot to advance our relations with our neighbours. first, good progress has been made with enlargement countries on the european integration of the western balkans. last friday we were happy to witness the signature of the accession treaty of our 28th member state – croatia – which will join in july 2013. this should constitute an incentive for the rest of the region to keep to the path of european reforms. the successful summit with our eastern neighbours hosted by the polish presidency in warsaw confirmed our ambition to create the necessary conditions to accelerate political association and further economic integration between the european union and interested partner countries within our enhanced neighbourhood policy. association agreements are being negotiated with four of the six eastern partners and deep and comprehensive free trade areas with three of them. this monday we started further negotiations with georgia and moldova. i will be travelling to kiev next monday, as we seek to conclude an association agreement with ukraine. this house has called for the conclusion of the negotiations by the end of the year. the ukrainian authorities need, however, to demonstrate that they abide by the principles and values that underpin this agreement, namely respect for democracy, the rule of law, human rights and judiciary independence. the establishment of the european endowment for democracy, an innovation also introduced by poland, will greatly enrich the range of instruments at our disposal to support the process of democratisation and consolidate the aspirations of those fighting for freedom, including in places in our neighbourhood where democracy and rule of law needs to be encouraged. finally, i will travel to warsaw tomorrow – once again – where i will participate in european development day, a commission initiative, this time in cooperation with the polish presidency. this shows clearly that, even in times of crisis, the european union does not forget about the need to show solidarity to developing countries and to the most poor of the world. as you remember, some time ago when we had this enlargement, there were some suspicions in the developing world that the fact that europe was enlarging showed that it conferred less interest and importance to the south of our planet. this did not happen; on the contrary, we are reinforcing our commitments to the developing world. as i said, these were considerable achievements under difficult circumstances. but this crisis is not behind us, and we have a lot of work ahead. as we move forward, i would like all member states to show the same level of commitment to europe as poland has shown. (applause) the polish presidency will be a tough act to follow. the challenge ahead will now be with our danish friends. in conclusion, let me very sincerely thank prime minister tusk, all his team and his government, the team dedicated to the presidency, for your leadership, your strong european commitment and your political courage. i think this was a great example for all the member states which are committed to a stronger european union. just before the beginning of the polish presidency of the council. the different proposals for a legal basis have now been approved and sent to the legislator. i would like to underline the mr president of the european parliament, honourable members of the parliament, guests, let me begin by giving you my warmest greetings and expressing my thanks and gratitude to you for having chosen me as a recipient of the sakharov prize for freedom of thought. this prize has huge symbolic and moral value. it is something that the people of libya appreciate. they have congratulated me on having been awarded the prize. it also provides further stimulus for the consolidation of the values we have always been in favour of, that is to say the creation of a democratic, constitutional state based upon the equality of all, a state where women enjoy the freedom to vote and stand in elections, to make their voices heard. women have made huge sacrifices in libya. women have laid down their lives. they have seen their nearest and dearest, their children die, to try to get rid of this totalitarian regime which we suffered from for more than 42 years – in prisons, with constant humiliation, constant violations of our human dignity. it was these years and years of dictatorship that eventually led young people to lay down their lives, to shed their blood, even though they had no weapons. the only weapon that they had was their commitment, their conviction. that is what won out in the end, thanks to the support from the international community and this european parliament. i would just like to express my gratitude to you for that. now we need to rebuild our country, to do so in a tolerant fashion, showing tolerance even to those who committed crimes, who targeted our sons, our brothers, those who destroyed houses, who violated human dignity. i am sure that you saw these things on television, all the crimes that were committed in libya. again we are grateful for the unambiguous economic, diplomatic and military support that europe provided. as i said, we had no weapons and the dictator tried to keep us down by force thanks to the links he had forged with certain countries, countries that supported him for various reasons – economic reasons sometimes, and other reasons. but all of these countries realised that ultimately the people would win. the people always remain. that is why we would like to thank europe for the position that it adopted and thank of course the whole of the international community. but we have to say that our european neighbours – our closest neighbours – were the first to support the libyan people, despite their lack of weapons. thanks to that support we managed to get rid of this totalitarian regime that had been in place for 42 years. i myself of course was a prisoner of conscience under gaddafi. i was in prison for 31 years, including nine years in solitary confinement. i was tortured, i was denied health care, but i did not lose hope. during all of those years i did not abandon my human dignity. in libya now we want to be treated on the same footing as everybody else; we do not want to be described as a nation of terrorists or people who have no right to life. we love life: our own lives and the lives of others as well. and we hope that the sakharov prize will allow us to make progress and allow other states still suffering from dictatorships to make progress too. please support us, and support us in trying to achieve those goals. we have a long way to go before our goals can be met but, thanks to patience, thanks to persistence, i am sure that we will achieve them. the first step is to set up a parliament and a constitution voted by the people. thank you once again for listening to me. in writing. − the envi report on fruit juices and certain similar products intended for human consumption is a document which contains a number of important elements. i believe that the quality of each product is ecological, ethical and social quality, and european products of high standard make healthy and especially sustainable nutrition possible. however, it should not be forgotten that 82% of orange juice comes from brazil and the usa, and the european processing industry is complementary to the fresh fruit trade. although there are still many issues to be resolved, including the naming of the names, i consider the report by mr andrés perello rodríguez to be well prepared and i voted in favour of its adoption. thank you, sir.
in writing. − the proposed amendments to council directive 2001/112/ec take account of technical progress in the production methods of juices, exclude sugars from the list of ingredients allowed for use in juices, order the provisions on flavourings and provide clear definitions of finished products and raw materials and intermediate products for their production. it is important that the amendments to the 'juice directive' address the health benefits and, above all, regulate the addition of sweeteners to juices, so that clear labelling of products makes it easier for consumers to distinguish juice from nectar (e.g. in the case of the labelling of juices derived from two or more fruits). the support to national fruit producers should also be taken into account. the entry into force of the amendments to the directive contributes to improving the quality of fruit juices and nectars in circulation and to harmonising their labelling. the amendments will also make it possible to harmonise the quality requirements for juices and nectars, which will contribute to improving the quality of the products.
in writing. − in more and more households, not only the washing machine but also the dishwasher are becoming standard in the home. so we use a lot more products that have a lot of phosphate. they are discharged into watercourses and then into reservoirs and contribute to over-fertilization. the rapporteur, mr bill newton dunn, rightly points out that we should do everything we can to reduce the risk of eutrophication, which is associated with a decrease in the transparency of water, the formation of algal shells on its surface and the mass extinction of aquatic fauna due to insufficient oxygen and light. overflowed reservoirs have a marked deterioration in the taste and smell of the water, making them unsuitable not only as a place for sports and recreation but also as a source of drinking water. the setting of weight limits for the amount of phosphate in a portion of detergent is a very good move, forcing manufacturers to introduce more concentrated, compact products on the market. the solution is to use products containing phosphorus in a proportion that depends on the hardness of the water in the area, or to mass-produce products that do not contain phosphate. member states should also make every effort to introduce technologies and appropriate equipment for the recovery of phosphorus due to its rare occurrence as an element.
in writing. − while we are concerned about the growing trend of cuts in national defence budgets and the associated risk of reducing the combat capability of member states' armies, i cannot support the report. actions to coordinate defence planning, pool joint ownership potential, strengthen cooperation in research and technological development and optimise military procurement are already being implemented under the north atlantic treaty. there is therefore no need to duplicate them within the union. i am also sceptical about the possibility of these initiatives being implemented as a complement to the coordination of nato's defence planning process. member countries spend a combined €200 billion a year on defence, which is only one third of us defence spending, while covering three quarters of nato's budget. the very low level of expenditure and, above all, the waste of the european members' resources, could threaten the alliance's continued existence and this should be our primary focus.
in writing. − the common security and defence policy is an essential value for the development of the freedom and democracy so important to the european union. i think that its role, its community character, is becoming more important in a time of crisis, when various budget cuts are being made as part of austerity. but we must remember that it is the military sector, the defence industry, that is the place of modern scientific research, of various innovative solutions, which are then taken over by the areas of the civilian economy and significantly influence their development. i would like to deal with two other problems in detail. first, i believe that the european external action service should have more specialists on important eu and global issues - such as energy security, climate and environmental issues, economic and development issues, finance and many others. this would greatly enhance the quality of the work of this service. secondly, the european union should develop its own services and strengthen the coordination of national disaster relief services. it should be an important pillar of our activities, complementing nato's activities. congratulations on a very interesting report.

in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the neighbourhood policy is of great strategic importance to the community countries. a balanced neighbourhood policy by the member states will contribute to progress and development in peace-building and democracy in neighbouring countries. for the partner countries, building a long-term neighbourhood policy gives hope of stability and a willingness to support the european union in building their internal development and social prosperity. i would like to point out that we should be concerned about the sustainable socioeconomic development of our neighbours. building a neighbourhood policy will also bring greater security and economic development to the union. events such as the arab spring and the situation in ukraine require us to adopt a modern approach to the outbreak of conflicts and to pursue a rational financial policy towards these countries. this project will allow us to influence the way we look at human rights, immigration and asylum policy. this document will also facilitate the analysis of the financial assistance provided. it should also be noted that member states should demonstrate a willingness to align their national interests with the common neighbourhood policy, taking into account the benefits for both parties and in particular for partner countries.
in writing. − the european union needs a new strategy for a european neighbourhood policy that is adapted to the socioeconomic and political conditions of each country bordering the european union. i think we should promote respect and democracy, human rights and democratic governance. we should further strengthen the multilateral dimension of the eastern partnership, taking into account the role of peripheral regions and euroregions, especially in the eu's external policy. this will also help us to achieve the objectives of cohesion policy, especially in border regions, which is why i voted in favour of the report by mário david and marek siwca on the european neighbourhood policy. thank you, sir.
in writing. - i believe that we should strive to strengthen the european neighbourhood policy in its political, financial and economic dimensions. i support efforts to strike a balance between developing the european union's relations with its eastern and southern neighbours, recognising their different aspirations and needs. i believe that the development of political contacts, economic convergence and the removal of trade barriers, including the reduction or abolition of the visa requirement, are particularly important. the strategic objective of the neighbourhood policy is to stimulate economic growth. removing administrative and legislative barriers and improving competitiveness are also important, but the fight against corruption is no less important. the clear benefits are improved conditions for association, increased media freedom, and respect for the rights of national minorities. there are still many issues that require further action by the european parliament and many challenges ahead, but i am confident that all the challenges facing the european neighbourhood policy will be successfully addressed.
in writing. - despite years of fighting terrorism, it is still a phenomenon in the modern world. the recent tragic events in norway show that the security of european countries can also be threatened by their own citizens. terrorism is used by both organized groups and individual extremists. terrorist activities are subject to a constant evolution of their criminal character. the legal framework and mechanisms to combat all its manifestations must therefore be systematically improved, which means that action must also be taken to ensure effective prevention. however, the union should not be the coordinator of the exchange of intelligence. national security is a matter for the member states. the reporting in this form does not reflect a sense of real danger. it does not specify how to improve police and judicial cooperation. it does not formulate specific solutions to ensure the security of citizens and to prevent the various forms of extremism in the member states. i abstained from the vote.
on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. the draft regulation under discussion has the potential to improve the transparency of the european institutions in the eyes of the public. if the principle of transparency is extended to the union's institutions, offices and agencies, then by analysing their work, by facilitating access to documents, citizens themselves may come to the conclusion that in some cases the eu's extensive bureaucracy is a form that outweighs the content and that its maintenance is not always justified, especially in times of crisis. in this context, i also do not think it is right to create new posts of officials, that is, information officers. ensuring that every natural or legal person in the european union has access to full, comprehensive information should be the right and the effort of every employee within his or her field of competence. at the same time, in order to increase the transparency of the technocratic application of law and the enactment of laws, the positive postulate of the draft regulation is to extend the access of citizens also to documents constituting delegated acts. information relating to security concerns should be given special protection.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, the commission white paper ‘roadmap to a single european transport area’, adopted on 28 march 2011, defines a vision for a competitive and resource-efficient transport system and a policy agenda for the coming years. i would like sincerely to thank the rapporteur, matthieu grosch, and the members of the committee on transport and tourism for the input given to the commission throughout this exercise. it all started with the report on the 2009 communication on a sustainable future for transport. i believe there is wide agreement on the importance of preserving an efficient and competitive transport sector. transport is an essential support for the internal market and the economic integration of all regions of europe in the global economy. transport is also an important economic sector itself, with 10 million jobs in transport services and another 8 million in the manufacture of transport vehicles. transport is also essential for social and territorial cohesion. this is why i am convinced that curbing mobility is not a sensible alternative in order to make transport sustainable. but i am also convinced that, without finding ways of using less and cleaner energy and of better exploiting infrastructure, we will be forced into such a detrimental alternative. the white paper sets a target for a 60% reduction of greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 with respect to 1990 and ten goals that will benchmark progress until that date. there are 40 concrete initiatives which the commission intends to take within the current mandate in order to address transport challenges. we are fully committed to this agenda. the commission will, in 2011, deliver about 20% of the initiatives listed in the white paper – and not the least important ones. i will continue, based on the wide support given in your report to several key proposals, such as the internalisation of external costs of transport; the single european sky; the maritime ‘blue belt’; urban sustainable mobility plans and, in general, the completion of the internal market in transport. as the commission announced in its work programme, i intend to put forward very ambitious proposals next year. concerning rail, the programme should include measures to develop the european single railway area. new legislation should also contribute to the development of clean fuel vehicles and priorities set for innovation and technological development. we will also make further steps towards the full internalisation of all externalities and for the elimination of tax distortions. i hope i can count on parliament’s continued support to make the vision outlined in the white paper a reality.
author of the draft opinion of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety. - mr president! - what are you doing? transport is the foundation of our economy and society. it contributes to economic growth and job creation. however, the development of this sector of the economy must be sustainable and linked to international cooperation. european infrastructure and transport system management should aim to increase the competitiveness and attractiveness of the european union as a whole, and this can only be achieved by eliminating the effects that restrict the free movement of transport between member states. in my opinion on the creation of a single european transport area, i focus on the need to move towards technologies based on non-fossil fuels, which are less harmful to air emissions, to reduce energy and fuel consumption by promoting clean driving and the use of fuel-saving technologies, and to support research to accelerate the introduction of eco-innovation and new technologies in transport. the development of infrastructure in the new member states, including road infrastructure, is also a very important element and should be reflected in the multiannual financial plans.
in writing. the last white paper on transport published by the commission in 2001 set out our framework and scope for action in the sector for the next 10 years. the european union's transport strategy has been largely based on the factors developed jointly there. it is important that the white paper currently being drawn up fully addresses the needs of the sector, while also identifying emerging trends and needs. it should be stressed that transport is so important to eu citizens because it defines the concept of mobility. eu citizens benefit directly from it, as it allows them to move for both their private and professional needs. let us remember that it also represents one of the freedoms of europe, namely freedom of movement. the rapporteur rightly supports long-term objectives, but he stresses that it is impossible to predict how new technologies will develop or what economic conditions we will have to face in the future, even from the perspective of the current crisis. the question that is very interesting is therefore: what are the challenges for european transport policy in 2050? i think it is appropriate to define a common strategy for all policy areas to be achieved by 2020. however, they should be subject to annual inspection.
madam president! the free movement of people and workers within the european union is one of the key benefits of integration. in the period of recovery from the economic and financial crisis, we should particularly support the mobility of european union citizens. despite the fact that freedom of movement and of employment in the member states has long been a core value of the union, union citizens continue to face many barriers and obstacles resulting from the different national legislative arrangements, but also, as is still the case for workers from bulgaria and romania, from the transitional periods introduced. currently, only 2% of eu citizens live in a member state other than their own. over 17% of people say they would like to work in another eu country, showing that there is untapped potential. the second transitional phase for workers from bulgaria and romania will end at the end of 2011. from now on, member states wishing to extend transitional periods will have to prove that the influx of workers from these countries will cause serious disruption to the labour market. each country has the right to introduce a transitional period, but as meps we should strive to make the principles on which such decisions are made clear and transparent, and to create a set of indicators to allow for consideration of such requests. many members in this chamber have raised these issues. next year, croatia will join the european union. i hope that, unless member states have clear evidence that croatian workers threaten the stability of their labour markets, they will open up and contribute to improving mobility in the european union. workers from my country, poland, have proven by their quality of work that it's worth opening the door to mobility.
madam president! i wanted to say that today's topic is extremely important in reference to the words that fell in this room from the mouth of the polish prime minister, the chairman of the polish presidency. today, one of the answers to the crisis is to deepen integration. the problems we have in the comprehensive system of restrictions on the free movement of persons in the form of schengen, in the form of transitional periods, which today discriminate to a large extent against the citizens of bulgaria and romania, must be addressed. we should be more courageous in our efforts to make the movement of workers an opportunity for the development of the european union and to overcome the crisis. we must now face the fact that one third of the citizens of the european union have no vocational qualifications. how are we to achieve the mobility we set out in the europe 2020 strategy if we do not fully open up labour markets for all member states, including in view of croatia's accession? i therefore call for courage and for our solutions to open up markets through the free movement of workers, so that europe's competitiveness is increasing. i therefore call on the commission to show courage and take action. the vote of parliament is therefore extremely important.
madam president! i would like to thank the rapporteur for this report. i'm a member of the delegation for afghanistan. i know that this country has been in a notorious war for 30 years, in this country all the foundations of a democratic and transparent state have been shaken, they simply did not exist. this country is being rebuilt. that is why it is so important to join forces, whether it is the un funds, the world bank funds or our european funds. they should be settled through similar channels, which must be based on a system of transparency, which must be based on measurable indicators of the effectiveness of the use of aid. i think we need to rehearse all the elements. it obviously requires a stronger government administration, which has its own goals, because the country needs to be rebuilt. but let's remember that ngos have to be supported in parallel, so the channel of distribution of funds by ngos is equally important. the private sector does not exist, and it is also key to redistribute resources that must be used efficiently. i therefore think that we should create exactly what the rapporteur has said - clear steps towards transparency, efficiency and above all we should settle them step by step on the basis of clear and legible principles.
madam president! thank you very much, rapporteur, for this report. i am a member of the delegation for central asia and we welcome the assumption of this strategy. in the area of the democratisation of human rights, we must ask ourselves whether the european union wants to be a global player that promotes values linked to human rights and freedom. to do this, we need to join forces decisively with the un and undp, because these activities are parallel and often unrelated. we can increase efficiency if we work together. that's the first and most important point. in the economic area, the energy issue and nabucco. unfortunately, our efforts are already a little behind schedule. the chinese, who have their own additional connection, have exploited and overtaken us in this area. we should be more active in the energy sector and in the whole of the rare earth strategy. i think we have a very good experience of democratic nation-building to pass on to these new countries with different degrees of democratization. let us use this great asset, let us also use it to act in parallel in the economic sphere and in the protection of human rights. then this strategy will surely work.
madam president! an economic crisis is usually a very difficult time not only for entrepreneurs but also for employees. companies, in their efforts to reduce operating costs, place far less emphasis on compliance with safety and health regulations. we must not forget that the european strategy for health and safety at work is implemented in specific economic circumstances, and these conditions have a major impact on its effectiveness. the greatest threat to workers today is the constant risk of job loss and the all too common phenomenon of mobbing that is closely linked to it. employers and supervisors can exploit their position, knowing that the situation on the labour market puts them in a privileged position. few people are able to resist the aggression they experience, knowing that it may result in the loss of their only source of income. and that's why i think we should focus on this phenomenon. there is no doubt that the lack of a common and uniform definition of the phenomenon of mobbing at european level is a major shortcoming. this is why i join the call of the commission and the member states to develop national strategies to combat violence in the workplace. however, these strategies must be based on a common definition of mobbing across member states and an effective campaign to raise awareness of rights. i am pleased to see that the commission has taken the initiative to present this report to the european parliament and to the council.
madam president! one of the key objectives of the europe 2020 strategy is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and make the union a world leader in green technologies. in the light of the current economic crisis, this objective is extremely ambitious and difficult to achieve. it is therefore to be welcomed that we have an effective instrument to achieve this, namely intelligent energy for europe. the decade of its existence has shown very clearly that the objectives and mechanisms adopted under the framework contribute to improving energy efficiency, promoting renewable energy sources and, above all, to the exchange of experience between scientists and experts in this field. it's worth it to not let that experience go to waste. it is important that the new edition of this programme is open to new technological and raw material opportunities that have emerged recently and that allow some member states, especially those where changes are urgent and necessary, to achieve real co2 reductions. the new energy sources that are giving europe energy independence and that need attention are, for example, the shale gas deposits recently discovered in poland. the success of the current edition of the programme is that every project financed and implemented can be verified and assessed in terms of the measurable results it brings. the main contribution is made by the experts and professional teams employed by the associated executive agency. it may be worth considering whether this experience could be transferred to other instruments and mechanisms in order to increase the effectiveness of the union and its member states' actions towards smart and sustainable development.
this program requires us to improve energy efficiency. europe continues to make unreasonable use of the energy resources at its disposal. it is essential that existing programmes aimed at improving efficiency reach an ever wider audience. public education in areas such as energy efficiency and reduction of energy consumption is the most effective way to build sustainable solutions in creating energy security and sustainable development. changes in the new policy must continue to go hand in hand with environmental protection. the key action remains the reduction of co2 emissions and the reduction of energy consumption. taking care of the environment is our responsibility to future generations, and the way to succeed in this is through a modern approach to energy and the way we use renewable energy.
madam president! i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr schwab, very warmly for the excellent report he has produced. however, i would like to draw attention to a rather curious situation: we are looking at the 2010 report almost 12 months after its completion. i think that in future parliament should do everything possible to speed up the work. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be able to take action to ensure that the competition rules are applied in a fair and transparent manner. the free movement of goods, services and capital stimulates the development of the single market while strengthening consumer protection. the key to stimulating competition and increasing the value of choice of articles is a balanced pricing policy. the lack of competition in the roaming market is a particularly striking example. despite the introduction of new framework legislation in this area, the need to increase price transparency remains evident. further action is therefore necessary to achieve the objective of eliminating the difference between roaming costs and national tariffs. in the food sector, too, the lack of price transparency and the complexity of the supply chain should be a focus. ensuring that consumers have more choice and avoid unfair discrimination will certainly help to improve the situation.
madam president! in times of crisis, europe needs to increase its competitiveness, which is a major contributor to its economic growth. the role of the common market is crucial here, and competition policy is the key to its proper functioning and development. competitiveness policy can be an effective tool in the fight against the crisis, but it must be properly targeted. we all remember the spectacular failure of the lisbon strategy, which was supposed to make the european union the most competitive economy in the world. attempts to make the union the most competitive economy in the world have failed because of a change in the paradigm of economic integration. all attempts to control the economy at european level, including the lisbon strategy, have failed. competition policy should therefore be used to unlock europe's economic potential, not as a tool for sophisticated economic engineering. we must not forget this, especially in times of crisis, when competition policy has a special role to play.
madam president! competitiveness policy defines the rules for the functioning of the single european market, which is the foundation of the european union and the source of its success. i want to draw attention to the following problems. firstly, mergers, acquisitions and takeovers improve the economic efficiency and strengthen the market position of a newly created economic entity, but let us remember that market domination, monopolisation, leads to a reduction in competitiveness and a deterioration in the consumer's situation. second, we have spent a lot of money in the past on bank bailouts. the taxpayer paid for it in the end. at the same time, the free food distribution scheme for the poorest in the european union, which costs only 500 million euros a year, has been blocked for the last two years. finally, the energy market should be monitored more closely, both at eu and national level, as the increase in energy costs is very burdensome for consumers. the same is true of the food market. congratulations on your report.
dear colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, commissioners, honourable guests, ‘if sparta and rome perished,’ wrote jean jacques rousseau, ‘what state can hope to last for ever?’ no human institutions are immortal. we europeans must not be deluded into thinking that our union is somehow an exception. to remain strong it requires an investment every day in our common future. to understand where we are today, we need a historic context. in this recent period of prosperity, we fell into the illusion that the eu could simply sail on forever. we have not prepared our community for difficult and more challenging times. we did not have enough political will and we did not convince our citizens of such a project. we even broke our own rules. discipline was lost. three years ago the financial crisis sailed across the atlantic. we were not prepared for such a situation. arguments about self-interest began to erode our belief in the common good. and now, our union has moved into a deep crisis whose causes are as much political and psychological, as economic. as president of the european parliament i served you, and europe’s citizens. i have been incredibly honoured by your choice of two-and-a-half years ago, given with such a great majority. i succeeded my dear friend hans-gert pöttering in office, whom i thank once again for his excellent leadership. i was competing for this post with ms eva-britt svensson who is not present with us today, but to whom i send my warmest regards. i also pay tribute to our colleagues mario mauro and graham watson, who supported my candidature to ensure the unity of this chamber. i did everything in order not to disappoint your trust. i knew that i could count on you, no matter what our views were. today i would like to give my report on the work of our parliament: your work, as well as mine. this is not a detailed report. you will find such a document in your mailboxes in the new year. however, i would like to present what we have achieved together, and what still remains ahead of us. you know as well as i do that my term as president coincided with an exceptionally difficult time for europe. first, we introduced the treaty of lisbon. second, we faced the crisis. third, we observed globalisation at an incredible speed. fourth, we faced the most important decisions for our future. i wish to outline these four points with you today. first, let us remind ourselves that in the summer of 2009 we faced the threat that the treaty of lisbon might not be ratified by all member states. i started from convincing the still unconvinced that we needed more europe. my first official visit was to ireland, just before the second referendum. then i went to meet the czech president. i will never forget that discussion. it started bluntly and ended very positively. the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon changed the way our european union functions. for me, the most important was parliament’s place in eu decision-making. we are now the parliament we always wanted to be. (applause)we are now the parliament we always wanted to be: a full co-legislator in a two-chamber structure. we achieved a lot, but this is a fight we all need to continue. to be strong is simply not enough; we need to use our power in everyday practice and to decide. i am proud that the european parliament, in cooperation with the other eu institutions, is ready to prepare in a few weeks’ time a deep and comprehensive programme to help solve our current economic problems. jean monnet once said ‘everybody is ambitious. the question is whether he or she is ambitious to be or ambitious to do’. we should be ambitious ‘to do’, of course. you, the members of the european parliament, co-decide on nearly all the essential policies and give your consent on almost all international agreements. who will ever forget our decision to block the swift agreement with the united states in order to protect the rights of our citizens? i remember the night before the vote, i received a phone call from the us secretary of state. i told her that as a former senator, she knows and understands about democratic oversight. she did, and she agreed later during her visit to the european parliament, that today we have a better agreement than the first one. our citizens expect that we exercise power, proper parliamentary scrutiny. in the spirit of lisbon we have pushed for greater accountability of the european commission. we negotiated a better framework agreement between parliament and the commission. the candidate for the president of the commission came for the first time to our political groups to discuss his five-year manifesto. we established the monthly question hour with the president of the european commission and commissioners. we used our powers to shape the new european external action service so that it was more accountable and representative for the community as a whole. we insisted on hearings of eu ambassadors to key posts and that the vice-president/high representative should report back to plenary on a regular basis. equally, we shaped a new relationship with the european council and its president. but with new powers comes increased responsibility and increased demands for credibility and transparency. so as a parliament we also had to respond to that. i am very proud today to say we introduced our own code of conduct for members. it was adopted with a huge majority and was applauded for its clarity and strength. i believe we should remain committed to the letter and the spirit of what the treaty of lisbon represents – using the european institutions and creating a common good and common solutions for the whole community. challenge number two was the need for action and overcoming the crisis. over the last two and a half years we had to deal with a series of very difficult economic and international challenges. we had a crisis within the eu but we also had a critical situation at our borders. when you elected me as president of the european parliament, we all thought that the international banking crisis was coming to an end. instead it came to our shores and took away wealth and jobs from millions of our citizens. responding to that challenge became our highest priority as the crisis brought an enormous threat to our citizens. a broad package of laws – the ‘six-pack’ – entered into force just two days ago and our european parliament can be proud of the role it played in shaping this legislation. it is a new economic anti-crisis shield making closer economic cooperation a reality. thanks to our firmness, attempts to weaken this shield were not successful. now it may even become a part of the new treaty under discussion. we passed legislation increasing the supervision of banks, insurers and the financial sector. for all three institutions responsible – commission, council and parliament – and with their support i proposed a first fast-track procedure for a legislation aiming to combat the crisis; similar to what we used when we established a permanent stability mechanism. on your behalf i have often stressed the need to complete the internal market and to boost growth and competitiveness. as part of the crisis reaction i was engaged in contacts with the rotating presidencies, the president of the commission, president rompuy of the european council and with the head of the euro group and the president of the ecb. our parliament called for more investment and for bigger support of research, development and green technologies. in today’s europe, just as it was in the 1950s, energy is at the heart of our economy. this is why i made a special appeal with jacques delors to create a genuine european energy community. i was proud that this plenary supported this idea. let us turn to the challenges we faced in our neighbourhood, both to the south and to the east. if you will permit me i would like to admit a difficult truth. for many years we looked for stability, while not being seriously engaged in defending human rights and building democracy in our neighbourhood. but long-term stability can only come from democracy. we learned this from our history but did not apply it to our closest neighbours. our arab neighbours have reminded us that freedom and democracy are for everybody. on the other hand we, european parliamentarians, were always strong defenders and supporters of all people fighting for freedom, democracy and human dignity. our annual sakharov prize is the most visible example of this. in parliament we were the first politicians to call for gaddafi to step down. when i spoke to protestors in tahrir square in cairo and freedom fighters in martyrs’ square in tripoli, they told me: ‘thank you, europe. thank you for believing and being with us.’ i heard from the prime minister of tunisia that ‘the only way for us is europe’. however we cannot support democracy only by words. our external policies and our internal policies must be linked as we, together with the european commission, proposed in our new neighbourhood policy. if we want to export our democratic model, we need to invest there and to open step-by-step our market for their goods and services. long-term democracy and stability can only come from growing prosperity – step-by-step. if i may add one additional remark: i visited the choucha refugee camp in tunisia. if we want to present ourselves as credible to our neighbours, we must respond to their expectations and help with their refugee crisis. three thousand people not having the possibility to go back to their countries is something that the eu should be able to deal with. the european union is a lighthouse, a beacon for people across the mediterranean, but also for those to the east of us: in georgia, moldova, ukraine and many others. this is why i urged, together with many of you, for the creation of the euronest parliamentary assembly. it is one of our successes. when i travelled from baku to yerevan, from tbilisi to chisinau, i tried to explain that sitting and negotiating at the same table gives hope for lasting peace. unfortunately, i regret the situation in belarus today seems to be worse than it was some thirty months ago. talking about the eu’s activities in our neighbourhood, i would like to make a general remark. i am a strong believer in the power of our parliamentary diplomacy. we are trusted both by society and local leaders. this was a success for example in moldova. one year ago i was actively involved in bringing the various parties to the negotiating table in the efforts to form a pro-european alliance and to move forward with their reforms. our european ‘soft power’ seems to be as strong as ‘hard power’ when we promote our values and create democratic institutions and procedures. we can see this in the western balkans for example. as i said, as a parliament we have pushed the human rights agenda very strongly; we have created the sakharov prize network as a permanent dialogue on human rights. you and i have spoken hundreds of times on various official visits – to china, to russia, to the south caucasus, in defence of individual cases. for someone who was born in an occupied country and brought up in an oppressed country, it is natural to argue for human rights and human dignity. i was proud to see the support i received from you when i came to standing up for this issue. we did not forget that in many countries in the world women are still oppressed and humiliated. i was a strong partisan of equal treatment of men and women –in politics, in business and in social and family life – in the world and in europe. women’s rights are simply human rights. point number three: today citizens’ ‘virtual participation’ is changing the world we live in. today citizens are much better connected. they are as well-informed as politicians are. this brings quite a new challenge. how to ensure credibility in the decision-making process? how to ensure trust for the activities of our politicians? what can be the role of the european parliament in this context? today a particular responsibility lies with the parliament – it is not only a guarantor of the stability of the political scene, but also has the task of creating a courageous vision for europe. the citizens expect that it will present such a vision and a new kind of european dream. reconnecting the citizens will help to give another non-economic meaning to the definition of deepening and widening of europe. governance, free markets, the single currency – these are absolutely insufficient as a basis for community. we need one more crucial factor. the most important one: european civic activity. as jean monnet said, ‘we are not uniting states, we are uniting human beings.’ let me address the citizens of europe directly. i understand that you may be disappointed, but europe in many respects is the best place in the world. it is our european diversity, creativity and openness that can best satisfy your aspirations and passions. log in to our common european space; it is your space. and please do not let yourself be persuaded that there is a contradiction between being a good pole and a good european, a good british citizen and a european citizen, a good spaniard and at the same time a good european. this alternative is an absolutely false one. europe allows you to discover the magic of the word ‘and’: being a good citizen of your town, region, country and your continent. paradoxically, through this crisis we are starting to see the emergence of a true demos. europeans can see how interdependent we are. one country can undermine the whole economy, but many countries working together can solve the problem. this is why i have pushed for greater dialogue with people and promoted the idea of a european civic space and in all my visits within the eu. democracy built in such a way could be stronger than financial markets which are so influential in our political decisions and everyday lives. and the last point is about planning for our european union, our common future. i believe that we need something like a new deal for europe. our real problem is the lack of mutual trust and the loss of a sense of meaning. the historian norman davis wrote in vanished kingdoms, ‘it is precisely through such a loss of purpose that powers fall’. we need a common project and not a mortgage on the next generation’s future. in the 1930s, while our continent was sliding towards tragedy, president roosevelt saved democracy and the free market economy in the united states of america with his new deal. today our crisis demands a new deal for europe. let me repeat shortly what i already said, and share my own vision of the future in three points. first, we need a new wave of political integration. for the long term, the community interest benefits our individual interest. the idea of a common civilisation and cultural space has been strong in europe for centuries. what we need today is to find the optimal political solution that will be fitting for our times. let me be very clear, we do not want a superstate. so let us decide how in practice we can realise the idea of ‘unity in diversity’, while redesigning the necessary solutions. while discussing possible treaty changes or new treaties, i want to recall that without a return to a genuine spirit of cooperation or – a ‘destiny shared in common’ as robert schuman put it – we will not succeed. change is not about new rules. it is about a commitment to live by those rules. this is about a state of mind. second, we need a new wave of economic integration. we need to create a real fiscal and economic union. john donne once said, ‘no man is an island’. i would say, no country is an island and i do not speak about geography. member states that want to go forward need to respect the treaty of lisbon. no country has the right to stop others working closer together. those who stay outside cannot expect to be main players. (applause)my hope remains that the frictions that have appeared using this intergovernmental method will lead to more, not less, use of the treaty of lisbon and the community method. for this reason i call for a greater involvement of the european parliament in this discussion and the decision-making process. third and last point, we need to create a true european civic space. as i mentioned earlier, while creating a new vision for europe we need to discuss issues which are close to each of us: security, the possibility to realise your own destiny, an active life in local communities, and the feeling of belonging. europe needs more solidarity, more responsibility, more respect for values, as well as enthusiasm. it was built on dreams and we have no right to throw those dreams away. in order to better reconnect with europeans, those who think of profit must also think of values. those who gain wealth must be responsible. those who are concerned about their prosperity – about which there is nothing wrong – must be concerned about equality, and those who believe in competition must come to believe in justice. my last sentences: i would like to thank each and every member of the european parliament for your contribution and cooperation. throughout my term in office i have played a part in resolving the tensions between the various eu institutions, leaders of member states, and the states themselves. on many occasions i have been close to losing hope that a settlement would be found. but in general, we reached a compromise. this is why i am optimistic today. i have never had doubts about a common europe. representing you in europe, and around the world, i was able to perceive the full, distinctive borders of the european project, as well as its exceptional, human, moral, economic and cultural potential. the european union is an incredible value, one worth working for and living in. but it is a value that can be created and used only if we are united. it is this very europe that i will always serve with energy and determination. it is not only as hungarian, czech, swedish, french or german men and women that we sit in this house. we also sit here as europeans, to solve european problems and come up with joint solutions. i dream of this european parliament, uniting so many nations, being a body making real changes on behalf of our citizens. (applause) mogę z wielką dumą powiedzieć: jestem polakiem i jestem europejczykiem i dlatego tak bardzo wierzę w naszą wspólną europejską przyszłość. nigdy nie bierzmy naszej europejskiej integracji jako danej raz na zawsze, musimy się codziennie o nią troszczyć. dziękuję bardzo!
